    3. MVI PATTERN — UNIDIRECTIONAL DATA FLOW

    MVI: Model-View-Intent


    Intent → user actions / events (not Android Intent)

    Model → immutable state

    View → renders state


    Flow: View → Intent → Reducer → New State → View


    Benefits over MVVM:

    ✅ Single immutable state — easier to debug, log, replay

    ✅ Predictable state transitions — reducer is a pure function

    ✅ Time-travel debugging possible

    ✅ Better for complex state machines (payments, checkout)


    Trade-offs:

    ❌ More boilerplate (sealed classes for Intent/State)

    ❌ Can be overkill for simple CRUD screens


    💡 Google Interview: "When would you use MVI over MVVM?" Answer: Payment flows, fintech, state machines, audit logging. MVVM is better for simple forms and CRUD.

    class="cm">// ── Sealed classes for Intent and State ──
sealed interface CheckoutIntent {
    data class LoadCart(val userId: String) : CheckoutIntent
    data class UpdateQuantity(val itemId: String, val qty: Int) : CheckoutIntent
    data class ApplyPromoCode(val code: String) : CheckoutIntent
    data object ProceedToPayment : CheckoutIntent
    data class SelectPaymentMethod(val method: PaymentMethod) : CheckoutIntent
    data object ConfirmPayment : CheckoutIntent
}

data class CheckoutState(
    val cartItems: List<CartItem> = emptyList(),
    val subtotal: Double = 0.0,
    val discount: Double = 0.0,
    val total: Double = 0.0,
    val promoCode: String? = null,
    val promoError: String? = null,
    val paymentMethod: PaymentMethod? = null,
    val checkoutStep: CheckoutStep = CheckoutStep.CART,
    val isProcessing: Boolean = false,
    val error: String? = null
)

enum class CheckoutStep { CART, PAYMENT_SELECTION, CONFIRMATION, SUCCESS, FAILED }

class="cm">// Side effects that should happen once (navigation, toasts)
sealed interface CheckoutEffect {
    data class ShowToast(val message: String) : CheckoutEffect
    data object NavigateToSuccess : CheckoutEffect
    data class NavigateToError(val reason: String) : CheckoutEffect
}

class="cm">// ── MVI ViewModel ──
class CheckoutViewModel(
    private val cartRepository: CartRepository,
    private val paymentRepository: PaymentRepository,
    private val promoRepository: PromoRepository
) : ViewModel() {

    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(CheckoutState())
    val state: StateFlow<CheckoutState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    class="cm">// One-time effects via Channel (not StateFlow — avoids re-delivery)
    private val _effects = Channel<CheckoutEffect>(Channel.BUFFERED)
    val effects: Flow<CheckoutEffect> = _effects.receiveAsFlow()

    fun processIntent(intent: CheckoutIntent) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            when (intent) {
                is CheckoutIntent.LoadCart -> handleLoadCart(intent.userId)
                is CheckoutIntent.UpdateQuantity -> handleUpdateQty(intent.itemId, intent.qty)
                is CheckoutIntent.ApplyPromoCode -> handleApplyPromo(intent.code)
                is CheckoutIntent.ProceedToPayment -> handleProceedToPayment()
                is CheckoutIntent.SelectPaymentMethod -> handleSelectPayment(intent.method)
                is CheckoutIntent.ConfirmPayment -> handleConfirmPayment()
            }
        }
    }

    class="cm">// Reducer pattern — pure state transformation
    private fun reduce(transform: CheckoutState.() -> CheckoutState) {
        _state.update { it.transform() }
    }

    private suspend fun handleLoadCart(userId: String) {
        reduce { copy(isProcessing = true) }
        cartRepository.getCart(userId)
            .onSuccess { items ->
                val subtotal = items.sumOf { it.price * it.quantity }
                reduce {
                    copy(cartItems = items, subtotal = subtotal,
                         total = subtotal, isProcessing = false)
                }
            }
            .onFailure { e ->
                reduce { copy(error = e.message, isProcessing = false) }
            }
    }

    private suspend fun handleConfirmPayment() {
        reduce { copy(isProcessing = true, checkoutStep = CheckoutStep.CONFIRMATION) }
        val currentState = _state.value

        paymentRepository.processPayment(
            amount = currentState.total,
            method = currentState.paymentMethod!!
        ).onSuccess {
            reduce { copy(checkoutStep = CheckoutStep.SUCCESS, isProcessing = false) }
            _effects.send(CheckoutEffect.NavigateToSuccess)
        }.onFailure { e ->
            reduce { copy(checkoutStep = CheckoutStep.FAILED, isProcessing = false, error = e.message) }
            _effects.send(CheckoutEffect.NavigateToError(e.message ?: class="st">"Payment failed"))
        }
    }

    private suspend fun handleApplyPromo(code: String) { class="cm">/* ... */ }
    private suspend fun handleUpdateQty(itemId: String, qty: Int) { class="cm">/* ... */ }
    private suspend fun handleProceedToPayment() { class="cm">/* ... */ }
    private suspend fun handleSelectPayment(method: PaymentMethod) { class="cm">/* ... */ }
}

    4. CLEAN ARCHITECTURE — USECASES

    UseCases (Interactors) encapsulate a single piece of business logic.


    Benefits:

    ✅ ViewModels stay thin (delegate to UseCases)

    ✅ Reusable across ViewModels

    ✅ Easy to unit test (pure Kotlin, no Android deps)

    ✅ Clear API boundary between UI and Data layers


    Convention:

    - One public method (invoke / execute)

    - Use operator fun invoke() for clean call syntax

    - Naming: VerbNounUseCase (GetArticlesUseCase, BookmarkArticleUseCase)

    class GetArticlesUseCase(
    private val articleRepository: ArticleRepository,
    private val userRepository: UserRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(
        filter: ArticleFilter,
        forceRefresh: Boolean = false
    ): Result<List<Article>> {
        return try {
            val userId = userRepository.getCurrentUserId()
            val articles = if (forceRefresh) {
                articleRepository.refreshArticles(userId)
            } else {
                articleRepository.getArticles(userId)
            }

            val filtered = when (filter) {
                ArticleFilter.ALL -> articles
                ArticleFilter.BOOKMARKED -> articles.filter { it.isBookmarked }
                ArticleFilter.RECENT -> articles.sortedByDescending { it.publishedAt }.take(20)
            }
            Result.success(filtered)
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            Result.failure(e)
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// UseCase returning a Flow (for observing data changes)
class ObserveArticlesUseCase(
    private val articleRepository: ArticleRepository
) {
    operator fun invoke(filter: ArticleFilter): Flow<List<Article>> {
        return articleRepository.observeArticles()
            .map { articles ->
                when (filter) {
                    ArticleFilter.ALL -> articles
                    ArticleFilter.BOOKMARKED -> articles.filter { it.isBookmarked }
                    ArticleFilter.RECENT -> articles.sortedByDescending { it.publishedAt }.take(20)
                }
            }
            .catch { emit(emptyList()) }
    }
}

    5. REPOSITORY PATTERN — SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH

    Repository sits between Domain and Data layers.


    Responsibilities:

    - Abstract data sources (network, local DB, cache)

    - Implement caching strategy (offline-first, cache-then-network)

    - Single source of truth (usually local DB)

    - Expose data as Flows/suspend functions


    Interview Tip: 💡 Google strongly favors offline-first architecture.

    Room is the SSOT. Network is a sync mechanism, not a data source.

    class ArticleRepositoryImpl(
    private val articleDao: ArticleDao,
    private val articleApi: ArticleApi,
    private val dispatchers: DispatcherProvider
) : ArticleRepository {

    class="cm">// Offline-first: observe local DB as the source of truth
    override fun observeArticles(): Flow<List<Article>> {
        return articleDao.observeAllArticles()
            .map { entities -> entities.map { it.toDomain() } }
            .flowOn(dispatchers.io)
    }

    override suspend fun getArticles(userId: String): List<Article> {
        return withContext(dispatchers.io) {
            class="cm">// Return cached data first
            val cached = articleDao.getAllArticles()
            if (cached.isNotEmpty() && !isStale(cached)) {
                returnclass="an">@withContext cached.map { it.toDomain() }
            }
            class="cm">// If stale or empty, fetch from network and cache
            refreshArticles(userId)
        }
    }

    override suspend fun refreshArticles(userId: String): List<Article> {
        return withContext(dispatchers.io) {
            val response = articleApi.getArticles(userId)
            val entities = response.map { it.toEntity() }
            class="cm">// Write to DB — observers will automatically emit
            articleDao.upsertAll(entities)
            entities.map { it.toDomain() }
        }
    }

    private fun isStale(articles: List<ArticleEntity>): Boolean {
        val latestUpdate = articles.maxOfOrNull { it.lastFetched } ?: 0L
        val fifteenMinutes = 15 * 60 * 1000L
        return System.currentTimeMillis() - latestUpdate > fifteenMinutes
    }
}

    6. VIEWMODEL DEEP DIVE

    ViewModel Key Facts:


    - Scoped to a ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity, Fragment, NavBackStackEntry)

    - Survives configuration changes (rotation, locale)

    - ❌ Does NOT survive process death (use SavedStateHandle)

    - Has viewModelScope (auto-cancelled in onCleared())

    - Should NOT hold references to Views, Activities, or Contexts


    Interview Question: How does ViewModel survive configuration changes?


    Answer: ViewModel is stored in ViewModelStore, which is retained via NonConfigurationInstance mechanism. When Activity is destroyed for config change, the ViewModelStore is passed to the new Activity instance.


    Follow-up: How is ViewModel shared between Fragments?


    Answer: Scope ViewModel to the Activity:

    val sharedVM: SharedViewModel by activityViewModels() Or scope to a NavGraph:

    val sharedVM: SharedViewModel by navGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph)


    ⚠️ GOTCHA: ViewModel scoped to Fragment is destroyed when Fragment is destroyed. ViewModel scoped to Activity lives as long as the Activity.

    class="cm">// Sharing ViewModel between Fragments via Navigation Graph scope
class StepOneFragment : Fragment() {
    class="cm">// Scoped to the checkout nav graph — shared with StepTwoFragment
    private val checkoutVM: CheckoutViewModel by navGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph)
}

class StepTwoFragment : Fragment() {
    class="cm">// Same ViewModel instance as StepOneFragment
    private val checkoutVM: CheckoutViewModel by navGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph)
}

    7. MVVM vs MVI — DECISION FRAMEWORK

    ┌────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
│ Criteria           │ MVVM                   │ MVI                     │
├────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
│ State management   │ Multiple StateFlows    │ Single immutable state  │
│ Complexity         │ Lower boilerplate      │ More boilerplate        │
│ Debugging          │ Harder (multiple       │ Easier (single state,   │
│                    │ state sources)         │ time-travel possible)   │
│ Best for           │ CRUD, forms, simple    │ Payments, checkout,     │
│                    │ list/detail            │ complex state machines  │
│ Testing            │ Test each flow         │ Test reducer function   │
│ Side effects       │ In ViewModel methods   │ Explicit Effect channel │
│ Scalability        │ Can get messy at scale │ Scales well             │
└────────────────────┴────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘

    💡 Google SDE-2 Answer:

    "I use MVVM for most screens because it's simpler and Google-recommended. I switch to MVI for screens with complex state transitions — payments, multi-step wizards, or anything where I need an audit trail of state changes. The key is choosing based on the screen's complexity, not applying one pattern everywhere."

    8. NAVIGATION COMPONENT

    Jetpack Navigation:

    - NavHost — container for destinations

    - NavController — manages backstack and navigation

    - NavGraph — defines routes/destinations

    - Safe Args — type-safe argument passing


    Key features:

    - Deep linking support

    - ViewModel scoping to NavGraph

    - Animation transitions

    - Conditional navigation (auth flows)

    class="cm">// Compose Navigation example
class="an">@Composable
fun AppNavigation() {
    val navController = rememberNavController()

    NavHost(navController = navController, startDestination = class="st">"article_list") {
        composable(class="st">"article_list") {
            ArticleListScreen(
                onArticleClick = { id ->
                    navController.navigate(class="st">"article_detail/$id")
                }
            )
        }
        composable(
            route = class="st">"article_detail/{articleId}",
            arguments = listOf(navArgument(class="st">"articleId") { type = NavType.StringType })
        ) { backStackEntry ->
            val articleId = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString(class="st">"articleId") ?: returnclass="an">@composable
            ArticleDetailScreen(articleId = articleId)
        }
    }
}

    9. MULTI-SOURCE DATA MERGING

    Real production apps rarely show data from a single source. A typical screen might combine:

    - Database (Room) for cached/persisted data

    - Network (Retrofit) for fresh data

    - In-memory state (user input, filters, sort order)


    Kotlin's combine() operator merges multiple Flows into a single stream. The Repository owns the data merging; the ViewModel owns the presentation logic.


    Interview Tip: 💡 Google loves asking "How would you build a search screen

    with filters, sorting, and offline support?" — this pattern is the answer.


    Key tools:

    combine() → merge N flows; emits whenever ANY input changes flatMapLatest {} → switch to a new flow when upstream emits (search query)

    debounce() → delay emission until user stops typing distinctUntilChanged() → skip duplicate emissions

    class="cm">// ── UI State for a search screen with filters ──
data class SearchScreenUiState(
    val query: String = class="st">"",
    val filter: SearchFilter = SearchFilter.ALL,
    val sortOrder: SortOrder = SortOrder.NEWEST,
    val results: List<Article> = emptyList(),
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val error: String? = null
)

enum class SearchFilter { ALL, BOOKMARKED, UNREAD }
enum class SortOrder { NEWEST, OLDEST, RELEVANCE }

class="cm">// ── Repository: merging DB + network ──
class SearchRepository(
    private val articleDao: ArticleDao,
    private val articleApi: ArticleApi,
    private val dispatchers: DispatcherProvider
) {
    class="cm">// Observe local DB as SSOT, but trigger network refresh in background
    fun observeSearchResults(query: String, filter: SearchFilter): Flow<List<Article>> {
        return articleDao.observeSearch(class="st">"%$query%")
            .map { entities -> entities.map { it.toDomain() } }
            .map { articles ->
                when (filter) {
                    SearchFilter.ALL -> articles
                    SearchFilter.BOOKMARKED -> articles.filter { it.isBookmarked }
                    SearchFilter.UNREAD -> articles.filter { !it.isRead }
                }
            }
            .onStart {
                class="cm">// Trigger network sync in background (fire-and-forget)
                withContext(dispatchers.io) {
                    try {
                        val remote = articleApi.search(query)
                        articleDao.upsertAll(remote.map { it.toEntity() })
                    } catch (_: Exception) { class="cm">/* offline is OK — DB is SSOT */ }
                }
            }
            .flowOn(dispatchers.io)
    }
}

class="cm">// ── ViewModel: combine() to merge user input + data ──
class SearchViewModel(
    private val searchRepository: SearchRepository,
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle
) : ViewModel() {

    class="cm">// Each user-controllable dimension is its own StateFlow
    private val queryFlow: MutableStateFlow<String> =
        MutableStateFlow(savedStateHandle[class="st">"query"] ?: class="st">"")

    private val filterFlow: MutableStateFlow<SearchFilter> =
        MutableStateFlow(savedStateHandle[class="st">"filter"] ?: SearchFilter.ALL)

    private val sortOrderFlow: MutableStateFlow<SortOrder> =
        MutableStateFlow(savedStateHandle[class="st">"sort"] ?: SortOrder.NEWEST)

    val uiState: StateFlow<SearchScreenUiState> = combine(
        queryFlow
            .debounce(300)                class="cm">// Wait 300ms after user stops typing
            .distinctUntilChanged(),       class="cm">// Skip if query hasn't actually changed
        filterFlow,
        sortOrderFlow
    ) { query, filter, sortOrder ->
        Triple(query, filter, sortOrder)
    }
        .flatMapLatest { (query, filter, sortOrder) ->
            class="cm">// Switch to a new data flow every time inputs change.
            class="cm">// flatMapLatest cancels the previous collection automatically.
            searchRepository.observeSearchResults(query, filter)
                .map { articles ->
                    val sorted = when (sortOrder) {
                        SortOrder.NEWEST -> articles.sortedByDescending { it.publishedAt }
                        SortOrder.OLDEST -> articles.sortedBy { it.publishedAt }
                        SortOrder.RELEVANCE -> articles class="cm">// API returns relevance-sorted
                    }
                    SearchScreenUiState(
                        query = query,
                        filter = filter,
                        sortOrder = sortOrder,
                        results = sorted,
                        isLoading = false
                    )
                }
                .onStart {
                    emit(SearchScreenUiState(
                        query = query, filter = filter,
                        sortOrder = sortOrder, isLoading = true
                    ))
                }
                .catch { e ->
                    emit(SearchScreenUiState(
                        query = query, filter = filter,
                        sortOrder = sortOrder, error = e.message
                    ))
                }
        }
        .stateIn(
            scope = viewModelScope,
            started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000),
            initialValue = SearchScreenUiState()
        )

    class="cm">// ── User actions ──
    fun onQueryChanged(query: String) {
        savedStateHandle[class="st">"query"] = query
        queryFlow.value = query
    }

    fun onFilterChanged(filter: SearchFilter) {
        savedStateHandle[class="st">"filter"] = filter
        filterFlow.value = filter
    }

    fun onSortChanged(sortOrder: SortOrder) {
        savedStateHandle[class="st">"sort"] = sortOrder
        sortOrderFlow.value = sortOrder
    }
}

    Why this pattern matters at Google scale:


    ✅ Reactive — any input change automatically triggers a new result

    ✅ Debounced — avoids hammering the DB/network on every keystroke

    ✅ Offline-first — Room is SSOT; network sync is best-effort

    ✅ Cancellation-safe — flatMapLatest cancels stale queries

    ✅ Process-death safe — SavedStateHandle persists user inputs

    ✅ Lifecycle-aware — WhileSubscribed stops work when UI is gone


    ⚠️ GOTCHA: combine() emits when ANY input changes. If you have 5 inputs and set all 5 in a row, you get 5 emissions. Use debounce() or conflate() if intermediate states are expensive.


    ⚠️ GOTCHA: debounce() delays ALL emissions, including the first one. If you want instant first result + debounced subsequent queries, use a custom operator or transformLatest with a conditional delay.

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: Your ViewModel has grown to 500+ lines. How do you refactor? A: Extract business logic into UseCases. Each UseCase = one operation. ViewModel becomes an orchestrator that delegates to UseCases.


    Q2: How do you handle one-time events (show toast, navigate)? A: Use Channel + receiveAsFlow() in ViewModel. SharedFlow with replay=0 also works but Channel guarantees delivery. Never use StateFlow for events (re-delivered on recomposition/collection restart).


    Q3: How do you share data between unrelated screens? A: Options (best → worst):

    1. Scope ViewModel to shared NavGraph

    2. Use Repository as SSOT — both VMs observe the same data source

    3. Navigation arguments for small, serializable data

    ❌ Static/global state, EventBus


    Q4: What's the difference between StateFlow and LiveData? A:

    - StateFlow requires an initial value; LiveData doesn't

    - StateFlow is Kotlin-native; LiveData is Android-specific

    - StateFlow doesn't auto-stop on lifecycle; needs repeatOnLifecycle

    - StateFlow uses equality check to skip duplicates; LiveData always notifies

    - StateFlow works in domain/data layers (no Android dependency)


    Q5: How does unidirectional data flow prevent bugs? A: State only changes in one place (ViewModel/Reducer). UI can't directly mutate state, so you can't have inconsistent state or race conditions. Every state change is traceable and testable.


    Q6: You have a search screen that combines a search query, filters, and Room data. The user types fast and the UI lags. How do you fix it? A: Three-pronged approach:

    1. debounce(300) on the query Flow — don't react to every keystroke

    2. flatMapLatest on the combined inputs — cancel stale queries

    3. Room as SSOT with network sync in onStart — no blocking network call The ViewModel uses combine(query, filter, sort).flatMapLatest { ... } to build a single reactive pipeline. WhileSubscribed(5000) in stateIn() keeps the pipeline alive briefly during config changes but stops work when the user truly leaves the screen.

    03 -- Jetpack Compose

    ============================================================================ 03 — JETPACK COMPOSE Google SDE-2 Interview Prep

    ============================================================================


    Topics Covered:

    1. Compose Mental Model — Declarative vs Imperative

    2. Composition, Recomposition & Skipping

    3. State Management (remember, rememberSaveable, derivedStateOf)

    4. State Hoisting Pattern

    5. Side Effects (LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, SideEffect, etc.)

    6. Compose Lifecycle & Phases

    7. Stability & Performance (Stable, Immutable annotations)

    8. CompositionLocal

    9. Custom Layouts & Modifiers

    10. Compose Compiler Internals

    11. Compose Navigation

    12. Material 3, Theming & Accessibility

    13. Compose Interop (AndroidView, ComposeView)


    ============================================================================

    1. DECLARATIVE VS IMPERATIVE — MENTAL MODEL

    Imperative (View System):

    val textView = findViewById<TextView>(R.id.title) textView.text = "Hello" textView.visibility = if (show) View.VISIBLE else View.GONE → You MUTATE existing view objects


    Declarative (Compose):

    @Composable fun Greeting(name: String) { Text("Hello, $name") } → You DESCRIBE what the UI should look like for a given state. → Compose framework handles creating/updating the actual UI nodes.


    💡 Key Insight: In Compose, you don't update UI — you re-describe it. The framework diffs the new description against the old one and applies only the necessary changes (similar to React's virtual DOM).

    2. COMPOSITION & RECOMPOSITION

    Composition: First time Compose executes your @Composable functions and builds the UI tree (slot table / composition).


    Recomposition: When state changes, Compose re-executes ONLY the composables that read that state. This is "smart recomposition".


    Interview Question: When does recomposition happen?


    Answer: When a State<T> object that was READ during composition changes. Compose tracks which composables read which state objects at runtime. Only those composables are re-executed.


    Follow-up: Can recomposition be skipped?


    Answer: Yes! If a composable's parameters haven't changed (by equality), Compose can skip re-executing it. This requires parameters to be:

    - Primitive types

    - @Stable or @Immutable annotated classes

    - Other composable functions (lambda stability)


    ⚠️ GOTCHA: Recomposition can happen in ANY ORDER and CONCURRENTLY. Never rely on execution order or side effects in composable functions. Never write to shared mutable state inside a composable.

    class="an">@Composable
fun RecompositionDemo() {
    var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }

    Column {
        class="cm">// This Text recomposes when `count` changes
        Text(class="st">"Count: $count")

        class="cm">// This Text does NOT recompose — it reads no state
        Text(class="st">"Static text")

        Button(onClick = { count++ }) {
            Text(class="st">"Increment")
        }
    }
}

    Positional Memoization:

    Compose identifies composables by their POSITION in the call tree, not by variable name. This is why:

    - The same composable function called twice creates two separate slots

    - key() is needed when positions can shift (dynamic lists)

    class="an">@Composable
fun PositionalMemoizationExample(showHeader: Boolean) {
    Column {
        if (showHeader) {
            Text(class="st">"Header")  class="cm">// Slot 0 when present
        }
        class="cm">// ⚠️ Without key(), this Text's slot shifts when showHeader changes,
        class="cm">// potentially losing its remembered state
        Text(class="st">"Content")

        class="cm">// ✅ Fix: Use key() to give stable identity
        key(class="st">"content") {
            Text(class="st">"Content")
        }
    }
}

    3. STATE MANAGEMENT

    State in Compose = any value that can change over time and affects the UI.


    mutableStateOf() → creates observable state

    remember { } → retains value across recompositions (NOT config change) rememberSaveable {} → retains across recomposition AND config change/process death

    derivedStateOf {} → computed state; recomposes only when result changes

    class="an">@Composable
fun StateManagementShowcase() {
    class="cm">// ── remember: survives recomposition, lost on config change ──
    var counter by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }

    class="cm">// ── rememberSaveable: survives recomposition + config change + process death ──
    var userInput by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(class="st">"") }

    class="cm">// ── derivedStateOf: only recomposes when the RESULT changes ──
    val items = remember { mutableStateListOf<String>() }
    val hasItems by remember { derivedStateOf { items.isNotEmpty() } }
    class="cm">// Even if items changes from [class="st">"a",class="st">"b"] to [class="st">"a",class="st">"c"], hasItems doesn't recompose
    class="cm">// because the boolean value (true) didn't change.

    class="cm">// ── snapshotFlow: convert Compose state to a Flow ──
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()
    LaunchedEffect(listState) {
        snapshotFlow { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex }
            .distinctUntilChanged()
            .filter { it > 5 }
            .collect { class="cm">/* Show class="st">"scroll to top" FAB */ }
    }

    class="cm">// ── collectAsStateWithLifecycle: safely collect Flow as Compose state ──
    class="cm">// Lifecycle-aware: stops collecting when UI goes to background
    class="cm">// ✅ Use this instead of collectAsState()
    val viewModel: MyViewModel = hiltViewModel()
    val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
}

    Interview Question: What's the difference between remember and rememberSaveable?


    remember:

    - Stores value in the Composition's slot table

    - Survives recomposition

    - Lost on configuration change (Activity recreation)

    - Can store ANY type


    rememberSaveable:

    - Backed by onSaveInstanceState Bundle

    - Survives config change AND process death

    - Limited to Bundle-compatible types (primitives, Parcelable, Serializable)

    - Custom types need a Saver


    Follow-up: How do you save a custom class with rememberSaveable?

    class="cm">// Custom Saver for rememberSaveable
data class ComposeSearchFilter(
    val query: String,
    val category: String,
    val sortBy: SortOrder
)

val ComposeSearchFilterSaver = run {
    val queryKey = class="st">"query"
    val categoryKey = class="st">"category"
    val sortKey = class="st">"sort"
    mapSaver(
        save = { filter ->
            mapOf(
                queryKey to filter.query,
                categoryKey to filter.category,
                sortKey to filter.sortBy.name
            )
        },
        restore = { map ->
            ComposeSearchFilter(
                query = map[queryKey] as String,
                category = map[categoryKey] as String,
                sortBy = SortOrder.valueOf(map[sortKey] as String)
            )
        }
    )
}

class="an">@Composable
fun SaveableSearchScreen() {
    var filter by rememberSaveable(stateSaver = ComposeSearchFilterSaver) {
        mutableStateOf(ComposeSearchFilter(class="st">"", class="st">"all", SortOrder.NEWEST))
    }
}

    4. STATE HOISTING

    State Hoisting = moving state UP to the caller so the composable is stateless.


    Pattern:

    - Stateful composable: owns state internally (via remember)

    - Stateless composable: receives state + event callbacks as parameters


    Benefits:

    ✅ Reusable — no internal state assumptions

    ✅ Testable — inject any state for testing

    ✅ Previewable — create @Preview with any state

    ✅ Single source of truth — parent controls the state


    Google's Rule: Hoist state to the lowest common ancestor that needs it.

    class="cm">// ❌ Bad: Stateful — hard to test, can't control externally
class="an">@Composable
fun SearchBarBad() {
    var query by remember { mutableStateOf(class="st">"") }
    TextField(value = query, onValueChange = { query = it })
}

class="cm">// ✅ Good: Stateless — state hoisted to caller
class="an">@Composable
fun SearchBar(
    query: String,
    onQueryChange: (String) -> Unit,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier
) {
    TextField(
        value = query,
        onValueChange = onQueryChange,
        modifier = modifier
    )
}

class="cm">// Stateful wrapper if needed
class="an">@Composable
fun SearchBarStateful() {
    var query by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(class="st">"") }
    SearchBar(query = query, onQueryChange = { query = it })
}

    5. SIDE EFFECTS — COMPLETE GUIDE

    Side effect = any work that escapes the scope of a composable function. Examples: API calls, analytics, registering listeners, writing to DB.


    Compose provides specific APIs because:

    - Composable functions can be called many times (recomposition)

    - They can be called in any order or concurrently

    - They can be skipped if the result is the same


    ⚠️ NEVER perform side effects directly in a composable body.

    class="an">@Composable
fun SideEffectsShowcase(userId: String, analyticsHelper: AnalyticsHelper) {

    class="cm">// ── LaunchedEffect ──
    class="cm">// Runs a suspend function when keys change. Cancels + restarts on key change.
    class="cm">// Use for: API calls, one-time operations, coroutine-based work
    LaunchedEffect(userId) {
        class="cm">// This cancels & restarts when userId changes
        val userData = repository.fetchUser(userId)
        class="cm">// update state...
    }

    class="cm">// ── LaunchedEffect(Unit) ──
    class="cm">// Runs ONCE when composable enters composition. Never restarts.
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        class="cm">// One-time initialization
        analyticsHelper.logScreenView(class="st">"profile")
    }

    class="cm">// ── DisposableEffect ──
    class="cm">// For registering/unregistering listeners. Has cleanup via onDispose.
    class="cm">// Use for: Lifecycle observers, broadcast receivers, callbacks
    val lifecycleOwner = LocalLifecycleOwner.current
    DisposableEffect(lifecycleOwner) {
        val observer = LifecycleEventObserver { _, event ->
            when (event) {
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_RESUME -> { class="cm">/* ... */ }
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_PAUSE -> { class="cm">/* ... */ }
                else -> {}
            }
        }
        lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(observer)
        onDispose {
            lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.removeObserver(observer)
        }
    }

    class="cm">// ── SideEffect ──
    class="cm">// Runs EVERY recomposition. No coroutine scope. Synchronous.
    class="cm">// Use for: Updating non-Compose state that needs to stay in sync
    SideEffect {
        analyticsHelper.setUserProperty(class="st">"screen", class="st">"profile_$userId")
    }

    class="cm">// ── rememberCoroutineScope ──
    class="cm">// Gets a CoroutineScope tied to the composable's lifecycle.
    class="cm">// Use for: Launching coroutines from callbacks (onClick, etc.)
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    Button(onClick = {
        scope.launch {
            class="cm">// Can do suspend work in response to user action
            repository.toggleBookmark(userId)
        }
    }) {
        Text(class="st">"Bookmark")
    }

    class="cm">// ── rememberUpdatedState ──
    class="cm">// Captures the latest value of a parameter for use in long-running effects.
    class="cm">// Prevents LaunchedEffect from capturing a stale closure.
    val currentOnTimeout by rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout)
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        delay(5000)
        currentOnTimeout()  class="cm">// Always calls the LATEST onTimeout, not the initial one
    }

    class="cm">// ── produceState ──
    class="cm">// Converts non-Compose state (Flow, callback) into Compose State.
    val imageState by produceState<ImageLoadState>(
        initialValue = ImageLoadState.Loading,
        key1 = imageUrl
    ) {
        value = try {
            val bitmap = imageLoader.load(imageUrl)
            ImageLoadState.Success(bitmap)
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            ImageLoadState.Error(e)
        }
    }
}

    ⚠️ GOTCHA — Side Effect Pitfalls:


    1. LaunchedEffect(Unit) with changing parameters:

    If you use a parameter inside LaunchedEffect(Unit), it captures the INITIAL value. Use rememberUpdatedState or add the param to keys.


    2. Forgetting onDispose in DisposableEffect:

    → Memory leak (listener not unregistered)


    3. Performing network calls directly in composable:

    @Composable fun Bad() { val data = api.fetchData() // ❌ Called on every recomposition! } → Use LaunchedEffect or move to ViewModel

    6. COMPOSE PHASES & LIFECYCLE

    Compose has 3 phases per frame:


    1. Composition → WHAT to show (runs @Composable functions, builds UI tree)

    2. Layout → WHERE to place it (measure + place each node)

    3. Drawing → HOW to render it (draws pixels to Canvas)


    Reading state in different phases:

    - State read in Composition → triggers recomposition

    - State read in Layout (via Modifier.layout) → triggers re-layout only

    - State read in Drawing (via Modifier.drawBehind) → triggers re-draw only


    💡 Performance Tip: Defer state reads to the latest possible phase. If state only affects position, read it in Layout phase. If state only affects visuals, read it in Drawing phase.

    class="an">@Composable
fun PhaseOptimizationExample() {
    var offset by remember { mutableStateOf(0f) }

    class="cm">// ❌ Reading offset in Composition — triggers full recomposition
    Box(modifier = Modifier.offset(x = offset.dp))

    class="cm">// ✅ Reading offset in Layout phase — skips Composition
    Box(modifier = Modifier.offset { IntOffset(offset.toInt(), 0) })

    class="cm">// ✅ Reading offset in Drawing phase — skips Composition AND Layout
    Box(modifier = Modifier.drawBehind {
        drawCircle(Color.Red, center = Offset(offset, 0f))
    })
}

    7. STABILITY & PERFORMANCE

    For Compose to skip recomposition, it must know if parameters changed. This requires types to be "stable" — their equals() is reliable.


    Automatically stable:

    - Primitives (Int, String, Boolean, Float, etc.)

    - data class with all stable fields

    - Enum classes

    - Function types (lambdas)


    Unstable (can't skip):

    - List, Set, Map (interfaces — implementation might be mutable)

    - Classes from external modules (Compose compiler can't verify)

    - var properties

    class="cm">// ❌ Unstable — List<T> is an interface; could be mutable
class="an">@Composable
fun UnstableExample(items: List<String>) { class="cm">/* Always recomposes */ }

class="cm">// ✅ Stable — ImmutableList is known to be immutable
class="an">@Composable
fun StableExample(items: ImmutableList<String>) { class="cm">/* Can skip recomposition */ }

class="cm">// ✅ Annotate your own classes
class="an">@Immutable  class="cm">// Promise to Compose: all fields are deeply immutable
data class ArticleUi(
    val id: String,
    val title: String,
    val author: String,
    val tags: ImmutableList<String>
)

class="an">@Stable  class="cm">// Promise to Compose: mutable, but changes are observable via Compose State
class CartState {
    var itemCount by mutableStateOf(0)
        private set
    fun addItem() { itemCount++ }
}

    Lambda Stability:


    ❌ Unstable lambda (captures unstable variable):

    items.forEach { item -> Button(onClick = { onItemClick(item) }) // New lambda each recomposition }


    ✅ Stable lambda via remember:

    val onClick = remember(item.id) { { onItemClick(item) } } Button(onClick = onClick)


    ✅ Or use method reference:

    Button(onClick = viewModel::onItemClick)

    8. COMPOSITIONLOCAL

    CompositionLocal provides implicit data down the composition tree. Like React's Context — avoids threading parameters through every composable.


    Built-in examples:

    LocalContext.current → Android Context

    LocalLifecycleOwner.current → Lifecycle owner

    LocalDensity.current → Screen density

    LocalConfiguration.current → Device configuration


    staticCompositionLocalOf → Value rarely changes (theme, DI). More efficient.

    compositionLocalOf → Value may change. Recomposes readers on change.

    class="cm">// Custom CompositionLocal
val LocalAnalytics = staticCompositionLocalOf<AnalyticsHelper> {
    error(class="st">"No AnalyticsHelper provided")
}

class="an">@Composable
fun AppRoot() {
    CompositionLocalProvider(LocalAnalytics provides AnalyticsHelperImpl()) {
        AppNavigation()  class="cm">// All descendants can access LocalAnalytics.current
    }
}

class="an">@Composable
fun DeepNestedScreen() {
    val analytics = LocalAnalytics.current  class="cm">// No parameter threading needed
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        analytics.logScreenView(class="st">"deep_nested")
    }
}

    ⚠️ When NOT to use CompositionLocal:

    - For data that only a few composables need (just pass as parameter)

    - For frequently changing data (performance overhead)

    - When it makes the composable harder to test


    ✅ Good uses: Theme, analytics, navigation, DI-provided dependencies

    9. CUSTOM LAYOUTS & MODIFIERS

    Custom Layout — when standard Row/Column/Box aren't enough. You get full control over measuring and placing children.

    class="an">@Composable
fun StaggeredGrid(
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,
    columns: Int = 2,
    content: class="an">@Composable () -> Unit
) {
    Layout(
        modifier = modifier,
        content = content
    ) { measurables, constraints ->
        val columnWidth = constraints.maxWidth / columns
        val itemConstraints = constraints.copy(
            minWidth = 0, maxWidth = columnWidth
        )

        val placeables = measurables.map { it.measure(itemConstraints) }
        val columnHeights = IntArray(columns)

        layout(constraints.maxWidth, constraints.maxHeight) {
            placeables.forEach { placeable ->
                val shortestColumn = columnHeights.indexOfMin()
                placeable.placeRelative(
                    x = shortestColumn * columnWidth,
                    y = columnHeights[shortestColumn]
                )
                columnHeights[shortestColumn] += placeable.height
            }
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// Custom Modifier
fun Modifier.shimmer(isLoading: Boolean): Modifier = composed {
    if (!isLoading) returnclass="an">@composed this

    val transition = rememberInfiniteTransition(label = class="st">"shimmer")
    val translateAnim by transition.animateFloat(
        initialValue = 0f,
        targetValue = 1000f,
        animationSpec = infiniteRepeatable(
            animation = tween(durationMillis = 1200, easing = LinearEasing),
            repeatMode = RepeatMode.Restart
        ),
        label = class="st">"shimmer_translate"
    )

    this.drawWithContent {
        drawContent()
        val brush = Brush.linearGradient(
            colors = listOf(
                Color.LightGray.copy(alpha = 0.6f),
                Color.LightGray.copy(alpha = 0.2f),
                Color.LightGray.copy(alpha = 0.6f)
            ),
            start = Offset(translateAnim - 200f, 0f),
            end = Offset(translateAnim, 0f)
        )
        drawRect(brush = brush)
    }
}

    10. COMPOSE COMPILER INTERNALS (ADVANCED)

    What the Compose compiler does to your @Composable functions:


    1. Adds a Composer parameter to every @Composable function fun Greeting(name: String) → fun Greeting(name: String, $composer: Composer, $changed: Int)


    2. Generates groups in the slot table:

    - startGroup / endGroup calls that track composable identity

    - Each call position gets a unique key


    3. Adds comparison checks ($changed bitmask):

    - Tracks which parameters changed since last composition

    - If nothing changed, can skip the composable entirely


    4. Transforms remember {} calls:

    - Stores/retrieves values from the slot table

    - Invalidates when keys change


    5. Generates restartable groups:

    - Each composable that reads state becomes a "restart scope"

    - When state changes, only that scope re-executes


    Interview Tip: 💡 Understanding this helps explain WHY:

    - @Composable functions can only call other @Composable functions

    - Compose can skip unchanged composables

    - Stability matters for performance

    11. COMPOSE NAVIGATION

    Navigation in Compose replaces the Fragment-based Navigation component.


    Core components:

    NavController → manages the back stack and navigation actions

    NavHost → container that swaps composables based on the current route

    NavGraph → set of destinations (composable routes)

    NavBackStackEntry → holds arguments and scoped state for a destination


    Interview Tip: 💡 Know both the string-based route API and the newer

    type-safe Kotlin Serializable route API (Navigation 2.8+).

    class="cm">// ── String-based route approach ──

class="an">@Composable
fun StringRouteNavigation() {
    val navController = rememberNavController()

    NavHost(
        navController = navController,
        startDestination = class="st">"home"
    ) {
        composable(class="st">"home") {
            HomeScreen(
                onArticleClick = { articleId ->
                    navController.navigate(class="st">"article/$articleId")
                },
                onProfileClick = {
                    navController.navigate(class="st">"profile")
                }
            )
        }

        composable(
            route = class="st">"article/{articleId}",
            arguments = listOf(
                navArgument(class="st">"articleId") { type = NavType.StringType }
            )
        ) { backStackEntry ->
            val articleId = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString(class="st">"articleId") ?: returnclass="an">@composable
            ArticleDetailScreen(articleId = articleId)
        }

        class="cm">// Optional arguments with default values
        composable(
            route = class="st">"search?query={query}&category={category}",
            arguments = listOf(
                navArgument(class="st">"query") {
                    type = NavType.StringType
                    defaultValue = class="st">""
                },
                navArgument(class="st">"category") {
                    type = NavType.StringType
                    defaultValue = class="st">"all"
                }
            )
        ) { backStackEntry ->
            val query = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString(class="st">"query") ?: class="st">""
            val category = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString(class="st">"category") ?: class="st">"all"
            SearchScreen(initialQuery = query, category = category)
        }

        class="cm">// Deep link support
        composable(
            route = class="st">"article/{articleId}",
            deepLinks = listOf(
                navDeepLink { uriPattern = class="st">"https:class="cm">//myapp.com/article/{articleId}" }
            )
        ) { class="cm">/* ... */ }
    }
}

class="cm">// ── Type-safe route approach (Navigation 2.8+, Kotlin Serializable) ──

class="an">@Serializable
data class ArticleRoute(val articleId: String)

class="an">@Serializable
data class SearchRoute(
    val query: String = class="st">"",
    val category: String = class="st">"all"
)

class="an">@Serializable
object HomeRoute

class="an">@Serializable
object ProfileRoute

class="an">@Composable
fun TypeSafeNavigation() {
    val navController = rememberNavController()

    NavHost(
        navController = navController,
        startDestination = HomeRoute
    ) {
        composable<HomeRoute> {
            HomeScreen(
                onArticleClick = { id -> navController.navigate(ArticleRoute(id)) }
            )
        }

        composable<ArticleRoute> { backStackEntry ->
            val route = backStackEntry.toRoute<ArticleRoute>()
            ArticleDetailScreen(articleId = route.articleId)
        }

        composable<SearchRoute> { backStackEntry ->
            val route = backStackEntry.toRoute<SearchRoute>()
            SearchScreen(initialQuery = route.query, category = route.category)
        }
    }
}

    Scoping ViewModels to a NavGraph:

    By default, ViewModels are scoped to the NavBackStackEntry of a destination. You can scope them to a nested nav graph to share across screens.

    class="an">@Composable
fun SharedViewModelExample(navController: NavHostController) {
    val parentEntry = remember(navController) {
        navController.getBackStackEntry(class="st">"checkout_graph")
    }
    val sharedViewModel: CheckoutViewModel = hiltViewModel(parentEntry)
}

    Custom back handling:

    BackHandler from activity-compose intercepts the system back button.

    class="an">@Composable
fun ScreenWithCustomBack(onBack: () -> Unit) {
    var hasUnsavedChanges by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    var showDialog by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }

    BackHandler(enabled = hasUnsavedChanges) {
        showDialog = true
    }

    if (showDialog) {
        AlertDialog(
            onDismissRequest = { showDialog = false },
            confirmButton = {
                TextButton(onClick = { showDialog = false; onBack() }) {
                    Text(class="st">"Discard")
                }
            },
            dismissButton = {
                TextButton(onClick = { showDialog = false }) { Text(class="st">"Cancel") }
            },
            title = { Text(class="st">"Unsaved changes") },
            text = { Text(class="st">"Discard your changes?") }
        )
    }
}

    ⚠️ Navigation Gotchas:

    1. Avoid creating a new NavController on recomposition — always use rememberNavController()

    2. navigate() adds to the back stack by default; use popUpTo for login/splash flows

    3. Don't pass complex objects as arguments — pass IDs and fetch from ViewModel/repository

    4. Use launchSingleTop = true to avoid duplicate destinations on rapid taps

    12. MATERIAL 3, THEMING & ACCESSIBILITY

    Material 3 (Material You) in Compose:


    MaterialTheme provides:

    colorScheme → color tokens (primary, secondary, surface, error, etc.)

    typography → text styles (displayLarge, titleMedium, bodySmall, etc.)

    shapes → corner rounding (small, medium, large, extraLarge)


    Dynamic Color (Material You — Android 12+):

    Colors derived from the user's wallpaper. Use dynamicDarkColorScheme() and dynamicLightColorScheme() with a fallback for older devices.

    class="an">@Composable
fun AppTheme(
    darkTheme: Boolean = isSystemInDarkTheme(),
    dynamicColor: Boolean = true,
    content: class="an">@Composable () -> Unit
) {
    val colorScheme = when {
        dynamicColor && Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.S -> {
            val context = LocalContext.current
            if (darkTheme) dynamicDarkColorScheme(context) else dynamicLightColorScheme(context)
        }
        darkTheme -> darkColorScheme(
            primary = Color(0xFFBB86FC),
            secondary = Color(0xFF03DAC6),
            background = Color(0xFF121212)
        )
        else -> lightColorScheme(
            primary = Color(0xFF6200EE),
            secondary = Color(0xFF03DAC6),
            background = Color(0xFFFFFBFE)
        )
    }

    MaterialTheme(
        colorScheme = colorScheme,
        typography = Typography(
            titleLarge = TextStyle(
                fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold,
                fontSize = 22.sp,
                lineHeight = 28.sp
            )
        ),
        shapes = Shapes(
            small = RoundedCornerShape(4.dp),
            medium = RoundedCornerShape(12.dp),
            large = RoundedCornerShape(16.dp)
        ),
        content = content
    )
}

    Accessibility in Compose:


    Compose uses a Semantics tree (parallel to the UI tree) that screen readers (TalkBack) and testing tools use to understand your UI.


    Key APIs:

    contentDescription → describes non-text elements (images, icons)

    semantics { } → attach semantic properties to a composable

    mergeDescendants → treat a subtree as a single accessible element

    clearAndSetSemantics → override all child semantics (useful for custom widgets)


    ⚠️ Touch target size: Material guidelines require at least 48dp × 48dp. Use Modifier.sizeIn(minWidth = 48.dp, minHeight = 48.dp) or Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize() (Material 3).

    class="an">@Composable
fun AccessibilityExample() {
    class="cm">// contentDescription for images
    Image(
        painter = painterResource(R.drawable.logo),
        contentDescription = class="st">"App logo",  class="cm">// Read by TalkBack
        modifier = Modifier.size(48.dp)
    )

    class="cm">// Decorative image — null contentDescription is intentional
    Icon(
        imageVector = Icons.Default.Star,
        contentDescription = null  class="cm">// Ignored by screen readers
    )

    class="cm">// mergeDescendants — card read as a single element
    Row(
        modifier = Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) { }
    ) {
        Image(
            painter = painterResource(R.drawable.avatar),
            contentDescription = null  class="cm">// Merged into parent
        )
        Column {
            Text(class="st">"Jane Doe")
            Text(class="st">"Senior Engineer")
        }
    }
    class="cm">// TalkBack reads: class="st">"Jane Doe, Senior Engineer" as one item

    class="cm">// clearAndSetSemantics — replace all child semantics
    Row(
        modifier = Modifier.clearAndSetSemantics {
            contentDescription = class="st">"Rating: 4 out of 5 stars"
        }
    ) {
        repeat(5) { index ->
            Icon(
                imageVector = if (index < 4) Icons.Filled.Star else Icons.Outlined.Star,
                contentDescription = null
            )
        }
    }

    class="cm">// Minimum touch target
    IconButton(
        onClick = { class="cm">/* ... */ },
        modifier = Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize()
    ) {
        Icon(Icons.Default.Close, contentDescription = class="st">"Close")
    }
}

    Focus management for screen readers:

    Use FocusRequester to programmatically move focus after state changes (e.g., after showing an error, move focus to the error message).

    class="an">@Composable
fun FocusManagementExample() {
    val focusRequester = remember { FocusRequester() }
    var showError by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }

    Column {
        if (showError) {
            Text(
                class="st">"Invalid input",
                color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.error,
                modifier = Modifier.focusRequester(focusRequester)
            )
            LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
                focusRequester.requestFocus()
            }
        }
        TextField(value = class="st">"", onValueChange = {})
    }
}
    Interview Tip: 💡 Google cares deeply about accessibility. Be ready to discuss:

    - How you'd make a custom component accessible

    - The difference between contentDescription and text for semantics

    - How mergeDescendants affects the TalkBack traversal order

    - Testing accessibility with Accessibility Scanner or Espresso

    13. COMPOSE INTEROP

    Compose ↔ View system interoperability is essential for incremental migration.


    Two directions:

    1. Compose inside Views: ComposeView (embed Compose in Fragment/Activity XML)

    2. Views inside Compose: AndroidView (embed legacy View widgets in Compose)


    Interview Tip: 💡 Google's recommended migration strategy is bottom-up —

    start by replacing individual screens or leaf components with Compose, while the Activity/Fragment shell remains.

    class="cm">// ── AndroidView: Embedding a View widget inside Compose ──

class="an">@Composable
fun MapComposable(
    onMapReady: (MapView) -> Unit,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier
) {
    var mapView: MapView? by remember { mutableStateOf(null) }

    AndroidView(
        factory = { context ->
            MapView(context).also {
                it.onCreate(null)
                mapView = it
            }
        },
        update = { view ->
            class="cm">// Called on every recomposition — update the View's state here
            view.getMapAsync { googleMap ->
                onMapReady(view)
            }
        },
        modifier = modifier
    )

    class="cm">// Handle lifecycle for the MapView
    val lifecycleOwner = LocalLifecycleOwner.current
    DisposableEffect(lifecycleOwner) {
        val observer = LifecycleEventObserver { _, event ->
            when (event) {
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_RESUME -> mapView?.onResume()
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_PAUSE -> mapView?.onPause()
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_DESTROY -> mapView?.onDestroy()
                else -> {}
            }
        }
        lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(observer)
        onDispose { lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.removeObserver(observer) }
    }
}

class="cm">// Wrapping an AdView (common real-world interop case)
class="an">@Composable
fun AdBanner(adUnitId: String, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    AndroidView(
        factory = { context ->
            AdView(context).apply {
                setAdSize(AdSize.BANNER)
                this.adUnitId = adUnitId
                loadAd(AdRequest.Builder().build())
            }
        },
        modifier = modifier
    )
}

class="cm">// ── ComposeView: Embedding Compose inside a Fragment ──

class ProfileFragment : Fragment() {
    override fun onCreateView(
        inflater: LayoutInflater,
        container: ViewGroup?,
        savedInstanceState: Bundle?
    ): View {
        return ComposeView(requireContext()).apply {
            setViewCompositionStrategy(
                ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed
            )
            setContent {
                AppTheme {
                    ProfileScreen()
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

    ViewCompositionStrategy — controls when Compose disposes:


    DisposeOnDetachedFromWindow → default; disposes when view detaches DisposeOnDetachedFromWindowOrReleasedFromPool → for RecyclerView items DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed → ✅ best for Fragments (matches view lifecycle)

    DisposeOnLifecycleDestroyed → ties to a specific Lifecycle


    ⚠️ Common Pitfalls:

    1. Theme inheritance: ComposeView doesn't inherit Material theme from XML. You must wrap content in your Compose theme.

    2. Lifecycle mismatch: Fragment's view lifecycle ≠ Fragment lifecycle. Always use DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed in Fragments.

    3. Inflation order: If mixing XML and Compose in the same layout, remember that AndroidView factory runs once, update runs on recomposition.

    4. Keyboard handling: IME behavior can differ between View and Compose text fields.

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: What's the difference between State and MutableState? A: State<T> is read-only interface. MutableState<T> extends it with a setter. Expose State<T> publicly, keep MutableState<T> private — same as StateFlow/MutableStateFlow pattern.


    Q2: Why shouldn't you use collectAsState for StateFlow from a ViewModel? A: collectAsState keeps collecting even when the app is in background. Use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() instead — it stops collecting in onStop and resumes in onStart, saving resources.


    Q3: What happens if you use var x = 0 instead of mutableStateOf? A: Compose won't track changes. The variable will change but recomposition won't be triggered. UI stays stale.


    Q4: How do you animate between two screens in Compose? A: AnimatedNavHost (Navigation Compose + animation), AnimatedContent, Crossfade, or SharedElement transitions (Compose 1.7+).


    Q5: What is the Snapshot system in Compose? A: Compose uses a snapshot system (similar to software transactional memory) to track state reads/writes. When mutableStateOf() is read during composition, the snapshot records it. When written to, all compositions that read it are scheduled for recomposition.


    Q6: How do you handle lists in Compose efficiently? A: LazyColumn/LazyRow with key parameter for stable identity. Use ImmutableList for skippable recomposition. Use derivedStateOf for computed list properties. Avoid creating new list instances in every recomposition.


    Q7: How would you implement a multi-screen checkout flow with shared state using Compose Navigation? A: Create a nested NavGraph for the checkout flow. Scope a shared CheckoutViewModel to the nested graph's NavBackStackEntry using hiltViewModel(navController.getBackStackEntry("checkout_graph")). All screens in the graph share the same ViewModel instance. On completion, pop the entire graph: navController.popBackStack("checkout_graph", inclusive = true).


    Q8: How do you make a custom rating bar accessible for TalkBack users? A: Use clearAndSetSemantics on the container to replace individual star semantics with a single description like "Rating: 4 out of 5 stars". Also add a stateDescription for the current value and an adjustable action (via semantics { }) so users can change the rating with swipe-up/swipe-down gestures in TalkBack.

    2. Dispatchers (Main, IO, Default, Unconfined)

    4. launch vs async — Concurrency Patterns

    5. Exception Handling (try-catch, SupervisorJob, CEH)

    6. Cancellation & Cooperative Cancellation
