    7. NETWORK CONNECTIVITY MONITORING

    class NetworkMonitor(context: Context) {
    private val connectivityManager =
        context.getSystemService(Context.CONNECTIVITY_SERVICE) as ConnectivityManager

    val isOnline: Flow<Boolean> = callbackFlow {
        val callback = object : ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback() {
            override fun onAvailable(network: Network) { trySend(true) }
            override fun onLost(network: Network) { trySend(false) }
            override fun onCapabilitiesChanged(
                network: Network,
                networkCapabilities: NetworkCapabilities
            ) {
                val hasInternet = networkCapabilities.hasCapability(
                    NetworkCapabilities.NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET
                )
                trySend(hasInternet)
            }
        }

        val request = NetworkRequest.Builder()
            .addCapability(NetworkCapabilities.NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET)
            .build()
        connectivityManager.registerNetworkCallback(request, callback)

        class="cm">// Emit current state
        val currentNetwork = connectivityManager.activeNetwork
        val capabilities = connectivityManager.getNetworkCapabilities(currentNetwork)
        trySend(capabilities?.hasCapability(NetworkCapabilities.NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET) == true)

        awaitClose { connectivityManager.unregisterNetworkCallback(callback) }
    }.distinctUntilChanged()
}

    8. WEBSOCKET & SERVER-SENT EVENTS

    WebSocket = full-duplex, persistent connection between client and server. SSE (Server-Sent Events) = one-way stream from server to client over HTTP.


    When to use what:

    WebSocket → bidirectional real-time (chat, gaming, collaborative editing)

    SSE → server-push only (live feeds, notifications, stock tickers)

    Polling → low-frequency updates, simplest to implement, highest latency


    Interview Tip: 💡 Google favors WebSocket for bidirectional and SSE for

    unidirectional streams. Know the trade-offs (connection overhead, proxy support, automatic reconnection).


    ⚠️ SSE advantages over WebSocket:

    - Built-in reconnection and event ID tracking

    - Works through HTTP proxies without special config

    - Simpler server implementation

    ⚠️ SSE limitations: text-only (no binary), unidirectional

    class="cm">// WebSocket client with OkHttp
class ArticleWebSocketClient(
    private val okHttpClient: OkHttpClient,
    private val onMessage: (String) -> Unit,
    private val onConnectionChange: (Boolean) -> Unit
) {
    private var webSocket: WebSocket? = null
    private var retryCount = 0
    private val maxRetries = 5
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO + SupervisorJob())

    fun connect() {
        val request = Request.Builder()
            .url(class="st">"wss:class="cm">//api.example.com/ws/articles")
            .build()

        webSocket = okHttpClient.newWebSocket(request, object : WebSocketListener() {
            override fun onOpen(webSocket: WebSocket, response: okhttp3.Response) {
                retryCount = 0
                onConnectionChange(true)
                class="cm">// Send auth or subscribe message
                webSocket.send(class="st">""class="st">"{"typeclass="st">":"subscribeclass="st">","channelclass="st">":"articlesclass="st">"}"class="st">"")
            }

            override fun onMessage(webSocket: WebSocket, text: String) {
                onMessage(text)
            }

            override fun onClosing(webSocket: WebSocket, code: Int, reason: String) {
                webSocket.close(1000, null)
                onConnectionChange(false)
            }

            override fun onFailure(
                webSocket: WebSocket,
                t: Throwable,
                response: okhttp3.Response?
            ) {
                onConnectionChange(false)
                reconnectWithBackoff()
            }
        })
    }

    private fun reconnectWithBackoff() {
        if (retryCount >= maxRetries) return
        val delayMs = (1000L * (1 shl retryCount)).coerceAtMost(30_000L) class="cm">// Exponential, cap 30s
        retryCount++
        scope.launch {
            delay(delayMs)
            connect()
        }
    }

    fun send(message: String) {
        webSocket?.send(message)
    }

    fun disconnect() {
        webSocket?.close(1000, class="st">"Client disconnect")
        scope.cancel()
    }
}

class="cm">// Server-Sent Events (SSE) with OkHttp
class SseClient(private val okHttpClient: OkHttpClient) {

    fun observeEvents(url: String): Flow<SseEvent> = callbackFlow {
        val request = Request.Builder()
            .url(url)
            .header(class="st">"Accept", class="st">"text/event-stream")
            .build()

        val call = okHttpClient.newCall(request)
        val response = call.execute()
        val source = response.body?.source() ?: run {
            close()
            returnclass="an">@callbackFlow
        }

        var eventType = class="st">""
        val dataBuilder = StringBuilder()

        try {
            while (!source.exhausted()) {
                val line = source.readUtf8Line() ?: break
                when {
                    line.startsWith(class="st">"event:") -> eventType = line.removePrefix(class="st">"event:").trim()
                    line.startsWith(class="st">"data:") -> dataBuilder.append(line.removePrefix(class="st">"data:").trim())
                    line.isEmpty() && dataBuilder.isNotEmpty() -> {
                        trySend(SseEvent(eventType, dataBuilder.toString()))
                        eventType = class="st">""
                        dataBuilder.clear()
                    }
                }
            }
        } finally {
            response.close()
        }

        awaitClose { call.cancel() }
    }
}

data class SseEvent(val event: String, val data: String)

    9. REMOTEMEDIATOR (OFFLINE-FIRST PAGING) — SUMMARY

    RemoteMediator = bridge between Paging 3 and a remote data source. It loads data from the network and caches it in Room. PagingSource then reads from Room (single source of truth).


    Flow:

    LazyColumn requests page → Pager asks PagingSource (Room) → if Room has data → display → if Room exhausted → RemoteMediator.load() called → fetches from API → inserts into Room → PagingSource emits new data


    Interview Tip: 💡 This is the Google-recommended pattern for offline-first

    paginated lists. Know the full flow end-to-end — it's a very common SDE-2 system design question.


    ⚠️ Key: The DB transaction in load() must be atomic — delete old data (on REFRESH) and insert new data in a single transaction.


    → See 05_data_persistence.kt § "PAGING 3 + ROOM" for the full RemoteMediator implementation, RemoteKey entity, DAO, Pager wiring, and Compose UI with LazyPagingItems.

    10. API DESIGN BEST PRACTICES

    REST Versioning:

    - URL versioning: /api/v1/articles (most common, Google uses this)

    - Header versioning: Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=1

    - Query param: /api/articles?version=1


    Pagination Contracts:


    Offset-based: ?page=3&limit=20

    ✅ Simple, supports random page access

    ❌ Inconsistent when data changes (duplicates/gaps on insert/delete)


    Cursor-based: ?cursor=abc123&limit=20

    ✅ Consistent results even with data changes

    ✅ Better performance (no OFFSET scan on DB side)

    ❌ No random page access, forward-only (or with prev_cursor)

    💡 Google/Twitter/Slack all use cursor-based pagination


    Error Envelope Pattern:

    Consistent error structure across all endpoints:

    class="cm">// Standardized error envelope
class="an">@Serializable
data class ApiErrorEnvelope(
    val error: ApiErrorDetail
)

class="an">@Serializable
data class ApiErrorDetail(
    val code: String,             class="cm">// Machine-readable: class="st">"ARTICLE_NOT_FOUND"
    val message: String,          class="cm">// Human-readable: class="st">"The article was not found"
    val target: String? = null,   class="cm">// Which field caused the error
    val details: List<ApiErrorDetail>? = null  class="cm">// Nested validation errors
)

    Idempotency Keys:

    Problem: network timeout on POST → did the server process it? Solution: client sends a unique key; server deduplicates.


    Client sends: POST /orders Header: Idempotency-Key: <UUID> Server: if key seen before → return cached response (no duplicate order) if key is new → process and store response keyed by Idempotency-Key


    ⚠️ Critical for payment, order creation, any non-idempotent mutation.


    gRPC (relevant at Google):

    - Protocol Buffers (protobuf) for serialization — smaller, faster than JSON

    - HTTP/2 based — multiplexing, header compression, bidirectional streaming

    - Strongly typed service contracts (.proto files)

    - Google uses gRPC extensively for internal microservice communication

    - On Android: use grpc-kotlin for coroutine-based stubs


    Interview Tip: 💡 Mentioning gRPC in a Google interview shows awareness of

    their tech stack. Know basic trade-offs vs REST (binary vs text, streaming support, tooling maturity, browser support).

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: What's the difference between Application and Network interceptors? A: Application interceptors: called once, see original request, can short-circuit. Network interceptors: called per network request (including redirects), can access Connection, see request after OkHttp modifications.


    Q2: How do you handle token refresh in a multi-threaded environment? A: Use OkHttp Authenticator or synchronize the refresh. With an interceptor: check 401, synchronize refresh (Mutex or synchronized), check if another thread already refreshed, retry with new token.


    Q3: How would you implement offline-first with Paging 3? A: Use RemoteMediator. It fetches from API, stores in Room. PagingSource reads from Room. UI always sees local data. RemoteMediator handles network fetch + DB upsert.


    Q4: What is ETag caching? A: Server sends ETag header with response. Client sends If-None-Match on next request. If data hasn't changed, server returns 304 (Not Modified), client uses cached version. Saves bandwidth, reduces server load.


    Q5: Retrofit with coroutines — what happens on network error? A: If the function returns Response<T>, you get a Response object (check isSuccessful). If it returns T directly, network errors throw IOException/HttpException. Always wrap in try-catch or safeApiCall.


    Q6: When would you choose WebSocket vs SSE vs polling? A: WebSocket: bidirectional real-time (chat, multiplayer). Full-duplex, binary + text support, but requires explicit reconnection logic. SSE: server-push only (live feeds, notifications). Built-in reconnect, works through HTTP proxies, text-only. Simpler than WebSocket. Polling: simplest, works everywhere, highest latency. Use for low-frequency updates where real-time isn't critical.


    Q7: Walk through how RemoteMediator coordinates network and local cache. A: Pager reads from Room via PagingSource. When Room data is exhausted, Pager calls RemoteMediator.load(). RemoteMediator fetches the next page from the API, then in a single DB transaction inserts the new data and remote keys into Room. Room's PagingSource is invalidated automatically (via InvalidationTracker), emitting the new page to the UI. On REFRESH, old data and keys are cleared before inserting. initialize() can skip refresh if cache is fresh (e.g., < 1 hour old).

    07 -- Android Internals

    ============================================================================ 07 — ANDROID INTERNALS Google SDE-2 Interview Prep

    ============================================================================


    Topics Covered:

    1. Android Process Model

    2. Low Memory Killer (LMK)

    3. Binder IPC Framework

    4. Handler / Looper / MessageQueue

    5. App Startup Flow (Cold / Warm / Hot)

    6. Activity Launch Sequence (Zygote → Activity)

    7. APK Structure & Build Process

    8. ART Runtime & Compilation (AOT, JIT, Profiles)

    9. View Rendering Pipeline

    10. ANRs (Application Not Responding)

    11. Memory Management Depth (Heap, GC, onTrimMemory)


    ============================================================================

    1. ANDROID PROCESS MODEL

    Each Android app runs in its OWN Linux process with its OWN Dalvik/ART VM.


    Process isolation provides:

    - Security: one app can't access another's memory

    - Stability: one app crashing doesn't bring down others

    - Resource management: OS can kill individual processes


    Components in the same app share the same process by default. You can assign components to separate processes via android:process in manifest.


    Interview Question: When would you use multiple processes? A: WebView (isolate crashes), heavy background services (separate heap), push notification handling (lightweight process for messages).

    ⚠️ Trade-off: Each process gets its own heap, singletons, and static state. Data sharing requires IPC (Binder, ContentProvider, files).

    2. LOW MEMORY KILLER (LMK)

    Android kills processes based on priority to free memory.


    Process priority (high → low, killed last → first):


    1. Foreground Process

    - Activity in onResume (user interacting)

    - Service bound to foreground Activity

    - BroadcastReceiver executing onReceive()


    2. Visible Process

    - Activity in onPause (partially visible, e.g., behind dialog)

    - Service bound to a visible Activity


    3. Service Process

    - Running a started Service (not bound, not foreground)

    - After ~30 minutes, demoted to cached


    4. Cached (Background) Process

    - Activity in onStop (not visible)

    - Kept for fast switching, but expendable

    - LRU list — oldest killed first


    5. Empty Process

    - No active components

    - Kept only for caching purposes

    - Killed first when memory needed


    Interview Tip: 💡 Explain how your architecture handles process death.

    SavedStateHandle, Room as SSOT, WorkManager for persistent work.

    3. BINDER IPC FRAMEWORK

    Binder = Android's inter-process communication (IPC) mechanism.


    How it works:

    1. Client calls a method on a proxy object

    2. Proxy serializes the call into a Parcel (marshalling)

    3. Parcel is sent to the Binder kernel driver

    4. Kernel driver forwards it to the server process

    5. Server deserializes (unmarshalling) and executes

    6. Response follows the same path back


    Everything in Android uses Binder under the hood:

    - startActivity() → talks to ActivityManagerService via Binder

    - bindService() → returns an IBinder to communicate

    - ContentResolver → talks to ContentProvider via Binder

    - Intents → serialized via Binder (hence the ~1MB limit)


    AIDL (Android Interface Definition Language):

    - Generates Binder boilerplate code

    - Used for cross-process service communication

    - Methods can be: oneway (async), in/out/inout params


    ⚠️ Binder Transaction Limit: ~1MB per process for ALL concurrent transactions. TransactionTooLargeException if exceeded (large Bundles, Bitmaps in Intents).

    4. HANDLER / LOOPER / MESSAGEQUEUE

    The foundation of Android's threading model:


    Looper → infinite loop that processes messages from a queue MessageQueue → FIFO queue of Messages and Runnables

    Handler → sends Messages/Runnables to a specific Looper's queue


    Main Thread = a thread with a Looper (created by ActivityThread.main()).


    Flow:

    Handler.post(runnable) → enqueues Runnable in MessageQueue Looper.loop() → dequeues and dispatches to Handler.handleMessage()


    Interview Question: How does runOnUiThread work? Answer: It checks if current thread is main thread. If yes, runs immediately. If no, posts to main Looper's Handler.


    Follow-up: How does Dispatchers.Main work under the hood? Answer: It uses a Handler attached to the main Looper to post coroutine resumption to the main thread's MessageQueue.

    class="cm">// How Handler/Looper work conceptually
class HandlerLooperExample {

    class="cm">// Creating a background thread with a Looper
    fun createBackgroundLooper() {
        val handlerThread = HandlerThread(class="st">"BackgroundThread")
        handlerThread.start()

        val backgroundHandler = Handler(handlerThread.looper)
        val mainHandler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())

        backgroundHandler.post {
            class="cm">// This runs on the background thread
            val result = heavyComputation()

            mainHandler.post {
                class="cm">// This runs on the main thread
                updateUI(result)
            }
        }
    }

    class="cm">// This is essentially what Dispatchers.Main does
    fun postToMainThread(block: () -> Unit) {
        val mainHandler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
        mainHandler.post(block)
    }
}

    5. APP STARTUP FLOW

    Cold Start (slowest):

    1. User taps app icon

    2. Linux kernel creates a new process (forked from Zygote)

    3. ART creates the Application object

    4. Application.onCreate() runs

    5. ActivityThread creates the main Activity

    6. Activity.onCreate() → onStart() → onResume()

    7. First frame drawn → app is interactive


    Warm Start:

    - Process exists but Activity was destroyed

    - Skips steps 2-4, starts from step 5

    - Faster because Application is already initialized


    Hot Start:

    - Process AND Activity exist (in onStop)

    - Just brings Activity to foreground

    - onRestart() → onStart() → onResume()


    💡 Google Metric: Cold start should be < 500ms for good UX. Time To Initial Display (TTID) and Time To Full Display (TTFD).


    Optimizing Cold Start:

    - Lazy-initialize libraries in Application.onCreate()

    - Use App Startup library (Jetpack) for ContentProvider initialization

    - Defer non-critical initialization to background

    - Use Baseline Profiles for AOT compilation of hot paths

    - Minimize work in Activity.onCreate()

    class="cm">// Optimized Application class
class OptimizedApplication : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()

        class="cm">// Only critical initialization here
        initializeCrashReporting()  class="cm">// Must be first

        class="cm">// Defer everything else
        val backgroundScope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default + SupervisorJob())
        backgroundScope.launch {
            initializeAnalytics()
            initializeRemoteConfig()
            preloadFonts()
        }
    }
}

    6. ZYGOTE & ACTIVITY LAUNCH SEQUENCE

    Zygote = template process that every Android app is forked from.


    Why Zygote?

    - Pre-loads common framework classes and resources

    - fork() is fast (copy-on-write memory)

    - New app process gets pre-warmed ART runtime


    Full Activity Launch Sequence:


    Launcher → startActivity(intent) → ActivityManagerService (system process, Binder IPC) → resolves Intent, checks permissions → if process doesn't exist: tells Zygote to fork → Zygote forks a new process → New process: ActivityThread.main() starts → Creates Looper, Handler for main thread → Binds to ActivityManagerService → AMS tells new process to create Application → Application.onCreate() → AMS tells process to launch Activity → Activity.onCreate() → onStart() → onResume() → WindowManager adds Activity's window → First frame rendered (TTID)

    7. APK STRUCTURE & BUILD PROCESS

    APK Contents:

    AndroidManifest.xml → compiled binary XML

    classes.dex → compiled bytecode (Dalvik Executable)

    resources.arsc → compiled resources table

    res/ → resources not compiled into resources.arsc

    lib/ → native libraries (arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a, x86_64)

    assets/ → raw files (accessed via AssetManager)

    META-INF/ → APK signature


    Build Process:

    .kt/.java → kotlinc/javac → .class → D8 → .dex R8 (release) → optimization, shrinking, obfuscation Resources → AAPT2 → compiled resources + R.java All combined → APK → zipalign → APK signing


    App Bundle (AAB):

    - Google Play generates optimized APKs per device

    - Split APKs: base + config (density, ABI, language)

    - Smaller downloads: user only gets what they need

    - Dynamic Feature Modules: download features on demand

    8. ART RUNTIME

    ART (Android Runtime) replaced Dalvik in Android 5.0.


    Compilation strategies:


    AOT (Ahead-Of-Time):

    - Compiles dex to native code at install time

    - Faster startup, higher storage cost

    - Used for frequently-used code paths


    JIT (Just-In-Time):

    - Compiles hot methods at runtime

    - Adapts to actual usage patterns

    - Profiles stored for future AOT compilation


    Profile-Guided Compilation:

    - JIT collects profiles of hot methods

    - On device idle/charging, AOT-compiles those methods

    - Baseline Profiles (developer-provided) + Cloud Profiles (from Play)


    Garbage Collection:

    - Concurrent, generational GC

    - Young generation: small, collected frequently (minor GC)

    - Old generation: large, collected rarely (major GC)

    - ⚠️ GC pauses can cause jank (skipped frames)

    - Avoid excessive allocations in onDraw() / composable recomposition

    9. VIEW RENDERING PIPELINE

    How a frame is rendered (View system):


    VSYNC signal (every 16.6ms for 60fps) → Choreographer dispatches frame callback → Input events processed → Animations updated → Measure pass (top-down, each view measures children) → Layout pass (top-down, each view positions children) → Draw pass (top-down, each view draws itself) → RenderThread → GPU renders display list → SurfaceFlinger composites all surfaces → Display shows frame


    Frame budget: 16.6ms (60fps) or 8.3ms (120fps) If frame takes longer → dropped frame → jank


    Common causes of jank:

    - Deep view hierarchies (too many measure/layout passes)

    - Overdraw (drawing the same pixel multiple times)

    - Main thread blocking (IO, heavy computation)

    - GC pauses from excessive allocation

    - Large bitmap decoding on main thread


    Compose rendering is different:

    Composition → Layout → Drawing (3 phases) Uses a slot table instead of a view tree Can skip phases if state hasn't changed

    10. ANRs (APPLICATION NOT RESPONDING)

    ANR = system dialog shown when the app is unresponsive to user input.


    ANR Triggers:

    - Input dispatch timeout: 5 seconds (touch/key event not handled)

    - BroadcastReceiver timeout: 10 seconds (onReceive not finished)

    - Service timeout: 20 seconds (onCreate/onStartCommand not finished)

    - ContentProvider timeout: published within 10 seconds of creation


    Root Cause: almost always main thread blocking.


    Common Causes:

    1. Synchronous disk I/O on main thread (SharedPreferences.commit(), DB queries)

    2. Synchronous network call on main thread

    3. Long-running computation on main thread (JSON parsing, bitmap decode)

    4. Lock contention — main thread waiting on a lock held by another thread

    5. Deadlock between main thread and a worker thread

    6. Slow BroadcastReceiver (doing IO in onReceive)

    7. Binder call to a slow or hung remote service


    Diagnosis Tools:

    - /data/anr/traces.txt → full thread dump at time of ANR

    - StrictMode → detects disk/network IO on main thread during development

    - Systrace / Perfetto → system-level trace showing thread activity

    - Android Studio Profiler → CPU trace reveals blocking calls

    - Google Play Console → ANR clusters with stack traces


    ⚠️ Google Play ANR Thresholds:

    - User-perceived ANR rate > 0.47% → "bad behavior" warning

    - User-perceived ANR rate > 8% → app may be deprioritized in Play Store

    - These are measured per active daily users, not sessions


    Interview Tip: 💡 When asked "how do you prevent ANRs?", don't just say

    "move work off main thread." Discuss StrictMode for detection, coroutines with Dispatchers.IO for I/O, and monitoring with Play Console vitals.

    class="cm">// StrictMode setup for detecting main thread violations in debug builds
class DebugApplication : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()

        if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
            StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(
                StrictMode.ThreadPolicy.Builder()
                    .detectDiskReads()
                    .detectDiskWrites()
                    .detectNetwork()
                    .detectCustomSlowCalls()
                    .penaltyLog()        class="cm">// Log to Logcat
                    .penaltyFlashScreen() class="cm">// Red border flash on violation
                    .build()
            )

            StrictMode.setVmPolicy(
                StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder()
                    .detectLeakedClosableObjects()
                    .detectLeakedSqlLiteObjects()
                    .detectActivityLeaks()
                    .penaltyLog()
                    .build()
            )
        }
    }
}

    11. MEMORY MANAGEMENT DEPTH

    ART Heap Structure:


    Young Generation (Nursery):

    - Where newly allocated objects live

    - Small, collected frequently (minor/young GC)

    - Most objects die young (generational hypothesis)

    - Uses a semi-space or copying collector


    Old Generation (Tenured):

    - Objects that survived multiple young GCs are promoted here

    - Larger, collected less frequently (major GC)

    - Uses a concurrent mark-sweep or compacting collector


    Large Object Space (LOS):

    - Objects > 12KB (typically large arrays, bitmaps)

    - Allocated separately to avoid fragmentation

    - Collected as part of major GC


    Native Heap vs Dalvik/ART Heap:

    - ART heap: managed by GC, holds Java/Kotlin objects

    - Native heap: unmanaged (malloc/free), holds native allocations

    - Bitmaps (API 26+): allocated on native heap, not ART heap

    - JNI allocations, NDK code, graphics buffers → native heap

    - Native leaks don't show in Memory Profiler heap dump — use malloc debug


    android:largeHeap="true":

    - Requests a larger Dalvik/ART heap (typically 256-512MB vs 128-256MB)

    ⚠️ Why it's usually wrong:

    - Does NOT fix memory leaks — just delays OOM

    - Longer GC pauses (more heap to scan)

    - System may kill your app sooner (uses more memory overall)

    - Legitimate use cases: photo/video editors, games with large assets


    Interview Tip: 💡 If asked about memory optimization, discuss the heap

    structure, then onTrimMemory for responding to pressure, and finally profiling tools (Memory Profiler, LeakCanary). Mentioning largeHeap as an anti-pattern shows depth.

    onTrimMemory / ComponentCallbacks2:


    Called by the system when memory is low. Your app should respond by releasing non-critical resources to avoid being killed.


    Levels (increasing severity):


    TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_MODERATE (5) → App is running, device is getting low on memory → Consider releasing non-essential caches


    TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOW (10) → App is running, device is quite low on memory → Release caches and reduce memory footprint


    TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICAL (15) → App is running, device is critically low → Release everything non-essential immediately


    TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN (20) → App's UI is no longer visible → Release UI-related resources (image caches, view caches)


    TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND (40) → App is in the LRU background list → Release as much as possible to survive longer


    TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATE (60) → App is in the middle of the LRU list → Getting close to being killed


    TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE (80) → App is near the end of the LRU list → Will be killed next if memory isn't freed

    class MemoryAwareApplication : Application() {  class="cm">// Application already implements ComponentCallbacks2

    private val imageCache = LruCache<String, Bitmap>(calculateMemoryCacheSize())

    override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {
        super.onTrimMemory(level)

        when {
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE -> {
                class="cm">// About to be killed — release everything
                imageCache.evictAll()
                clearAllCaches()
            }
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND -> {
                class="cm">// In background LRU — release most caches
                imageCache.trimToSize(imageCache.maxSize() / 4)
                clearNonEssentialCaches()
            }
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN -> {
                class="cm">// UI hidden — release UI caches
                imageCache.trimToSize(imageCache.maxSize() / 2)
            }
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICAL -> {
                class="cm">// Running but critical — reduce aggressively
                imageCache.trimToSize(imageCache.maxSize() / 8)
            }
            level >= ComponentCallbacks2.TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOW -> {
                class="cm">// Running but low — reduce caches
                imageCache.trimToSize(imageCache.maxSize() / 4)
            }
        }
    }

    private fun calculateMemoryCacheSize(): Int {
        val maxMemory = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / 1024  class="cm">// KB
        return (maxMemory / 8).toInt()  class="cm">// Use 1/8th of available memory
    }

    private fun clearAllCaches() { class="cm">/* release all in-memory caches */ }
    private fun clearNonEssentialCaches() { class="cm">/* release non-UI caches */ }
}

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: What is Zygote and why does Android use it? A: Zygote is a special process started at boot that pre-loads framework classes and resources. All app processes are forked from Zygote via fork(), which is fast because of copy-on-write memory semantics. This means each new app starts with framework already in memory.


    Q2: Explain the Binder transaction size limit and its implications. A: ~1MB per process for ALL concurrent transactions. This affects:

    - Intent extras (don't put large data in Intents)

    - onSaveInstanceState Bundles (keep small)

    - ContentProvider queries (use ContentResolver with cursors, not full data) Exceeding causes TransactionTooLargeException.


    Q3: Why can't you touch the UI from a background thread? A: Android's View system is NOT thread-safe. ViewRootImpl.checkThread() verifies all UI operations happen on the thread that created the view hierarchy (main thread). This is enforced to prevent race conditions during measure/layout/draw passes.


    Q4: How do Baseline Profiles improve app performance? A: They provide a list of "hot" classes and methods to the ART compiler. These are AOT-compiled at install time, so they're native code on first launch. Without profiles, JIT compilation causes slower first run. Can improve startup by 20-30%.


    Q5: What happens when you call startActivity()? A: Intent is sent via Binder to ActivityManagerService (AMS) in the system_server process. AMS resolves the Intent, checks permissions, determines target component, and instructs the target process to create/resume the Activity. If the process doesn't exist, AMS tells Zygote to fork a new one first.


    Q6: Your app has a high ANR rate. How do you diagnose and fix it? A: 1. Check Play Console ANR clusters for stack traces.

    2. Look at /data/anr/traces.txt for the thread dump — find what the main thread was blocked on (lock, I/O, binder call).

    3. Enable StrictMode in debug to catch disk/network on main thread.

    4. Use Systrace/Perfetto to see main thread activity around the ANR.

    5. Common fixes: move I/O to Dispatchers.IO, use SharedPreferences.apply() instead of commit(), use async BroadcastReceiver with goAsync() for long work, avoid holding locks across threads.


    Q7: Explain onTrimMemory levels and how you'd respond to memory pressure. A: onTrimMemory is called with increasing severity levels (5→80). RUNNING_* levels (5/10/15): app is foreground but device is low — progressively reduce caches. UI_HIDDEN (20): release UI resources. BACKGROUND/MODERATE/COMPLETE (40/60/80): app is in background LRU, risk of being killed — release everything non-essential. Implementation: use LruCache.trimToSize() to progressively shrink, clear image/data caches, release held resources. Responding properly keeps your app alive longer in the background.

    1. UI PERFORMANCE — JANK & OVERDRAW

    Jank = dropped frames. Occurs when frame takes longer than 16.6ms (60fps).


    Common Causes:

    1. Main thread blocking (IO, heavy computation)

    2. Deep view hierarchies (nested LinearLayouts)

    3. Overdraw (multiple layers drawing on the same pixel)

    4. Expensive onDraw() operations

    5. Layout thrashing (requestLayout() called too often)

    6. Large bitmap decoding on main thread


    Overdraw Levels:

    No overdraw (1x) → white/no tint 1x overdraw (2x) → blue 2x overdraw (3x) → green 3x overdraw (4x) → red — needs optimization


    Fixing Overdraw:

    - Remove unnecessary backgrounds (window background under Activity background)

    - Use clipRect() in custom views

    - Flatten view hierarchies

    - Use android:windowBackground for splash instead of Activity background

    </LinearLayout>
</LinearLayout>
*/

class="cm">// ✅ Flat hierarchy with ConstraintLayout

</ConstraintLayout>

class ArticleAdapter : ListAdapter<Article, ArticleViewHolder>(ArticleDiffCallback()) {

}

            class="cm">// ❌ Creates new lambda on every recomposition
            class="cm">// ArticleItem(article, onClick = { viewModel.onClick(article.id) })

            class="cm">// ✅ Stable reference — Compose can skip recomposition of ArticleItem
            val onClick = remember(article.id) { { viewModel.onClick(article.id) } }
            ArticleItem(article, onClick = onClick)
        }
    }
}

    4. MEMORY OPTIMIZATION

    Common Memory Leaks in Android:


    1. Static reference to Activity/Context Fix: Use Application Context or WeakReference


    2. Inner class holding implicit reference to outer Activity Fix: Use static inner class + WeakReference


    3. Handler with Activity reference Fix: Use lifecycleScope.launch instead


    4. Unregistered listeners (LocationManager, SensorManager, BroadcastReceiver) Fix: Unregister in onPause/onStop/onDestroyView


    5. Fragment View binding not cleared in onDestroyView Fix: Set _binding = null in onDestroyView


    6. Coroutine scope outliving the component Fix: Use viewModelScope, lifecycleScope, viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope


    7. ViewModel holding View/Activity reference Fix: Never pass View or Activity to ViewModel

    class="cm">// ❌ Classic memory leak — anonymous inner class holds Activity reference
class LeakyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        class="cm">// ❌ Runnable holds implicit reference to this Activity
        val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
        handler.postDelayed({
            class="cm">// This keeps Activity alive for 10 seconds even after onDestroy
            updateUI()
        }, 10_000)
    }
}

class="cm">// ✅ Fixed with lifecycleScope
class SafeActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            delay(10_000)
            class="cm">// Automatically cancelled when Activity is destroyed
            updateUI()
        }
    }
}

    Bitmap Memory Management:

    - Bitmaps are the #1 source of OOM crashes

    - A 4000x3000 photo at ARGB_8888 = 48MB of heap!


    Solutions:

    1. Use image loading libraries (Coil, Glide) — they handle caching + sampling

    2. inSampleSize — decode at reduced resolution

    3. Bitmap.Config.RGB_565 — half memory (no alpha), good for photos

    4. BitmapFactory.Options.inBitmap — reuse bitmap memory

    fun decodeSampledBitmap(
    resources: Resources,
    resId: Int,
    reqWidth: Int,
    reqHeight: Int
): Bitmap {
    class="cm">// First pass: decode bounds only (no memory allocation)
    val options = BitmapFactory.Options().apply {
        inJustDecodeBounds = true
    }
    BitmapFactory.decodeResource(resources, resId, options)

    class="cm">// Calculate sample size
    options.inSampleSize = calculateInSampleSize(options, reqWidth, reqHeight)
    options.inJustDecodeBounds = false

    return BitmapFactory.decodeResource(resources, resId, options)
}

fun calculateInSampleSize(
    options: BitmapFactory.Options,
    reqWidth: Int,
    reqHeight: Int
): Int {
    val (height, width) = options.outHeight to options.outWidth
    var sampleSize = 1
    if (height > reqHeight || width > reqWidth) {
        val halfHeight = height / 2
        val halfWidth = width / 2
        while (halfHeight / sampleSize >= reqHeight && halfWidth / sampleSize >= reqWidth) {
            sampleSize *= 2
        }
    }
    return sampleSize
}

    5. BATTERY OPTIMIZATION

    Doze Mode (API 23+):

    When device is stationary, unplugged, screen off:

    - Network access suspended

    - Alarms deferred

    - GPS/Wi-Fi scanning stopped

    - JobScheduler/WorkManager deferred

    - Periodic maintenance windows allow batched work


    App Standby Buckets (API 28+):

    Active → currently in use, no restrictions

    Working → recently used, mild restrictions

    Frequent → used regularly, more restrictions

    Rare → hardly used, heavy restrictions Restricted → not used + misbehaving, very heavy restrictions


    Battery optimization checklist:

    ✅ Use WorkManager with constraints (not AlarmManager)

    ✅ Batch network requests

    ✅ Use Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) instead of polling

    ✅ Minimize wake locks

    ✅ Use JobScheduler for deferrable work

    ✅ Reduce GPS accuracy when possible

    ✅ Use Fused Location Provider

    6. APK SIZE OPTIMIZATION

    APK size directly impacts install conversion rates. Every 6MB increase → 1% drop in install rate (Google data).


    Optimization techniques:


    R8 (ProGuard successor):

    - Code shrinking — removes unused classes/methods

    - Obfuscation — shortens names (a, b, c)

    - Optimization — inlines methods, simplifies code

    - Resource shrinking — removes unused resources


    App Bundle (AAB):

    - Dynamic delivery — users download only what they need

    - Split APKs — per density, ABI, language

    - Dynamic feature modules — on-demand module download

    - Typically 15-20% smaller than universal APK


    Other techniques:

    - Use WebP instead of PNG (25-34% smaller)

    - Vector drawables instead of multiple density PNGs

    - Remove unused libraries

    - Use android.enableR8.fullMode=true in gradle.properties

    - Compress native libraries: android.bundle.enableUncompressedNativeLibs=true

    class="cm">// build.gradle.kts — R8 configuration
class="cm">/*
android {
    buildTypes {
        release {
            isMinifyEnabled = true       class="cm">// Code shrinking
            isShrinkResources = true     class="cm">// Resource shrinking
            proguardFiles(
                getDefaultProguardFile(class="st">"proguard-android-optimize.txt"),
                class="st">"proguard-rules.pro"
            )
        }
    }
}
*/

    7. STARTUP OPTIMIZATION

    Goal: Cold start < 500ms (Google benchmark)


    Techniques:


    1. Lazy initialization:

    Don't initialize everything in Application.onCreate(). Use by lazy {} or Hilt's @Inject for on-demand creation.


    2. App Startup library:

    Replaces multiple ContentProviders (which run before Application.onCreate) with a single one that initializes libraries efficiently.


    3. Baseline Profiles:

    Pre-compile critical code paths (splash → home screen). 20-30% startup improvement typical.


    4. Splash Screen API (API 31+):

    System-managed splash screen — shows while app initializes. Replaces custom splash Activity pattern.


    5. Reduce main thread work:

    Move initialization to background threads. Use Dispatchers.Default for CPU-bound init.

    class="cm">// App Startup library
class AnalyticsInitializer : Initializer<Analytics> {
    override fun create(context: Context): Analytics {
        return Analytics.init(context)
    }

    override fun dependencies(): List<Class<out Initializer<*>>> {
        class="cm">// Declare dependencies — these initialize first
        return listOf(CrashReportingInitializer::class.java)
    }
}

    8. PROFILING TOOLS

    Android Studio Profiler:


    CPU Profiler:

    - System Trace → see thread activity, frame rendering, system events

    - Method Trace → see exact method calls and durations

    - Use for: finding jank, slow methods, main thread blocking


    Memory Profiler:

    - Real-time heap usage graph

    - Heap dump → see all live objects

    - Allocation tracking → see where objects are created

    - Use for: finding memory leaks, excessive allocations


    Network Profiler:

    - Timeline of network requests

    - Request/response inspection

    - Use for: finding redundant calls, large payloads


    Energy Profiler:

    - CPU, Network, GPS, Wake Lock usage

    - Use for: finding battery drain causes


    LeakCanary:

    - Automatic memory leak detection in debug builds

    - Detects: Activity, Fragment, ViewModel, View, Service leaks

    - Shows leak trace (reference chain) for debugging


    Macrobenchmark & Microbenchmark:

    - Macrobenchmark: measures app-level metrics (startup, scrolling)

    - Microbenchmark: measures code-level metrics (function timing)

    - Both provide deterministic, reproducible results

    9. NETWORK OPTIMIZATION

    Connection Pooling & HTTP/2 Multiplexing:

    - OkHttp maintains a ConnectionPool (default: 5 idle connections, 5 min keepalive)

    - HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests over a single TCP connection

    - Reduces latency from TCP handshake + TLS negotiation

    - Configure: ConnectionPool(maxIdleConnections, keepAliveDuration, timeUnit)


    Request Batching & Deduplication:

    - Batch multiple small requests into one (e.g., GraphQL, batch REST endpoints)

    - Deduplicate identical in-flight requests (return same Deferred/Flow to callers)

    - OkHttp automatically deduplicates concurrent requests to the same URL with the same Cache-Control behavior


    Compression:

    - OkHttp adds Accept-Encoding: gzip automatically

    - Server must support Content-Encoding: gzip

    - Reduces payload size by 60-80% for JSON/text responses

    - Don't manually gzip if OkHttp handles transparent decompression


    Prefetching Strategies:

    - Prefetch next page of paginated data when user is near the end

    - Prefetch likely navigation targets (e.g., article detail when scrolling list)

    - Use WorkManager or idle time for background prefetch

    ⚠️ Balance: prefetching wastes bandwidth if user doesn't use the data


    Reducing Payload Size:

    - Request only needed fields (sparse fieldsets, GraphQL partial queries)

    - Use Protocol Buffers (protobuf) instead of JSON for smaller payloads

    - Paginate — don't fetch entire collections

    - Use delta sync / If-Modified-Since / ETag for incremental updates


    Image Optimization:

    - WebP: 25-34% smaller than PNG, supports transparency and animation

    - Progressive loading: show low-quality placeholder, load full-res async

    - Thumbnails: request server-side resized images matching display size

    - Coil/Glide handle disk caching, memory caching, and downsampling


    Interview Tip: 💡 Discuss the full stack — client-side (pooling, caching,

    compression) AND API-side (pagination, field selection, image CDN).

    10. PERFETTO & SYSTRACE

    Perfetto = modern system-level tracing tool (replaces Systrace). Captures kernel-level + userspace events across ALL processes.


    What Perfetto captures:

    - CPU scheduling (which threads run on which cores)

    - Binder transactions

    - Rendering pipeline (Choreographer, RenderThread, SurfaceFlinger)

    - Disk I/O, memory allocations

    - Custom trace sections (android.os.Trace / androidx.tracing)


    How to capture:

    1. Android Studio → Profiler → CPU → System Trace (uses Perfetto)

    2. Command line: adb shell perfetto -o /data/misc/perfetto-traces/trace.pb

    3. On-device: Developer Options → System Tracing

    4. Open traces at ui.perfetto.dev


    Reading a Perfetto trace:

    - Each row = a thread or process

    - Colored blocks = trace sections (slices)

    - Look for long slices on the main thread (> 16ms = jank source)

    - "Choreographer#doFrame" → the frame boundary

    - Gaps between slices = thread was sleeping or waiting


    Identifying jank:

    - Find frames where doFrame > 16.6ms

    - Check what's on the main thread during that frame:

    → Long measure/layout? Deep view hierarchy → Binder transaction? Slow IPC call → Lock contention? Deadlock or resource competition → Disk I/O? Blocking read on main thread


    Perfetto vs Android Studio Profiler:

    - Profiler: easier UI, integrated in IDE, app-scoped

    - Perfetto: system-wide, more detail, better for cross-process issues

    - Use Profiler for quick checks, Perfetto for deep investigation


    Adding custom trace sections:

    class="cm">// Custom trace sections for identifying slow code paths
class TracedRepository(private val dao: ArticleDao, private val api: ArticleApiService) {

    suspend fun loadArticles(): List<Article> {
        class="cm">// Appears as class="st">"ArticleRepository.loadArticles" in Perfetto/Systrace
        return Trace.beginAsyncSection(class="st">"ArticleRepository.loadArticles", 0).let {
            try {
                val cached = traceSection(class="st">"loadFromDb") { dao.getAll() }
                if (cached.isNotEmpty()) return cached

                val remote = traceSection(class="st">"fetchFromApi") { api.getArticles(1).body()!! }
                val entities = remote.articles.map { it.toEntity() }
                traceSection(class="st">"saveToDb") { dao.insertAll(entities) }
                entities.map { it.toDomain() }
            } finally {
                Trace.endAsyncSection(class="st">"ArticleRepository.loadArticles", 0)
            }
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// Helper for synchronous trace sections
inline fun <T> traceSection(label: String, block: () -> T): T {
    Trace.beginSection(label)
    return try {
        block()
    } finally {
        Trace.endSection()
    }
}

    11. ANDROID VITALS

    Android Vitals = performance metrics dashboard in Google Play Console. Google uses these metrics to determine app quality and search ranking.


    Core Vitals (affect store visibility):


    ANR Rate:

    - User-perceived ANR rate (ANRs / daily active users)

    - Bad threshold: > 0.47%

    - Excessive threshold: > 8%

    - Main cause: main thread blocking (IO, locks, slow binder calls)


    Crash Rate:

    - User-perceived crash rate

    - Bad threshold: > 1.09%

    - Excessive threshold: > 8%

    - Includes Java/Kotlin exceptions AND native crashes


    Slow Rendering (Frozen Frames):

    - Frames that take > 700ms to render

    - Bad threshold: > 0.1% of sessions

    - Caused by main thread blocking during frame rendering


    Excessive Wakeups:

    - AlarmManager wakeups that wake the device from Doze

    - Bad threshold: > 10 wakeups per hour

    - Fix: use WorkManager, avoid exact alarms unless necessary


    Stuck Background Wake Locks:

    - Wake locks held for > 1 hour while in background

    - Fix: always set timeout on wake locks, release in finally blocks


    Using Vitals to Drive Performance Work:

    1. Check Play Console weekly for vitals regressions

    2. Correlate regressions with app version releases

    3. Use ANR/crash clusters → group by stack trace → prioritize by volume

    4. Set up alerting for threshold violations

    5. Track vitals improvement as a team OKR


    ⚠️ Apps with bad vitals get:

    - Warning badge in Play Store listing

    - Lower search ranking and recommendations

    - Potential removal from featured placements


    Interview Tip: 💡 Mentioning Android Vitals shows you think about production

    quality, not just feature development. Know the thresholds and how you'd set up a process to monitor and improve them.

    12. BASELINE PROFILES

    Baseline Profiles = developer-provided list of critical code paths for AOT compilation.


    How it works:

    1. Developer writes a Macrobenchmark test that exercises critical user journeys

    2. BaselineProfileRule records which classes/methods are touched

    3. Generated profile is bundled in the APK/AAB

    4. At install time, ART AOT-compiles these methods (instead of interpreting/JIT)

    5. On first launch: profiled code runs as native machine code


    Benefits:

    - 20-30% faster cold startup (typical improvement)

    - Smoother first-time scrolling (avoids JIT compilation stutters)

    - Consistent performance from first launch

    - Cloud Profiles (Play Store) complement developer-provided profiles


    ⚠️ Without Baseline Profiles:

    First launch → ART interprets bytecode → JIT compiles hot methods over time → First run is noticeably slower than subsequent runs


    Interview Tip: 💡 Baseline Profiles are a Google-created technology.

    Demonstrating hands-on knowledge (Macrobenchmark, BaselineProfileRule, CI integration) is a strong signal for SDE-2 performance questions.

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: Your app drops frames during scrolling. How do you diagnose and fix it? A: 1. Enable "Profile GPU rendering" bars in Developer Options

    2. Run System Trace in CPU Profiler — identify long frames

    3. Check for main thread blocking (IO, heavy computation)

    4. Check Layout Inspector for deep hierarchies

    5. Enable Debug GPU Overdraw to find overdraw

    6. Check RecyclerView: ensure DiffUtil, no allocations in onBind

    7. For Compose: check recomposition counts, use Composition tracing


    Q2: How do you detect and fix memory leaks? A: Detection: LeakCanary (auto), Memory Profiler (manual heap dump) Common fixes:

    - Null out binding in onDestroyView

    - Use viewLifecycleOwner for observers

    - Use Application Context in singletons

    - Cancel coroutines/callbacks in appropriate lifecycle methods


    Q3: Your APK is 80MB. How do you reduce it? A: 1. Enable R8 (minifyEnabled + shrinkResources)

    2. Switch to App Bundle (AAB)

    3. Analyze APK with Android Studio's APK Analyzer

    4. Convert PNGs to WebP, use vector drawables

    5. Remove unused libraries and native ABIs

    6. Use dynamic feature modules for large features

    7. Enable proguard for all build types


    Q4: Explain Baseline Profiles and how they improve performance. A: Developer-defined list of critical code paths (classes + methods). ART AOT-compiles these at install time instead of waiting for JIT. Result: faster startup (no interpretation/JIT compilation overhead). Create with Macrobenchmark library, generate with BaselineProfileRule. CI integration: regenerate on release branches, verify with benchmarks.


    Q5: How does R8 differ from ProGuard? A: R8 is Google's replacement for ProGuard. Key differences:

    - Faster build times (single-step DEX + shrink)

    - Better code optimization (more aggressive inlining)

    - Kotlin-aware (understands Kotlin metadata)

    - Full mode: more aggressive (breaks some reflection patterns)

    - Uses same ProGuard rules format


    Q6: How would you use Perfetto to diagnose a jank issue? A: 1. Capture a system trace via Android Studio Profiler or adb shell perfetto.

    2. Open at ui.perfetto.dev.

    3. Find the main thread row and locate Choreographer#doFrame slices.

    4. Identify frames exceeding 16.6ms.

    5. Inspect what's happening in that frame: long measure/layout (deep hierarchy), binder transactions (slow IPC), lock contention, or disk I/O. Cross-reference with RenderThread for GPU work.

    6. Add custom Trace.beginSection()/endSection() to narrow down the specific code path causing the delay.


    Q7: What are Android Vitals and how do they affect your app? A: Android Vitals is the Play Console dashboard tracking core performance metrics: ANR rate (> 0.47% is bad), crash rate (> 1.09% is bad), frozen frames (> 0.1% sessions), excessive wakeups, stuck wake locks. Apps exceeding thresholds get warning badges, lower search ranking, and reduced recommendations. Use vitals to prioritize performance work: correlate regressions with releases, use ANR/crash clusters to find root causes, and track improvement over time.

    09 -- Background Work

    ============================================================================ 09 — BACKGROUND WORK Google SDE-2 Interview Prep

    ============================================================================


    Topics Covered:

    1. Choosing the Right API (Decision Framework)

    2. WorkManager — Persistent & Deferrable Work

    3. Foreground Services

    4. Broadcast Receivers

    5. Background Execution Limits

    6. AlarmManager

    7. Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)

    8. Foreground Service Launch Restrictions (API 31+)


    ============================================================================

    1. CHOOSING THE RIGHT BACKGROUND API

    Decision Framework:


    ┌──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Requirement                  │ API to Use                                │
├──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Must complete even if app    │ WorkManager                               │
│ closes or device restarts    │                                           │
├──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Needs immediate execution    │ Coroutines (viewModelScope)               │
│ while user is in app         │                                           │
├──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ User-initiated long task     │ Foreground Service                        │
│ (music, navigation, upload)  │                                           │
├──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Exact timing required        │ AlarmManager (setExactAndAllowWhileIdle)  │
│ (reminders, alarms)          │                                           │
├──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ React to system events       │ BroadcastReceiver                         │
│ (boot, connectivity)         │                                           │
├──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Periodic background sync     │ WorkManager (PeriodicWorkRequest)         │
│                              │                                           │
└──────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

    💡 Default answer: WorkManager for almost all background work. It handles Doze, battery optimization, and guarantees execution.

    2. WORKMANAGER — PERSISTENT & DEFERRABLE WORK

    WorkManager features:

    ✅ Survives app restart and device reboot

    ✅ Constraint-based execution (network, battery, charging)

    ✅ Chaining (sequential and parallel work)

    ✅ Exponential backoff for retries

    ✅ Input/Output data passing

    ✅ Unique work (prevent duplicates)

    ✅ Expedited work (runs immediately, even under Doze)

    ✅ Observable work status via LiveData/Flow


    Under the hood: Uses JobScheduler (API 23+) or AlarmManager + BroadcastReceiver.

    class="cm">// Simple Worker
class SyncWorker(
    context: Context,
    params: WorkerParameters
) : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {

    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        val userId = inputData.getString(class="st">"USER_ID") ?: return Result.failure()

        return try {
            val api = ApiService.create()
            val localDb = AppDatabase.getInstance(applicationContext)

            class="cm">// Fetch from API
            val articles = api.getArticles(userId)

            class="cm">// Store locally
            localDb.articleDao().upsertAll(articles.map { it.toEntity() })

            class="cm">// Pass output data to next worker in chain
            val outputData = workDataOf(
                class="st">"SYNC_COUNT" to articles.size,
                class="st">"LAST_SYNC" to System.currentTimeMillis()
            )
            Result.success(outputData)

        } catch (e: IOException) {
            if (runAttemptCount < 3) {
                Result.retry()  class="cm">// Exponential backoff
            } else {
                Result.failure(workDataOf(class="st">"ERROR" to e.message))
            }
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            Result.failure(workDataOf(class="st">"ERROR" to e.message))
        }
    }

    class="cm">// Show notification for long-running work (API 31+ requires this for expedited)
    override suspend fun getForegroundInfo(): ForegroundInfo {
        val notification = NotificationCompat.Builder(applicationContext, class="st">"sync_channel")
            .setContentTitle(class="st">"Syncing articles...")
            .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_sync)
            .setProgress(0, 0, true)
            .build()
        return ForegroundInfo(SYNC_NOTIFICATION_ID, notification)
    }

    companion object {
        const val SYNC_NOTIFICATION_ID = 1001
    }
}

class="cm">// Scheduling Work
class WorkScheduler(private val context: Context) {

    class="cm">// One-time work with constraints
    fun scheduleSync(userId: String) {
        val constraints = Constraints.Builder()
            .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED)
            .setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true)
            .build()

        val inputData = workDataOf(class="st">"USER_ID" to userId)

        val syncRequest = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
            .setConstraints(constraints)
            .setInputData(inputData)
            .setBackoffCriteria(
                BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL,
                WorkRequest.MIN_BACKOFF_MILLIS,
                TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS
            )
            .addTag(class="st">"sync")
            .build()

        class="cm">// KEEP: if existing work is running, keep it. Don't enqueue duplicate.
        WorkManager.getInstance(context)
            .enqueueUniqueWork(class="st">"article_sync", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, syncRequest)
    }

    class="cm">// Periodic work
    fun schedulePeriodicSync() {
        val periodicSync = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>(
            repeatInterval = 1, TimeUnit.HOURS,
            flexInterval = 15, TimeUnit.MINUTES  class="cm">// Window for execution
        )
            .setConstraints(
                Constraints.Builder()
                    .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.UNMETERED) class="cm">// Wi-Fi only
                    .build()
            )
            .addTag(class="st">"periodic_sync")
            .build()

        WorkManager.getInstance(context)
            .enqueueUniquePeriodicWork(
                class="st">"periodic_article_sync",
                ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.UPDATE,
                periodicSync
            )
    }

    class="cm">// Chaining workers
    fun scheduleChainedWork() {
        val downloadWork = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<DownloadWorker>().build()
        val processWork = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<ProcessWorker>().build()
        val uploadWork = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<UploadWorker>().build()

        class="cm">// Sequential chain: download → process → upload
        WorkManager.getInstance(context)
            .beginWith(downloadWork)
            .then(processWork)
            .then(uploadWork)
            .enqueue()
    }

    class="cm">// Parallel then sequential
    fun scheduleParallelWork() {
        val fetchArticles = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<FetchArticlesWorker>().build()
        val fetchUsers = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<FetchUsersWorker>().build()
        val mergeWork = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<MergeDataWorker>().build()

        class="cm">// fetchArticles + fetchUsers run in PARALLEL, then mergeWork runs
        WorkManager.getInstance(context)
            .beginWith(listOf(fetchArticles, fetchUsers))
            .then(mergeWork)
            .enqueue()
    }

    class="cm">// Observing work status
    fun observeSync(workId: UUID): Flow<WorkInfo> {
        return WorkManager.getInstance(context)
            .getWorkInfoByIdFlow(workId)
    }

    class="cm">// Expedited work (API 31+)
    fun scheduleExpedited(userId: String) {
        val request = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
            .setInputData(workDataOf(class="st">"USER_ID" to userId))
            .setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST)
            .build()

        WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueue(request)
    }
}

    3. FOREGROUND SERVICES

    Foreground Service = visible ongoing operation (notification required).


    Use cases: Music playback, navigation, file upload/download, fitness tracking.


    API 34+ Changes:

    - Must declare foreground service TYPE in manifest

    - Types: camera, dataSync, health, location, mediaPlayback, mediaProjection, microphone, phoneCall, remoteMessaging, shortService, specialUse

    - Must have corresponding permission for each type


    ⚠️ API 35+: dataSync type has a 6-hour time limit. Use WorkManager for longer sync operations.

    class MusicPlaybackService : Service() {

    private var mediaPlayer: MediaPlayer? = null

    override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
        val notification = createNotification()

        class="cm">// Must call within 5 seconds of startForegroundService()
        startForeground(NOTIFICATION_ID, notification)

        when (intent?.action) {
            ACTION_PLAY -> startPlayback(intent.getStringExtra(class="st">"TRACK_URL"))
            ACTION_PAUSE -> pausePlayback()
            ACTION_STOP -> {
                stopPlayback()
                stopForeground(STOP_FOREGROUND_REMOVE)
                stopSelf()
            }
        }

        return START_STICKY  class="cm">// Restart if killed by system
    }

    override fun onBind(intent: Intent?): IBinder? = null

    private fun createNotification(): Notification {
        val channel = NotificationChannel(
            class="st">"music_playback", class="st">"Music Playback",
            NotificationManager.IMPORTANCE_LOW
        )
        val notificationManager = getSystemService(NotificationManager::class.java)
        notificationManager.createNotificationChannel(channel)

        return NotificationCompat.Builder(this, class="st">"music_playback")
            .setContentTitle(class="st">"Playing music")
            .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_music)
            .addAction(R.drawable.ic_pause, class="st">"Pause", pausePendingIntent)
            .addAction(R.drawable.ic_stop, class="st">"Stop", stopPendingIntent)
            .setStyle(
                androidx.media.app.NotificationCompat.MediaStyle()
                    .setShowActionsInCompactView(0, 1)
            )
            .build()
    }

    companion object {
        const val NOTIFICATION_ID = 2001
        const val ACTION_PLAY = class="st">"PLAY"
        const val ACTION_PAUSE = class="st">"PAUSE"
        const val ACTION_STOP = class="st">"STOP"
    }
}

    Service types and their return values:


    START_STICKY → restart with null Intent if killed (music player)

    START_NOT_STICKY → don't restart if killed (one-time operation) START_REDELIVER_INTENT → restart with last Intent (file download)

    4. BROADCAST RECEIVERS

    BroadcastReceiver listens for system-wide or app-specific events.


    Registration:

    Manifest-declared → survives app death (limited since API 26) Context-registered → lives as long as registering component


    API 26+ restrictions:

    Most implicit broadcasts can NOT be manifest-declared. Exceptions: BOOT_COMPLETED, LOCALE_CHANGED, MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED Use WorkManager or context-registered receivers instead.

    class="cm">// ✅ Modern approach: NetworkCallback (replaces deprecated CONNECTIVITY_ACTION)
class NetworkConnectivityObserver(context: Context) {

    private val connectivityManager =
        context.getSystemService(Context.CONNECTIVITY_SERVICE) as ConnectivityManager

    val isOnline: Flow<Boolean> = callbackFlow {
        val callback = object : ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback() {
            override fun onAvailable(network: Network) { trySend(true) }
            override fun onLost(network: Network) { trySend(false) }
        }

        val request = NetworkRequest.Builder()
            .addCapability(NetworkCapabilities.NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET)
            .build()
        connectivityManager.registerNetworkCallback(request, callback)

        class="cm">// Emit current state
        val currentNetwork = connectivityManager.activeNetwork
        val capabilities = connectivityManager.getNetworkCapabilities(currentNetwork)
        trySend(capabilities?.hasCapability(NetworkCapabilities.NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET) == true)

        awaitClose { connectivityManager.unregisterNetworkCallback(callback) }
    }.distinctUntilChanged()
}

class="cm">// Usage in ViewModel — schedule sync when connectivity returns
class ConnectivityAwareViewModel(
    private val networkObserver: NetworkConnectivityObserver,
    private val workManager: WorkManager
) : ViewModel() {
    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            networkObserver.isOnline
                .filter { it }  class="cm">// Only when connected
                .collect {
                    workManager.enqueueUniqueWork(
                        class="st">"connectivity_sync",
                        ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP,
                        OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>().build()
                    )
                }
        }
    }
}

    ⚠️ ConnectivityManager.CONNECTIVITY_ACTION is deprecated (API 28+). Always use NetworkCallback + callbackFlow for modern connectivity monitoring. See also: 06_networking.kt → NetworkMonitor for a complete implementation.

    Local Broadcasts (deprecated):

    LocalBroadcastManager was deprecated in favor of:

    - SharedFlow / StateFlow for in-app events

    - LiveData for lifecycle-aware observation These are more efficient (no IPC overhead).

    5. BACKGROUND EXECUTION LIMITS

    API 26+ Background Execution Limits:

    - Background services stopped ~1 minute after app goes to background

    - Most implicit broadcasts can't be manifest-registered

    - Background location limited to a few times per hour


    API 28+ App Standby Buckets restrict:

    - Job scheduling frequency

    - Alarm execution

    - Network access

    - FCM message priority


    API 31+ Exact Alarm Restrictions:

    - Need SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM permission (user can revoke)

    - Or USE_EXACT_ALARM (for alarm/timer apps, auto-granted)


    API 34+ Foreground Service Restrictions:

    - Must declare foreground service type

    - BOOT_COMPLETED receiver can't launch foreground services for some types


    💡 Interview Strategy: Always mention these restrictions when discussing background work. Shows awareness of real-world Android constraints.

    6. ALARMMANAGER

    AlarmManager fires an Intent at a specified time, even if the app is not running.


    Clock types:

    RTC → wall-clock time, does NOT wake device

    RTC_WAKEUP → wall-clock time, WAKES device

    ELAPSED_REALTIME → time since boot, does NOT wake device ELAPSED_REALTIME_WAKEUP → time since boot, WAKES device


    Scheduling methods:

    set() → inexact, batched with other alarms (API 19+)

    setExact() → exact time, but deferred during Doze setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() → exact time, fires even in Doze (limited to ~1/9 min)

    setAlarmClock() → treated as user-visible alarm clock; always fires, shows alarm icon in status bar


    Permissions (API 31+):

    SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM → required for setExact / setExactAndAllowWhileIdle user can revoke in Settings → Alarms & Reminders

    USE_EXACT_ALARM → for alarm clock / timer apps (auto-granted, not revocable)


    ⚠️ Always check canScheduleExactAlarms() before scheduling on API 31+. If revoked, fall back to inexact or guide user to Settings.


    AlarmManagerCompat (Jetpack) provides backward-compatible helpers:

    AlarmManagerCompat.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(alarmManager, type, triggerAt, pi)


    When to use AlarmManager vs WorkManager:

    AlarmManager → exact-time delivery matters (medication reminders, alarm clocks)

    WorkManager → task must complete but timing is flexible (sync, uploads)


    Interview Tip: 💡 "I use AlarmManager only when the user expects something

    at a precise time. For everything else, WorkManager is the better choice."

    class="cm">// Reminder alarm example
class ReminderAlarmScheduler(private val context: Context) {

    fun scheduleReminder(reminderId: Int, triggerAtMillis: Long, title: String) {
        val alarmManager = context.getSystemService(Context.ALARM_SERVICE) as AlarmManager

        val intent = Intent(context, ReminderReceiver::class.java).apply {
            putExtra(class="st">"REMINDER_ID", reminderId)
            putExtra(class="st">"TITLE", title)
        }
        val pendingIntent = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(
            context, reminderId, intent,
            PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
        )

        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.S) {
            class="cm">// API 31+: check permission before scheduling exact alarm
            if (alarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms()) {
                alarmManager.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(
                    AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, triggerAtMillis, pendingIntent
                )
            } else {
                class="cm">// Guide user to Settings or fall back to inexact
                alarmManager.setAndAllowWhileIdle(
                    AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, triggerAtMillis, pendingIntent
                )
            }
        } else {
            AlarmManagerCompat.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(
                alarmManager, AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, triggerAtMillis, pendingIntent
            )
        }
    }

    fun cancelReminder(reminderId: Int) {
        val alarmManager = context.getSystemService(Context.ALARM_SERVICE) as AlarmManager
        val intent = Intent(context, ReminderReceiver::class.java)
        val pendingIntent = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(
            context, reminderId, intent,
            PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
        )
        alarmManager.cancel(pendingIntent)
    }
}

class ReminderReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
        val title = intent.getStringExtra(class="st">"TITLE") ?: class="st">"Reminder"
        val reminderId = intent.getIntExtra(class="st">"REMINDER_ID", 0)

        val notification = NotificationCompat.Builder(context, class="st">"reminders")
            .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_reminder)
            .setContentTitle(title)
            .setPriority(NotificationCompat.PRIORITY_HIGH)
            .setAutoCancel(true)
            .build()

        val manager = context.getSystemService(Context.NOTIFICATION_SERVICE) as NotificationManager
        manager.notify(reminderId, notification)
    }
}

    7. FIREBASE CLOUD MESSAGING (FCM)

    FCM delivers push messages from your server to the device.


    Message types:

      ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Type             │ Behavior                                        │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Notification msg │ System tray auto-display when app is background │
  │                  │ onMessageReceived() ONLY when app is foreground │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Data message     │ Always delivered to onMessageReceived()         │
  │                  │ App handles display/processing in ALL states    │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Both (combined)  │ Notification shown by system in background,     │
  │                  │ data payload in intent extras of launcher       │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    Priority:

    HIGH → wake device immediately, bypass Doze for up to ~10 seconds (quota-limited; overuse downgrades to NORMAL) NORMAL → delivered on next maintenance window during Doze


    Topic messaging:

    Subscribe: FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().subscribeToTopic("news") Server sends to "/topics/news" — delivered to all subscribers.


    FCM + Doze:

    - HIGH priority messages can wake the device during Doze

    - Limited to ~10 high-priority messages per hour per app

    - Use high priority only for user-visible, time-sensitive messages


    Interview Tip: ⚠️ "I always use data-only messages for full control.

    Notification messages are convenient but you lose control when the app is in the background."

            }

        class="cm">// Notification messages when app is in FOREGROUND
        message.notification?.let { notification ->
            showNotification(notification.title ?: class="st">"", notification.body ?: class="st">"")
        }
    }
