    8. FOREGROUND SERVICE LAUNCH RESTRICTIONS (API 31+)

    Starting with API 31 (Android 12), apps CANNOT start a foreground service from the background. Doing so throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException.


    Exemptions (cases where background FGS launch IS allowed):

    ✅ User taps a notification (PendingIntent with FROM_NOTIFICATION)

    ✅ Alarm callback (setAlarmClock, or exact alarm with SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM)

    ✅ HIGH-priority FCM message (within ~10 second window)

    ✅ Device owner / profile owner apps

    ✅ App is in the temporary allowlist (system-granted)

    ✅ Companion device manager role

    ✅ BOOT_COMPLETED for some FGS types (but NOT all — e.g., not mediaPlayback)


    BroadcastReceiver restrictions:

    - Manifest-declared receivers that fire in background CANNOT start FGS

    - Context-registered receivers CAN start FGS if the app is still "visible"

    - BOOT_COMPLETED is an exception but has type-specific limitations


    Recommended alternatives:

    1. WorkManager with setExpedited() — runs immediately, short-lived

    2. Show notification first, let user tap to trigger FGS

    3. Use setAlarmClock() to get into the allowlist for time-critical work


    API 34+ additional restrictions:

    - Must declare foregroundServiceType in manifest

    - Specific permissions required per type

    - dataSync type has 6-hour limit (API 35+)


    Interview Tip: 💡 "On API 31+, I default to WorkManager expedited work for

    urgent background tasks. I only use FGS when the user explicitly triggers the action from the foreground or through a notification."

    class="cm">// Handling FGS restriction: prefer WorkManager expedited for background-started work
class BackgroundTaskHandler(private val context: Context) {

    fun handleUrgentTask(taskData: String) {
        if (isAppInForeground()) {
            class="cm">// Safe to start FGS from foreground
            val intent = Intent(context, UploadService::class.java).apply {
                putExtra(class="st">"DATA", taskData)
            }
            ContextCompat.startForegroundService(context, intent)
        } else {
            class="cm">// Background: use WorkManager expedited instead
            val request = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<UploadWorker>()
                .setInputData(workDataOf(class="st">"DATA" to taskData))
                .setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST)
                .build()
            WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueue(request)
        }
    }

    private fun isAppInForeground(): Boolean {
        val activityManager = context.getSystemService(Context.ACTIVITY_SERVICE) as ActivityManager
        val appProcesses = activityManager.runningAppProcesses ?: return false
        return appProcesses.any {
            it.importance == ActivityManager.RunningAppProcessInfo.IMPORTANCE_FOREGROUND &&
                it.processName == context.packageName
        }
    }
}

    ⚠️ Common mistake: catching ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException and silently ignoring it. The work never runs. Always have a fallback.


    Pattern for FCM-triggered FGS:

    1. Receive HIGH-priority FCM data message

    2. In onMessageReceived(), you have ~10 seconds

    3. Call startForegroundService() within that window

    4. If the window is missed, fall back to WorkManager

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: How would you implement a photo upload that survives app kill? A: Use WorkManager with CoroutineWorker. Constraints: NetworkType.CONNECTED Pass photo URI as input data. Show progress via setForeground() notification. Use unique work to prevent duplicate uploads. Chain: compress → upload → cleanup.


    Q2: WorkManager vs JobScheduler vs AlarmManager — when to use each? A: WorkManager: Almost all persistent background work. Abstracts over JobScheduler/AlarmManager. Constraint-based, chainable, observable. JobScheduler: Direct API for scheduled work (WorkManager uses this internally). AlarmManager: Only for exact-time requirements (actual alarm clock, reminders).


    Q3: What happens to a Foreground Service when the user force-stops the app? A: It's killed immediately. START_STICKY won't restart it. Force-stop also cancels WorkManager, AlarmManager, and kills the process. Only BOOT_COMPLETED or FCM can restart components after force-stop.


    Q4: How do you handle WorkManager work that depends on previous work's output? A: Chain workers with then(). Output data from one worker becomes input data for the next. For parallel work merging, use InputMerger (ArrayCreatingInputMerger or OverwritingInputMerger).


    Q5: What's the difference between expedited work and foreground service? A: Expedited work: short-lived, high priority, runs even under Doze. Has a quota (OS limits how often). Falls back to regular work if exceeded. Foreground Service: long-running, visible to user via notification. No time limit (except dataSync type on API 35+).


    Q6: What's the difference between FCM data messages and notification messages? A: Data messages: always delivered to onMessageReceived() regardless of app state. You have full control over parsing, display, and behavior. Notification messages: system auto-displays when app is in background. onMessageReceived() only fires in foreground. Combined messages get notification in background and data in the launcher intent's extras — easy to miss. Best practice: use data-only messages for full control in production apps.


    Q7: How do you handle starting a Foreground Service from the background on API 31+? A: You can't — it throws ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException. Solutions: (1) Use WorkManager with setExpedited() for urgent short-lived tasks. (2) Show a notification and let the user tap to start the FGS (FROM_NOTIFICATION). (3) Use a high-priority FCM message — gives ~10 seconds to call startForegroundService(). (4) For alarm-like use cases, setAlarmClock() puts the app on the temporary allowlist. Always have a WorkManager fallback — never silently fail.

    1. WHY DI MATTERS

    Dependency Injection = providing an object's dependencies from the outside rather than the object creating them itself.


    Benefits:

    ✅ Testability — swap real implementations with fakes/mocks

    ✅ Loose coupling — classes don't know about concrete implementations

    ✅ Reusability — same class works with different dependencies

    ✅ Scoping — control object lifetime (singleton, per-screen, etc.)

    ✅ Separation of concerns — class focuses on its job, not creation of deps


    Without DI:

    class="cm">// ❌ Tight coupling — hard to test, hard to change
class BadRepository {
    private val api = RetrofitClient.create(ArticleApi::class.java)  class="cm">// Hardcoded
    private val db = Room.databaseBuilder(class="cm">/*...*/).build()           class="cm">// Hardcoded
}

class="cm">// ✅ Dependencies injected — testable, flexible
class GoodRepository(
    private val api: ArticleApi,         class="cm">// Interface — can be faked
    private val dao: ArticleDao,         class="cm">// Interface — can be faked
    private val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher  class="cm">// Can use TestDispatcher
)

    2. HILT — COMPLETE SETUP

    Hilt = Google's recommended DI framework for Android. Built on top of Dagger 2. Reduces boilerplate significantly.


    Setup requires:

    1. @HiltAndroidApp on Application class

    2. @AndroidEntryPoint on Activities, Fragments, Services

    3. @Inject on constructors (for classes) or @Module + @Provides (for 3rd party)

    4. @HiltViewModel on ViewModels

    class="cm">// Step 1: Application
class="an">@HiltAndroidApp
class MyApplication : Application()

    class="an">@Provides

    3. HILT SCOPING & COMPONENTS

    Hilt Component Hierarchy:


    SingletonComponent → Application lifetime ↓ ActivityRetainedComponent → ViewModel lifetime (survives config change) ↓

    ViewModelComponent → ViewModel instance lifetime ↓

    ActivityComponent → Activity lifetime ↓

    FragmentComponent → Fragment lifetime ↓

    ViewComponent → View lifetime ↓ ViewWithFragmentComponent → View in Fragment lifetime


    Also: ServiceComponent (parallel to ActivityComponent)


    Scope annotations:

    @Singleton → one instance for entire app @ActivityRetainedScoped → one per Activity (survives config change)

    @ViewModelScoped → one per ViewModel instance

    @ActivityScoped → one per Activity instance

    @FragmentScoped → one per Fragment instance


    ⚠️ Default (no scope): new instance every time it's injected. This is often what you want for lightweight classes.

    Qualifier annotations for providing different instances of same type

    class="an">@Qualifier
class="an">@Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY)
annotation class IoDispatcher

class="an">@Qualifier
class="an">@Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY)
annotation class DefaultDispatcher

class="an">@Qualifier
class="an">@Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY)
annotation class MainDispatcher

class="an">@Module
class="an">@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object DispatcherModule {
    class="an">@Provides
    class="an">@IoDispatcher
    fun provideIoDispatcher(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO

    class="an">@Provides
    class="an">@DefaultDispatcher
    fun provideDefaultDispatcher(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default

    class="an">@Provides
    class="an">@MainDispatcher
    fun provideMainDispatcher(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Main
}

    4. HILT + VIEWMODEL, WORKMANAGER, COMPOSE

    class="cm">// ViewModel with Hilt
class="an">@HiltViewModel
class ArticleViewModel class="an">@Inject constructor(
    private val getArticlesUseCase: GetArticlesUseCase,
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle  class="cm">// Auto-provided by Hilt
) : ViewModel() {

    val searchQuery = savedStateHandle.getStateFlow(class="st">"query", class="st">"")

    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(ArticleUiState())

    fun search(query: String) {

class="cm">// WorkManager with Hilt
class="an">@HiltWorker
class SyncWorker class="an">@AssistedInject constructor(
    class="an">@Assisted context: Context,
    class="an">@Assisted params: WorkerParameters,
    private val repository: ArticleRepository  class="cm">// Injected by Hilt
) : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {

    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        return try {
            repository.sync()
            Result.success()
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            Result.retry()
        }
    }
}

    5. DAGGER 2 FUNDAMENTALS

    Hilt is built on Dagger 2. Knowing Dagger helps understand Hilt internals.


    Key Dagger concepts:


    @Component → interface that connects @Module providers with @Inject consumers

    @Module → class that provides dependencies

    @Provides → method in Module that creates an instance

    @Binds → abstract method that binds an interface to implementation

    @Inject → marks constructor or field for injection

    @Scope → controls instance lifetime @Subcomponent → child component that inherits from parent


    Dagger generates code at compile time (no reflection = fast).


    Hilt eliminates the need to:

    - Create Component interfaces manually

    - Write Component.Factory or Component.Builder

    - Manage component hierarchy

    - Inject into Activities/Fragments manually


    Interview Question: What's the difference between @Provides and @Binds? @Provides: creates instances, can have logic, returns concrete type @Binds: maps interface to implementation, no instance creation, must be abstract @Binds is more efficient (generates less code)

    6. MANUAL DI (WITHOUT FRAMEWORK)

    For small apps or when asked "how would you do DI without Hilt/Dagger?"


    Pattern: Service Locator or Manual Constructor Injection

    class="cm">// Manual DI container
class AppContainer(private val context: Context) {

    class="cm">// Singletons
    private val json: Json by lazy {
        Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }
    }

    private val okHttpClient: OkHttpClient by lazy {
        OkHttpClient.Builder()
            .connectTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .build()
    }

    private val retrofit: Retrofit by lazy {
        Retrofit.Builder()
            .baseUrl(class="st">"https:class="cm">//api.example.com/v1/")
            .client(okHttpClient)
            .build()
    }

    private val database: AppDatabase by lazy {
        Room.databaseBuilder(context, AppDatabase::class.java, class="st">"app_db").build()
    }

    class="cm">// Provide dependencies
    val articleApi: ArticleApi by lazy { retrofit.create(ArticleApi::class.java) }
    val articleDao: ArticleDao by lazy { database.articleDao() }

    val articleRepository: ArticleRepository by lazy {
        ArticleRepositoryImpl(articleApi, articleDao, Dispatchers.IO)
    }

    val getArticlesUseCase: GetArticlesUseCase by lazy {
        GetArticlesUseCase(articleRepository)
    }
}

class="cm">// Usage in Application class
class ManualDIApplication : Application() {
    val container by lazy { AppContainer(this) }
}

    8. @ENTRYPOINT — ACCESSING HILT FROM NON-HILT CLASSES

    @EntryPoint lets you access Hilt-managed dependencies from classes that Hilt does NOT inject into (ContentProvider, legacy code, third-party libraries).


    Why needed:

    - Hilt only injects into @AndroidEntryPoint-annotated Android classes

    - ContentProvider is created BEFORE Application.onCreate() — Hilt isn't ready

    - Some classes are instantiated by the framework, not by you


    Pattern:

    1. Define an @EntryPoint interface inside the consuming class

    2. Annotate it with @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)

    3. Access it via EntryPointAccessors.fromApplication()


    ⚠️ Use sparingly. If you find yourself using @EntryPoint often, the class should probably be refactored to use constructor injection instead.

    class ArticleContentProvider : ContentProvider() {

    class="cm">// Step 1: Declare what you need from the Hilt graph
    class="an">@EntryPoint
    class="an">@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
    interface ArticleContentProviderEntryPoint {
        fun articleRepository(): ArticleRepository
        fun json(): Json
    }

    private lateinit var repository: ArticleRepository
    private lateinit var json: Json

    override fun onCreate(): Boolean {
        class="cm">// Step 2: Access the Hilt graph via EntryPointAccessors
        val entryPoint = EntryPointAccessors.fromApplication(
            context!!.applicationContext,
            ArticleContentProviderEntryPoint::class.java
        )
        repository = entryPoint.articleRepository()
        json = entryPoint.json()
        return true
    }

    override fun query(
        uri: Uri, projection: Array<String>?, selection: String?,
        selectionArgs: Array<String>?, sortOrder: String?
    ): Cursor? {
        class="cm">// Use injected repository to serve data
        return null class="cm">// Implementation depends on URI matching
    }

    override fun getType(uri: Uri): String? = null
    override fun insert(uri: Uri, values: ContentValues?): Uri? = null
    override fun delete(uri: Uri, sel: String?, args: Array<String>?): Int = 0
    override fun update(uri: Uri, values: ContentValues?, sel: String?, args: Array<String>?): Int = 0
}
    Interview Tip: 💡 "@EntryPoint is the escape hatch when you can't use

    constructor injection. ContentProvider is the most common use case because it's created before the Hilt component is ready."

    9. MULTI-MODULE DI

    Hilt in multi-module projects:


    Structure:

    :app → @HiltAndroidApp, @AndroidEntryPoint

    :core:network → NetworkModule (@InstallIn SingletonComponent)

    :core:database → DatabaseModule (@InstallIn SingletonComponent) :feature:articles → ArticleViewModel, feature-scoped modules


    Key rules:


    1. Each module defines its own @Module classes with @InstallIn. Hilt's annotation processor aggregates all modules at compile time.


    2. The :app module must depend on all modules (directly or transitively) for Hilt to see their @Module and @EntryPoint annotations.


    3. api vs implementation for DI modules:

    - Use api if the module exposes types that other modules inject (e.g., :core:network provides OkHttpClient used by :feature:articles)

    - Use implementation if the module's bindings are internal only

    - Rule of thumb: interfaces go in api, implementations in implementation


    4. Avoiding duplicate singletons:

    - @Singleton in :core:network guarantees one instance app-wide

    - If two feature modules each provide their own OkHttpClient, you get duplicates. Centralize shared singletons in :core modules.

    - Use @Qualifier to differentiate when you intentionally want multiple instances (e.g., authenticated vs unauthenticated OkHttpClient)


    5. Interface + implementation split:

    - Define interface in a :core:data-api module (no Hilt dependency)

    - Provide implementation in :core:data-impl with @Binds

    - Feature modules depend only on :core:data-api


    ⚠️ Common pitfall: using @InstallIn(ActivityComponent::class) in a library module. Library modules should almost always use SingletonComponent or ActivityRetainedComponent to avoid lifecycle assumptions.

    class="cm">// :core:network module
class="an">@Module
class="an">@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object CoreNetworkModule {

    class="an">@Provides
    class="an">@Singleton
    fun provideOkHttpClient(): OkHttpClient {
        return OkHttpClient.Builder()
            .connectTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .readTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .build()
    }

    class="an">@Provides
    class="an">@Singleton
    class="an">@Qualifier
    annotation class AuthenticatedClient

    class="an">@Provides
    class="an">@Singleton
    class="an">@AuthenticatedClient
    fun provideAuthenticatedClient(
        authInterceptor: AuthInterceptor
    ): OkHttpClient {
        return OkHttpClient.Builder()
            .addInterceptor(authInterceptor)
            .connectTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .build()
    }
}

class="cm">// :feature:articles module — depends on :core:network via api/implementation
class="an">@Module
class="an">@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object ArticleNetworkModule {

    class="an">@Provides
    class="an">@Singleton
    fun provideArticleApi(
        class="an">@AuthenticatedClient okHttpClient: OkHttpClient
    ): ArticleApi {
        return Retrofit.Builder()
            .baseUrl(class="st">"https:class="cm">//api.example.com/v1/")
            .client(okHttpClient)
            .build()
            .create(ArticleApi::class.java)
    }
}
    Interview Tip: 💡 "In multi-module projects, I keep shared singletons

    in :core modules and use @Qualifier when multiple instances of the same type are needed. Feature modules only declare feature-scoped bindings."

    10. WORKMANAGER + HILT CONFIGURATION

    @HiltWorker requires custom WorkManager initialization because Hilt needs to supply its own WorkerFactory to inject dependencies into Workers.


    Steps:

    1. Disable default WorkManager initializer in AndroidManifest

    2. Implement Configuration.Provider in your Application class

    3. Inject HiltWorkerFactory and return it in workManagerConfiguration

    4. Annotate your Worker with @HiltWorker and use @AssistedInject


    Why custom initialization? Default WorkManager uses the built-in WorkerFactory that only knows how to call Worker(context, params). @HiltWorker needs additional constructor params (your injected dependencies), which only HiltWorkerFactory can provide.

    class="cm">// Step 1: Disable default initializer in AndroidManifest.xml
class="cm">/*
<provider
    android:name=class="st">"androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"
    android:authorities=class="st">"${applicationId}.androidx-startup"
    android:exported=class="st">"false"
    tools:node=class="st">"merge">
    <meta-data
        android:name=class="st">"androidx.work.WorkManagerInitializer"
        android:value=class="st">"androidx.startup"
        tools:node=class="st">"remove" />
</provider>
*/

class="cm">// Step 2: Application class with custom WorkManager config
class="an">@HiltAndroidApp
class MyApp : Application(), Configuration.Provider {

    class="an">@Inject
    lateinit var workerFactory: HiltWorkerFactory

    override val workManagerConfiguration: Configuration
        get() = Configuration.Builder()
            .setWorkerFactory(workerFactory)
            .setMinimumLoggingLevel(
                if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) android.util.Log.DEBUG
                else android.util.Log.ERROR
            )
            .build()
}

class="cm">// Step 3: Worker with class="an">@HiltWorker
class="an">@HiltWorker
class ArticleSyncWorker class="an">@AssistedInject constructor(
    class="an">@Assisted context: Context,
    class="an">@Assisted params: WorkerParameters,
    private val repository: ArticleRepository,
    private val notificationHelper: NotificationHelper
) : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {

    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        return try {
            val count = repository.syncAll()
            if (count > 0) {
                notificationHelper.showSyncComplete(count)
            }
            Result.success()
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            if (runAttemptCount < 3) Result.retry() else Result.failure()
        }
    }

    override suspend fun getForegroundInfo(): ForegroundInfo {
        val notification = notificationHelper.buildSyncProgressNotification()
        return ForegroundInfo(SYNC_NOTIFICATION_ID, notification)
    }

    companion object {
        const val SYNC_NOTIFICATION_ID = 3001
    }
}

    ⚠️ Common mistake: forgetting to disable the default initializer. WorkManager will crash at runtime with "WorkManager is already initialized" because both the default and custom initializers try to run.


    Interview Tip: 💡 "The three pieces to remember for @HiltWorker are:

    disable the default initializer, implement Configuration.Provider, and use @AssistedInject with @Assisted for context and params."

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: What's the difference between @Singleton and no scope in Hilt? A: @Singleton: one instance for entire app lifetime (cached in SingletonComponent). No scope: new instance created every time it's injected. Use @Singleton for expensive objects (OkHttpClient, Database). Use no scope for lightweight objects (UseCases, mappers).


    Q2: How does Hilt handle ViewModel creation? A: @HiltViewModel + @Inject constructor. Hilt generates a custom ViewModelProvider.Factory that creates the ViewModel with injected dependencies. SavedStateHandle is auto-provided.


    Q3: When would you use @Binds vs @Provides? A: @Binds when mapping interface → implementation (no logic needed). @Provides when: creating 3rd party objects, complex creation logic, or when the module isn't abstract. @Binds generates less code.


    Q4: How do you provide different implementations for debug/release? A: Create separate modules in debug/ and release/ source sets. Or use @Qualifier annotations with different @Provides methods. Or use Hilt's @TestInstallIn to replace modules in tests.


    Q5: What's the advantage of Dagger/Hilt over Koin? A: Dagger/Hilt: compile-time validation (catches errors at build time), no runtime overhead (generated code), better performance. Koin: simpler setup, DSL-based, runtime resolution (errors at runtime), slight runtime overhead. Google recommends Hilt for production apps.


    Q6: What is @EntryPoint and when would you use it? A: @EntryPoint is an interface annotated with @InstallIn that lets you access Hilt-managed dependencies from classes Hilt doesn't inject into. Primary use case: ContentProvider (created before Application.onCreate()). Also useful for legacy code, third-party library callbacks, or any class where you can't use @Inject constructor. Access it via EntryPointAccessors.fromApplication(). Use sparingly — prefer refactoring to constructor injection when possible.


    Q7: How does Hilt work in a multi-module Gradle project? A: Each module defines its own @Module + @InstallIn classes. Hilt's annotation processor aggregates all modules at compile time in the :app module. Shared singletons (OkHttpClient, Database) belong in :core modules. Use @Qualifier to differentiate multiple instances of the same type. Use api dependency for types other modules inject, implementation for internal-only bindings. Avoid @InstallIn(ActivityComponent) in libraries — use SingletonComponent or ActivityRetainedComponent instead.

    1. TESTING PYRAMID & STRATEGY

    Testing Pyramid (bottom to top):


    / E2E Tests \ ← Slow, flaky, few / Integration \ ← Medium speed, moderate / Unit Tests \ ← Fast, reliable, many /___________________\


    Google's recommendation for Android:

    70% Unit Tests → ViewModel, Repository, UseCase, utils

    20% Integration → Screen tests, Navigation, Room + DAO

    10% E2E Tests → Critical user flows


    Key principles:

    - Test behavior, not implementation

    - Tests should be fast, reliable, and independent

    - One assertion per test (when practical)

    - Test names describe the scenario and expected outcome

    - Use Given-When-Then or Arrange-Act-Assert pattern

    2. UNIT TESTING FUNDAMENTALS

    Tools:

    JUnit 4/5 → test framework

    MockK → mocking library (Kotlin-friendly)

    Truth → assertion library (Google)

    Turbine → Flow testing library kotlinx-coroutines-test → coroutine testing utilities

    class="cm">// Basic unit test structure
class ArticleMapperTest {

    class="an">@Test

        class="cm">// Arrange
        val response = ArticleResponse(
            id = class="st">"123",
            title = class="st">"Kotlin Coroutines",
            content = class="st">"Deep dive into coroutines",
            authorName = class="st">"John",
            publishedAt = 1700000000000,
            tags = listOf(class="st">"kotlin", class="st">"android")
        )

        class="cm">// Act
        val entity = response.toEntity()

        class="cm">// Assert
        assertEquals(class="st">"123", entity.id)
        assertEquals(class="st">"Kotlin Coroutines", entity.title)
        assertEquals(class="st">"John", entity.authorName)
        assertEquals(2, entity.tags.size)
    }

    class="an">@Test

        val response = ArticleResponse(
            id = class="st">"123",
            title = class="st">"Title",
            content = class="st">"Content",
            authorName = class="st">"Author",
            publishedAt = 0,
            tags = emptyList(),
            readTimeMinutes = null
        )

        val entity = response.toEntity()

        assertEquals(0, entity.readTimeMinutes)
    }
}

            val loading = awaitItem()
            assertTrue(loading.isLoading)

            class="cm">// Then success

        fakeDao.insertAll(stale)

    5. TESTING COROUTINES & FLOWS

    Key testing utilities:


    runTest { } → runs test with virtual time (no real delays)

    advanceUntilIdle() → advance all pending coroutines

    advanceTimeBy(ms) → advance virtual clock by specific amount StandardTestDispatcher() → manual advancement (deterministic) UnconfinedTestDispatcher → immediate execution (less control)

    Turbine (.test { }) → structured Flow testing with assertions

    class FlowTestExample {

    class="an">@Test
    fun `debounced search flow emits correct results`() = runTest {
        val searchFlow = MutableSharedFlow<String>()
        val resultFlow = searchFlow
            .debounce(300)
            .filter { it.length >= 2 }
            .distinctUntilChanged()
            .map { query -> class="st">"Results for: $query" }

        resultFlow.test {
            searchFlow.emit(class="st">"k")       class="cm">// Too short, filtered
            searchFlow.emit(class="st">"ko")      class="cm">// Will be debounced
            searchFlow.emit(class="st">"kot")     class="cm">// Replaces class="st">"ko" during debounce

            advanceTimeBy(301)

            assertEquals(class="st">"Results for: kot", awaitItem())

            searchFlow.emit(class="st">"kot")     class="cm">// Same value, distinctUntilChanged skips
            advanceTimeBy(301)
            expectNoEvents()           class="cm">// No emission

            searchFlow.emit(class="st">"kotlin")
            advanceTimeBy(301)
            assertEquals(class="st">"Results for: kotlin", awaitItem())

            cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// MainDispatcherRule for ViewModel tests
class MainDispatcherRule(
    private val testDispatcher: TestDispatcher = UnconfinedTestDispatcher()
) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(description: Description) {
        Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher)
    }
    override fun finished(description: Description) {
        Dispatchers.resetMain()
    }
}

    6. UI TESTING — ESPRESSO

    Espresso = UI testing framework for the View system.


    Core API:

    onView(matcher) → find a view

    .perform(action) → interact with it

    .check(assertion) → verify its state

    class="an">@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class ArticleListFragmentTest {

    class="an">@get:Rule
    val activityRule = ActivityScenarioRule(MainActivity::class.java)

    7. UI TESTING — COMPOSE

    Compose Testing API:

    composeTestRule.onNodeWithText("text") → find by text

    .onNodeWithTag("tag") → find by test tag

    .onNodeWithContentDescription("desc") → find by accessibility

    .performClick() → click action

    .performTextInput("text") → type text

    .assertIsDisplayed() → visibility check

    .assertTextEquals("text") → text content check

    8. FAKES VS MOCKS

    Google prefers FAKES over MOCKS.


    Fake:

    - Working implementation with shortcuts (in-memory DB, static data)

    - Tests behavior, not implementation details

    - Reusable across tests

    - More resilient to refactoring


    Mock:

    - Verifies method calls and arguments

    - Tightly coupled to implementation

    - Brittle — breaks when implementation changes

    - Good for verifying interactions (e.g., analytics calls)


    Interview Tip: 💡 "I prefer fakes for data-providing dependencies

    (repositories, APIs, DAOs) and mocks for verifying interactions (analytics, logging, notifications)."

    class="cm">// Fake Repository
class FakeArticleRepository : ArticleRepository {
    private val articles = mutableListOf<Article>()
    private val flow = MutableStateFlow<List<Article>>(emptyList())
    private var shouldFail = false
    private var delayMs = 0L

    fun setArticles(list: List<Article>) {
        articles.clear()
        articles.addAll(list)
        flow.value = list
    }

    fun setShouldFail(fail: Boolean) { shouldFail = fail }
    fun setDelay(ms: Long) { delayMs = ms }

    override fun observeArticles(): Flow<List<Article>> = flow

    override suspend fun getArticles(userId: String): List<Article> {
        if (delayMs > 0) delay(delayMs)
        if (shouldFail) throw IOException(class="st">"Fake error")
        return articles.toList()
    }

    override suspend fun refreshArticles(userId: String): List<Article> {
        if (shouldFail) throw IOException(class="st">"Fake error")
        return articles.toList()
    }
}

class="cm">// Using MockK for interaction verification

    class="an">@Test

        tracker.onScreenViewed(class="st">"article_detail")

        verify { analytics.logEvent(class="st">"screen_view", mapOf(class="st">"screen" to class="st">"article_detail")) }
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun `analytics not called for excluded screens`() {
        val tracker = ScreenTracker(analytics)

        tracker.onScreenViewed(class="st">"splash")

        verify(exactly = 0) { analytics.logEvent(any(), any()) }
    }

    9. ROBOLECTRIC

    Robolectric lets you run tests that depend on Android framework classes on the JVM — no emulator or device needed.


    How it works:

    - Provides "shadow" classes that simulate Android framework behavior

    - Intercepts calls to android.* classes and routes them to shadows

    - Runs as a regular JUnit test (in test/ not androidTest/)


    When to use Robolectric vs instrumented tests:

    Robolectric → fast feedback loop, CI-friendly, Activity/Fragment lifecycle tests, testing code that uses Context, SharedPreferences, Resources

    Instrumented → real device behavior, hardware-dependent features, Espresso UI tests, Room with actual SQLite, accurate rendering tests


    Shadow classes:

    - ShadowApplication, ShadowActivity, ShadowLooper, ShadowAlarmManager, etc.

    - You can create custom shadows for your own classes

    - Access via Shadows.shadowOf(instance) to inspect internal state


    Limitations & gotchas:

    ⚠️ Rendering is not pixel-accurate (no real GPU)

    ⚠️ Some native APIs are not fully simulated (camera, Bluetooth)

    ⚠️ Shadow behavior may differ from real Android in edge cases

    ⚠️ Slower startup than pure unit tests (class loading overhead)

    ⚠️ Needs @Config(sdk = [X]) to pin SDK version for consistent behavior


    Interview Tip: 💡 "I use Robolectric when I need Android framework classes

    but want JVM speed. For anything that depends on real device behavior — especially UI rendering and SQLite — I use instrumented tests."

    class="an">@RunWith(RobolectricTestRunner::class)
class="an">@Config(sdk = [34])
class NotificationSchedulerTest {

    private val context: Context = ApplicationProvider.getApplicationContext()

    class="an">@Test
    fun `scheduleReminder sets alarm via AlarmManager`() {
        val alarmManager = context.getSystemService(Context.ALARM_SERVICE) as AlarmManager
        val shadowAlarmManager = Shadows.shadowOf(alarmManager)

        val scheduler = ReminderAlarmScheduler(context)
        val triggerTime = System.currentTimeMillis() + 60_000

        scheduler.scheduleReminder(1, triggerTime, class="st">"Test Reminder")

        val nextAlarm = shadowAlarmManager.nextScheduledAlarm
        assertNotNull(nextAlarm)
        assertEquals(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, nextAlarm.type)
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun `activity launches with correct intent extras`() {
        val intent = Intent(context, ArticleDetailActivity::class.java).apply {
            putExtra(class="st">"ARTICLE_ID", class="st">"123")
        }

        val scenario = ActivityScenario.launch<ArticleDetailActivity>(intent)
        scenario.onActivity { activity ->
            assertEquals(class="st">"123", activity.intent.getStringExtra(class="st">"ARTICLE_ID"))
        }
    }
}

class SharedPreferencesTest {

        val prefs = context.getSharedPreferences(class="st">"settings", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)

    10. ROOM TESTING

    Room testing strategy:


    In-memory database → fast, no disk I/O, auto-cleared between tests MigrationTestHelper → verifies schema migrations don't lose data

    DAO tests → instrumented tests (real SQLite) for accuracy


    Why instrumented (not Robolectric)? Room uses real SQLite under the hood. Robolectric's SQLite shadow can differ in behavior (e.g., foreign key enforcement, WAL mode). Google recommends instrumented tests for Room.


    Interview Tip: 💡 "I always test Room with an in-memory database on a real

    device or emulator to ensure SQLite behavior matches production."

    class="an">@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class ArticleDaoTest {

    private lateinit var database: AppDatabase
    private lateinit var dao: ArticleDao

    class="an">@Before
    fun setup() {
        val context = ApplicationProvider.getApplicationContext<Context>()
        database = Room.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder(context, AppDatabase::class.java)
            .allowMainThreadQueries()  class="cm">// OK for tests only
            .build()
        dao = database.articleDao()
    }

    class="an">@After
    fun tearDown() {
        database.close()
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun insertAndRetrieveArticle() = runTest {
        val article = ArticleEntity(
            id = class="st">"1", title = class="st">"Testing Room", content = class="st">"Content",
            authorName = class="st">"Author", publishedAt = System.currentTimeMillis()
        )

        dao.insert(article)

        val result = dao.getArticleById(class="st">"1")
        assertNotNull(result)
        assertEquals(class="st">"Testing Room", result?.title)
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun upsertReplacesExistingArticle() = runTest {
        val original = ArticleEntity(id = class="st">"1", title = class="st">"Original", content = class="st">"V1")
        val updated = ArticleEntity(id = class="st">"1", title = class="st">"Updated", content = class="st">"V2")

        dao.insert(original)
        dao.upsert(updated)

        val result = dao.getArticleById(class="st">"1")
        assertEquals(class="st">"Updated", result?.title)
        assertEquals(class="st">"V2", result?.content)
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun deleteRemovesArticle() = runTest {
        val article = ArticleEntity(id = class="st">"1", title = class="st">"To Delete", content = class="st">"Content")
        dao.insert(article)

        dao.deleteById(class="st">"1")

        val result = dao.getArticleById(class="st">"1")
        assertNull(result)
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun observeArticlesEmitsOnChange() = runTest {
        dao.observeAll().test {
            assertEquals(emptyList<ArticleEntity>(), awaitItem())

            val article = ArticleEntity(id = class="st">"1", title = class="st">"New", content = class="st">"Content")
            dao.insert(article)

            val updated = awaitItem()
            assertEquals(1, updated.size)
            assertEquals(class="st">"New", updated.first().title)

            cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
        }
    }
}

class="an">@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class MigrationTest {

    class="an">@get:Rule
    val helper = MigrationTestHelper(
        InstrumentationRegistry.getInstrumentation(),
        AppDatabase::class.java.canonicalName,
        FrameworkSQLiteOpenHelperFactory()
    )

    class="an">@Test
    fun migrate1To2() {
        class="cm">// Create database at version 1
        helper.createDatabase(class="st">"test_db", 1).apply {
            execSQL(class="st">"INSERT INTO articles (id, title, content) VALUES ('1', 'Test', 'Content')")
            close()
        }

        val db = helper.runMigrationsAndValidate(class="st">"test_db", 2, true, MIGRATION_1_2)

        class="cm">// Verify data survived migration and new column has default value
        val cursor = db.query(class="st">"SELECT * FROM articles WHERE id = '1'")

    11. MOCKWEBSERVER

    OkHttp MockWebServer provides a local HTTP server for testing API interactions.


    Why use it:

    - Test real HTTP behavior (serialization, headers, error codes)

    - Verify request format (path, method, headers, body)

    - Simulate network conditions (slow responses, timeouts, errors)

    - No flaky network dependency in CI


    How it works:

    1. Start MockWebServer on localhost

    2. Point Retrofit at mockWebServer.url("/")

    3. Enqueue mock responses

    4. Execute API calls — they hit the local server

    5. Verify requests with takeRequest()


    Interview Tip: 💡 "I use MockWebServer to test the full networking stack —

    Retrofit, converters, interceptors — without real network calls. Fakes are great for repository tests, but MockWebServer catches serialization bugs that fakes miss."

    class ArticleApiTest {

    private lateinit var mockWebServer: MockWebServer
    private lateinit var api: ArticleApi

    class="an">@Before
    fun setup() {
        mockWebServer = MockWebServer()
        mockWebServer.start()

        val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder()
            .baseUrl(mockWebServer.url(class="st">"/"))
            .client(OkHttpClient.Builder().build())
            .addConverterFactory(Json.asConverterFactory(class="st">"application/json".toMediaType()))
            .build()

        api = retrofit.create(ArticleApi::class.java)
    }

    class="an">@After
    fun tearDown() {
        mockWebServer.shutdown()
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun `getArticles parses response correctly`() = runTest {
        val json = class="st">""class="st">"
            [
                {"idclass="st">": "1class="st">", "titleclass="st">": "Kotlin Coroutinesclass="st">", "contentclass="st">": "Deep diveclass="st">"},
                {"idclass="st">": "2class="st">", "titleclass="st">": "Jetpack Composeclass="st">", "contentclass="st">": "Modern UIclass="st">"}
            ]
        "class="st">"".trimIndent()

        mockWebServer.enqueue(
            MockResponse()
                .setResponseCode(200)
                .setBody(json)
                .setHeader(class="st">"Content-Type", class="st">"application/json")
        )

        val articles = api.getArticles(class="st">"user1")

        assertEquals(2, articles.size)
        assertEquals(class="st">"Kotlin Coroutines", articles[0].title)
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun `getArticles sends correct request`() = runTest {
        mockWebServer.enqueue(MockResponse().setBody(class="st">"[]").setResponseCode(200))

        api.getArticles(class="st">"user1")

        val request = mockWebServer.takeRequest()
        assertEquals(class="st">"GET", request.method)
        assertTrue(request.path!!.contains(class="st">"user1"))
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun `getArticles throws on server error`() = runTest {
        mockWebServer.enqueue(MockResponse().setResponseCode(500))

        try {
            api.getArticles(class="st">"user1")
            fail(class="st">"Expected HttpException")
        } catch (e: HttpException) {
            assertEquals(500, e.code())
        }
    }

    class="an">@Test
    fun `getArticles handles slow response`() = runTest {
        mockWebServer.enqueue(
            MockResponse()
                .setBody(class="st">"[]")
                .setBodyDelay(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        )

        val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
            .readTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .build()

        val slowApi = Retrofit.Builder()
            .baseUrl(mockWebServer.url(class="st">"/"))
            .client(client)
            .addConverterFactory(Json.asConverterFactory(class="st">"application/json".toMediaType()))
            .build()
            .create(ArticleApi::class.java)

        try {
            slowApi.getArticles(class="st">"user1")
            fail(class="st">"Expected timeout")
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            assertTrue(e is java.net.SocketTimeoutException)
        }
    }
}

    12. SCREENSHOT / VISUAL REGRESSION TESTING

    Screenshot testing catches unintended visual changes by comparing UI snapshots against golden (reference) images.


    Tools:


    1. Paparazzi (Cash App / Square):

    - Runs on JVM — no emulator needed

    - Renders Android views and Compose using layoutlib (the same renderer Android Studio uses for previews)

    - Records golden images, then verifies against them in CI

    - Commands: ./gradlew :app:recordPaparazziDebug (record) ./gradlew :app:verifyPaparazziDebug (verify)


    2. Compose Preview Screenshot Testing (Google, experimental):

    - Uses @Preview composables as screenshot test sources

    - Runs on JVM with layoutlib

    - Tightly integrated with Compose preview workflow

    - Commands: ./gradlew updateDebugScreenshotTest (record) ./gradlew validateDebugScreenshotTest (verify)


    When to use:

    ✅ Design system components (buttons, cards, inputs)

    ✅ Complex layouts with multiple states (loading, error, empty, populated)

    ✅ Dark mode / light mode verification

    ✅ Accessibility — large font / RTL layout checks

    ✅ Preventing accidental regressions in shared components


    CI integration:

    - Run verify task in CI pipeline on every PR

    - Record task generates/updates golden images (commit to repo)

    - Failed verification produces a diff image showing what changed

    - Review diffs in PR to decide if changes are intentional


    ⚠️ Gotchas:

    - Golden images are platform-sensitive (record + verify on same OS/JDK)

    - Dynamic content (timestamps, animations) must be pinned for determinism

    - Large golden image repos can bloat git — consider LFS


    Interview Tip: 💡 "I use Paparazzi for screenshot tests because it runs

    on JVM, making it fast and CI-friendly. It's especially valuable for design system components where visual regressions are costly."

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: How do you test a ViewModel that uses viewModelScope? A: Use MainDispatcherRule to replace Dispatchers.Main with TestDispatcher. Use runTest {} for coroutine testing. Use advanceUntilIdle() to complete all pending coroutines. Use Turbine for Flow assertions.


    Q2: How do you test Room database operations? A: Use Room.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder() for fast, isolated tests. Run on Android device/emulator (instrumented test). Test: insert → query → verify. Test: migration paths.


    Q3: What makes a good test? A: Fast, isolated, repeatable, self-validating, timely (FIRST). Tests behavior not implementation. Clear name describes scenario. Single reason to fail. Arranges minimal context.


    Q4: How do you handle flaky tests? A: Identify the flakiness source: timing (use TestDispatcher, IdlingResource), shared state (isolate tests), network (use fakes). For Espresso: use IdlingResource for async operations. For Compose: use waitUntil {} for async assertions.


    Q5: When do you use instrumented tests vs local tests? A: Local (JVM): ViewModel, UseCase, Repository, mappers — fast feedback. Instrumented (device): Room DB, UI tests, integration tests. Rule of thumb: run as much as possible locally.


    Q6: When would you use Robolectric vs instrumented tests? A: Robolectric: when you need Android framework classes (Context, SharedPreferences, Activity lifecycle) but want JVM speed. Great for CI pipelines — no emulator needed. Instrumented: when behavior must match real Android exactly — Room/SQLite, hardware features, pixel-accurate UI rendering, multi-process scenarios. Robolectric's shadows approximate real behavior but can diverge in edge cases, so anything SQLite or rendering-sensitive should run instrumented.


    Q7: How do you use MockWebServer to test API interactions? A: Start MockWebServer, point Retrofit's baseUrl at mockWebServer.url("/"). Enqueue MockResponse objects with status codes, JSON bodies, and headers. Execute API calls — they hit the local server. Use takeRequest() to verify the request method, path, headers, and body. Simulate errors with setResponseCode(500), slow responses with setBodyDelay(), and timeouts by combining delay with a short client timeout. This tests the full networking stack including serialization and interceptors.

    1. RUNTIME PERMISSIONS MODEL

    Permission types:

    Normal → granted automatically at install (INTERNET, VIBRATE)

    Dangerous → requires runtime request (CAMERA, LOCATION, CONTACTS)

    Special → requires Settings intent (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, WRITE_SETTINGS)


    Permission groups:

    ⚠️ Don't rely on groups — Google can change grouping at any time. Always request the specific permission you need.


    API 33+ changes:

    - POST_NOTIFICATIONS is now a runtime permission

    - Photo picker doesn't need READ_MEDIA_IMAGES for basic access

    - Granular media permissions (READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, READ_MEDIA_AUDIO)


    API 34+ changes:

    - Partial photo/video access (user selects specific files)

    - READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED for partial access

    class="cm">// Modern permission handling with Activity Result API
class PermissionActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    class="cm">// Single permission
    private val cameraPermissionLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
    ) { isGranted ->
        if (isGranted) {
            openCamera()
        } else {
            class="cm">// Check if we should show rationale
            if (shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)) {
                showRationaleDialog()
            } else {
                class="cm">// User permanently denied — direct to Settings
                showSettingsDialog()
            }
        }
    }

    class="cm">// Multiple permissions
    private val locationPermissionLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.RequestMultiplePermissions()
    ) { permissions ->
        val fineLocationGranted = permissions[Manifest.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION] ?: false
        val coarseLocationGranted = permissions[Manifest.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION] ?: false

        when {
            fineLocationGranted -> enablePreciseLocation()
            coarseLocationGranted -> enableApproximateLocation()
            else -> showLocationDeniedMessage()
        }
    }

    fun requestCameraPermission() {
        when {
            ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(
                this, Manifest.permission.CAMERA
            ) == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED -> {
                openCamera()
            }
            shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(Manifest.permission.CAMERA) -> {
                showRationaleDialog()
            }
            else -> {
                cameraPermissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
            }
        }
    }
}

    2. NETWORK SECURITY CONFIGURATION

    Network Security Config (res/xml/network_security_config.xml):

    Controls app's network security behavior declaratively.


    Key features:

    - Cleartext traffic policy (HTTP vs HTTPS)

    - Custom trust anchors (CA certificates)

    - Certificate pinning

    - Debug overrides


    API 28+: Cleartext (HTTP) blocked by default. API 24+: User-installed CAs not trusted by default.

    class="cm">// Example network_security_config.xml
class="cm">/*
<?xml version=class="st">"1.0" encoding=class="st">"utf-8"?>
<network-security-config>
    <!-- Default: HTTPS only, system CAs only -->
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted=class="st">"false">
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src=class="st">"system" />
        </trust-anchors>
    </base-config>

    <!-- Exception: allow cleartext for local dev server -->
    <domain-config cleartextTrafficPermitted=class="st">"true">
        <domain includeSubdomains=class="st">"true">10.0.2.2</domain>
    </domain-config>

    <!-- Certificate pinning for production API -->
    <domain-config>
        <domain includeSubdomains=class="st">"true">api.example.com</domain>
        <pin-set expiration=class="st">"2027-12-31">
            <pin digest=class="st">"SHA-256">base64EncodedPin1=</pin>
            <pin digest=class="st">"SHA-256">base64EncodedBackupPin=</pin>
        </pin-set>
    </domain-config>

    <!-- Debug only: trust user-installed CAs for proxy tools -->
    <debug-overrides>
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src=class="st">"user" />
        </trust-anchors>
    </debug-overrides>
</network-security-config>
*/

    3. CERTIFICATE PINNING

    Certificate pinning = only trust specific certificates for a domain. Prevents MITM attacks even with a compromised CA.


    Approaches:

    1. Network Security Config (XML) — recommended

    2. OkHttp CertificatePinner — programmatic

    3. TrustManager — custom low-level


    ⚠️ Always include a backup pin — if the primary cert is rotated, you need a fallback to avoid bricking the app.

    class="cm">// OkHttp certificate pinning
fun createPinnedClient(): OkHttpClient {
    val certificatePinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
        .add(
            class="st">"api.example.com",
            class="st">"sha256/AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=",  class="cm">// Primary
            class="st">"sha256/BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB="   class="cm">// Backup
        )
        .build()

    return OkHttpClient.Builder()
        .certificatePinner(certificatePinner)
        .build()
}

    4. ANDROID KEYSTORE SYSTEM

    Android Keystore = hardware-backed secure storage for cryptographic keys.


    Key features:

    - Keys never leave the secure hardware (TEE/Strongbox)

    - Keys can require user authentication (biometric)

    - Keys can have validity periods

    - Extraction is computationally infeasible


    Use cases:

    - Encrypting local data

    - Signing data for API authentication

    - Biometric-gated key access

    object KeystoreHelper {

    private const val KEY_ALIAS = class="st">"app_encryption_key"

    fun getOrCreateKey(): SecretKey {
        val keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance(class="st">"AndroidKeyStore")
        keyStore.load(null)

        class="cm">// Return existing key if available
        keyStore.getKey(KEY_ALIAS, null)?.let { return it as SecretKey }

        class="cm">// Generate new key
        val keyGenerator = KeyGenerator.getInstance(
            KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_AES, class="st">"AndroidKeyStore"
        )
        keyGenerator.init(
            KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(
                KEY_ALIAS,
                KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT
            )
                .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM)
                .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE)
                .setKeySize(256)
                .setUserAuthenticationRequired(false)
                .build()
        )
        return keyGenerator.generateKey()
    }

    fun encrypt(data: ByteArray): Pair<ByteArray, ByteArray> {
        val key = getOrCreateKey()
        val cipher = Cipher.getInstance(class="st">"AES/GCM/NoPadding")
        cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key)
        val iv = cipher.iv
        val encrypted = cipher.doFinal(data)
        return Pair(iv, encrypted)
    }

    fun decrypt(iv: ByteArray, encryptedData: ByteArray): ByteArray {
        val key = getOrCreateKey()
        val cipher = Cipher.getInstance(class="st">"AES/GCM/NoPadding")
        val spec = GCMParameterSpec(128, iv)
        cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, key, spec)
        return cipher.doFinal(encryptedData)
    }
}

    5. ENCRYPTED STORAGE

    EncryptedSharedPreferences (AndroidX Security):

    - AES-256 encryption for keys and values

    - Backed by Android Keystore

    - Drop-in replacement for SharedPreferences

    fun createEncryptedPrefs(context: Context): SharedPreferences {
    val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(context)
        .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
        .build()

    return EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
        context,
        class="st">"secure_prefs",
        masterKey,
        EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
        EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
    )
}

class="cm">// Store sensitive tokens
fun storeAuthToken(prefs: SharedPreferences, token: String) {
    prefs.edit().putString(class="st">"auth_token", token).apply()

}

    6. BIOMETRIC AUTHENTICATION

    class BiometricHelper(private val activity: FragmentActivity) {

    fun authenticate(
        onSuccess: () -> Unit,
        onError: (String) -> Unit
    ) {
        val biometricManager = BiometricManager.from(activity)
        when (biometricManager.canAuthenticate(BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_STRONG)) {
            BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_SUCCESS -> {
                showBiometricPrompt(onSuccess, onError)
            }
            BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_NO_HARDWARE ->
                onError(class="st">"No biometric hardware")
            BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_HW_UNAVAILABLE ->
                onError(class="st">"Biometric hardware unavailable")
            BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_NONE_ENROLLED ->
                onError(class="st">"No biometrics enrolled")
        }
    }

    private fun showBiometricPrompt(
        onSuccess: () -> Unit,
        onError: (String) -> Unit
    ) {
        val promptInfo = BiometricPrompt.PromptInfo.Builder()
            .setTitle(class="st">"Authenticate")
            .setSubtitle(class="st">"Verify your identity")
            .setNegativeButtonText(class="st">"Cancel")
            .setAllowedAuthenticators(BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_STRONG)
            .build()

        val biometricPrompt = BiometricPrompt(
            activity,
            ContextCompat.getMainExecutor(activity),
            object : BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback() {
                override fun onAuthenticationSucceeded(result: BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationResult) {
                    onSuccess()
                }

                override fun onAuthenticationError(errorCode: Int, errString: CharSequence) {
                    onError(errString.toString())
                }

                override fun onAuthenticationFailed() {
                    class="cm">// Don't close dialog — user can retry
                }
            }
        )

        biometricPrompt.authenticate(promptInfo)
    }
}

    8. PROGUARD / R8 — CODE OBFUSCATION

    R8 is the default code shrinker/obfuscator in Android (replaced ProGuard). Same rule format as ProGuard, but faster and Kotlin-aware.


    Three stages:

    1. Shrinking — removes unused classes, methods, fields

    2. Obfuscation — renames classes/members to short meaningless names (a, b, c)

    3. Optimization — inlines methods, removes dead branches, simplifies code


    R8 full mode vs compat mode:

    Compat (default): behaves like ProGuard — safe, fewer surprises Full mode: more aggressive optimizations — may break reflection-based code Enable: android.enableR8.fullMode=true in gradle.properties


    Mapping files:

    R8 produces mapping.txt (maps obfuscated names → original names). Upload to Play Console → crash stack traces are auto-deobfuscated. Keep mapping files for every release build you ship.

    class="cm">// Example proguard-rules.pro
class="cm">/*
# ── Keep rules ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Keep entire class (class name + all members)
-keep class com.example.model.** { *; }

# Keep class members only (class can be renamed)
-keepclassmembers class com.example.model.User {
    <fields>;
}

# Keep class name only (members can be renamed)
-keepnames class com.example.api.ApiResponse

# ── Common rules needed ─────────────────────────────────────────────

# Retrofit (uses reflection for interface proxies)
-keepattributes Signature
-keepattributes *Annotation*
-keep class retrofit2.** { *; }
-keepclassmembers,allowobfuscation interface * {
    class="an">@retrofit2.http.* <methods>;
}

# Kotlinx Serialization
-keepattributes *Annotation*, InnerClasses
-keep,includedescriptorclasses class com.example.**$$serializer { *; }
-keepclassmembers class com.example.** {
    *** Companion;
}

# Parcelable
-keep class * implements android.os.Parcelable {
    public static final ** CREATOR;
}

# Enum classes
-keepclassmembers enum * {
    public static **[] values();
    public static ** valueOf(java.lang.String);
}

# Keep R8 from stripping Google Play Integrity / SafetyNet
-keep class com.google.android.play.core.** { *; }
*/

    9. CONTENT PROVIDER SECURITY

    Content Providers expose structured data between apps. Major security concern: they're an IPC attack surface.


    Key attributes:

    exported="false" → only your app can access (default for API 31+ if no intent-filter)

    exported="true" → other apps can query/insert/update/delete


    Permissions:

    android:readPermission → required to query android:writePermission → required to insert/update/delete

    android:permission → required for both read and write


    Path-level permissions (android:pathPermission):

    Different permissions for different URI paths.


    grantUriPermissions:

    Allows temporary access to specific URIs even without the full permission. Essential for sharing files via FileProvider.


    SQL injection prevention:

    NEVER concatenate user input into queries. Use selection args (parameterized queries) or Room.

    class="cm">// Secure ContentProvider with FileProvider for sharing files
class="cm">/*
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<provider
    android:name=class="st">"androidx.core.content.FileProvider"
    android:authorities=class="st">"${applicationId}.fileprovider"
    android:exported=class="st">"false"
    android:grantUriPermissions=class="st">"true">
    <meta-data
        android:name=class="st">"android.support.FILE_PROVIDER_PATHS"
        android:resource=class="st">"class="an">@xml/file_paths" />
</provider>
*/

class="cm">// Sharing a file securely with another app
fun shareFile(context: Context, file: File) {
    val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(
        context,
        class="st">"${context.packageName}.fileprovider",
        file
    )

    val shareIntent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
        type = class="st">"application/pdf"
        putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_STREAM, uri)
        class="cm">// Grant read-only access to the receiving app
        addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)
    }
    context.startActivity(Intent.createChooser(shareIntent, class="st">"Share file"))
}

class="cm">// Parameterized queries prevent SQL injection
class SecureProvider : ContentProvider() {

    override fun query(
        uri: Uri,
        projection: Array<String>?,
        selection: String?,
        selectionArgs: Array<String>?,  class="cm">// ← always use selection args
        sortOrder: String?
    ): Cursor? {
        class="cm">// ✅ Safe: parameterized
        class="cm">// SELECT * FROM notes WHERE author = ?   selectionArgs = [class="st">"Alice"]

        class="cm">// ❌ Dangerous: string concatenation
        class="cm">// class="st">"SELECT * FROM notes WHERE author = '$userInput'"
        class="cm">// userInput = class="st">"'; DROP TABLE notes; --"

        return db.query(class="st">"notes", projection, selection, selectionArgs, null, null, sortOrder)
    }

    class="cm">// ... other required overrides
    override fun onCreate(): Boolean = true
    override fun getType(uri: Uri): String? = null
    override fun insert(uri: Uri, values: ContentValues?): Uri? = null
    override fun delete(uri: Uri, sel: String?, selArgs: Array<String>?): Int = 0
    override fun update(uri: Uri, values: ContentValues?, sel: String?, selArgs: Array<String>?): Int = 0

    10. WEBVIEW SECURITY

    WebView is one of the most dangerous components on Android. It's essentially a browser engine with access to native APIs.


    JavaScript interface risks:

    @JavascriptInterface exposes Kotlin/Java methods to JS code. Only annotated methods are exposed (API 17+), but any loaded page can call them.

    ⚠️ Never expose sensitive methods. Validate the calling URL.


    Common attack vectors:

    - XSS via injected scripts in loaded content

    - URL scheme hijacking (intent://, javascript://)

    - File access (file:// can read local files if enabled)

    - Mixed content (HTTPS page loading HTTP resources)

    - Deep link manipulation


    Cookie isolation:

    WebView cookies are shared across all WebViews in the app. Use CookieManager to clear cookies after sensitive sessions. Third-party cookies are blocked by default on API 33+.


    Safe Browsing (API 26+):

    Google Safe Browsing checks URLs against known malicious sites. Enabled by default. Shows an interstitial warning for dangerous sites. Set android:enableSafeBrowsing="true" in manifest (opt-in for older APIs).

    class SecureWebViewActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var webView: WebView

    fun setupSecureWebView() {
        webView = WebView(this)

        webView.settings.apply {
            class="cm">// Only enable JavaScript if absolutely necessary
            javaScriptEnabled = true

            class="cm">// ❌ Disable file access — prevents file:// attacks
            allowFileAccess = false
            allowFileAccessFromFileURLs = false
            allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs = false

            class="cm">// ❌ Disable content provider access via WebView
            allowContentAccess = false

            class="cm">// Block mixed content (HTTPS page loading HTTP resources)
            mixedContentMode = WebSettings.MIXED_CONTENT_NEVER_ALLOW

            class="cm">// Disable geolocation
            setGeolocationEnabled(false)
        }

        class="cm">// Validate URLs before loading
        webView.webViewClient = object : WebViewClient() {
            private val allowedHosts = setOf(class="st">"example.com", class="st">"www.example.com")

            override fun shouldOverrideUrlLoading(
                view: WebView,
                request: WebResourceRequest
            ): Boolean {
                val url = request.url
                class="cm">// Block non-HTTPS and untrusted hosts
                if (url.scheme != class="st">"https" || url.host !in allowedHosts) {
                    return true  class="cm">// Block navigation
                }
                return false  class="cm">// Allow navigation
            }
        }

        class="cm">// Safe JavaScript interface — minimal exposure
        webView.addJavascriptInterface(SafeBridge(), class="st">"AndroidBridge")
    }
}

class SafeBridge {
    class="an">@JavascriptInterface
    fun getAppVersion(): String {
        class="cm">// ✅ Safe: returns non-sensitive info
        return BuildConfig.VERSION_NAME
    }

    class="cm">// ❌ Never expose methods like: getAuthToken(), executeCommand(), readFile()
}

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: How do you securely store an auth token on Android? A: Use EncryptedSharedPreferences backed by Android Keystore. Keys are stored in hardware-backed security (TEE/Strongbox). Token is AES-256 encrypted at rest. Never store in plain SharedPreferences or in code/BuildConfig.


    Q2: What's the difference between certificate pinning in XML vs OkHttp? A: XML (network_security_config): declarative, handles backup pins, expiration dates, debug overrides. Recommended by Google. OkHttp CertificatePinner: programmatic, more control, but must handle updates manually. Both prevent MITM attacks.


    Q3: How do you handle the "Don't ask again" permission scenario? A: shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale returns false in two cases:

    1. First time asking (never denied) — just request

    2. User selected "Don't ask again" — show dialog directing to Settings Distinguish by tracking if you've asked before (DataStore flag).


    Q4: What is FLAG_SECURE and when would you use it? A: window.setFlags(FLAG_SECURE, FLAG_SECURE) prevents:

    - Screenshots of the Activity

    - Screen recording of the Activity

    - Preview in recent apps (shows blank) Use for: banking, password, sensitive data screens.


    Q5: How does Android Keystore differ from just encrypting with a password? A: Keystore keys never leave the secure hardware (TEE). Even root access can't extract the key material. Password-based encryption: key is in app memory — extractable. Keystore also supports biometric-gated access.

    1. KOTLIN MULTIPLATFORM (KMP)

    KMP = share Kotlin code between Android, iOS, Desktop, Web.


    What to share:

    ✅ Business logic (UseCases, domain models)

    ✅ Networking (Ktor client)

    ✅ Data persistence (SQLDelight)

    ✅ Serialization (kotlinx.serialization)

    ✅ State management

    ❌ UI (platform-specific; though Compose Multiplatform is emerging)

    ❌ Platform APIs (camera, sensors, notifications)


    Project structure:

    shared/

    commonMain/ → shared Kotlin code

    androidMain/ → Android-specific implementations

    iosMain/ → iOS-specific implementations

    androidApp/ → Android app module

    iosApp/ → iOS Xcode project


    expect/actual mechanism:

    expect → declares platform-specific API in commonMain actual → provides implementation in each platform module

    class="cm">// Common code (commonMain)
expect class PlatformLogger() {
    fun log(message: String)
}

class="cm">// Android implementation (androidMain)
actual class PlatformLogger {
    actual fun log(message: String) {
        android.util.Log.d(class="st">"KMP", message)
    }
}

class="cm">// Shared UseCase
class GetArticlesUseCase(
    private val repository: ArticleRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(): Result<List<Article>> {
        return repository.getArticles()
    }
}

    💡 Google's KMP investment:

    - Official support for KMP in Android Studio

    - Jetpack libraries being made KMP-compatible (Room, DataStore)

    - Google uses KMP internally for cross-platform code sharing


    Interview Question: When would you recommend KMP? A: When you have Android + iOS apps with significant shared business logic. Not worth it for: small apps, UI-heavy apps, or if team has no iOS devs. Start by sharing data/domain layers. Don't share UI initially.

    2. APP MODULARIZATION

    Modularization = splitting your app into multiple Gradle modules.


    Benefits:

    ✅ Build speed (only changed modules recompile)

    ✅ Code ownership (team per module)

    ✅ Strict dependency boundaries (can't accidentally access internals)

    ✅ Reusability (library modules shared across apps)

    ✅ Testability (test modules in isolation)

    ✅ Dynamic delivery (download features on demand)


    Module types:

    :app → main application module (entry point)

    :core:network → networking abstractions

    :core:database → Room database

    :core:common → shared utilities

    :core:ui → shared composables, theme

    :core:model → domain models :feature:articles → article list & detail screens

    :feature:profile → user profile screens :feature:settings → settings screens


    Dependency rules:

    :feature modules → depend on :core modules (not other :feature modules)

    :core modules → can depend on other :core modules

    :app module → depends on all :feature modules


    💡 Navigation between feature modules:

    Use Navigation Component with deep links or a shared navigation module. Features don't know about each other — they navigate via routes/URIs.

    class="cm">// Module structure example
class="cm">/*
project/
├── app/                          class="cm">// Entry point, DI setup
│   └── build.gradle.kts
├── core/
│   ├── common/                   class="cm">// Extensions, utils
│   ├── model/                    class="cm">// Domain data classes
│   ├── database/                 class="cm">// Room DB, DAOs, entities
│   ├── network/                  class="cm">// Retrofit, API services
│   ├── data/                     class="cm">// Repositories
│   └── ui/                       class="cm">// Shared Compose components, theme
├── feature/
│   ├── articles/                 class="cm">// Article screens + ViewModel
│   ├── profile/                  class="cm">// Profile screens + ViewModel
│   └── settings/                 class="cm">// Settings screens + ViewModel
└── build-logic/                  class="cm">// Convention plugins
    └── convention/
*/

    Interview Question: How do you handle navigation between feature modules that don't know about each other?


    A: Options:

    1. Deep link routes — each feature declares routes, navigation module maps them

    2. Interface-based — navigation interface in :core, implemented in :app

    3. Navigation Component with NavGraphs per feature + shared routes

    4. BASELINE PROFILES (SUMMARY)

    Baseline Profiles tell ART which code paths to AOT-compile at install time.


    Impact: 20-30% faster startup, smoother interactions.


    Quick summary:

    1. Write a Macrobenchmark that exercises critical user journeys

    2. BaselineProfileRule generates a profile file

    3. Profile is bundled with AAB/APK

    4. At install, ART AOT-compiles listed methods as native code

    5. Cloud Profiles from Play Store complement developer-provided profiles


    → See 08_performance_optimization.kt § "BASELINE PROFILES" for the full implementation: BaselineProfileGenerator, StartupBenchmark, CI integration, and Gradle setup.

    5. ANDROID 15/16 PLATFORM CHANGES

    Android 15 (API 35):

    - 16KB page size support (for newer hardware)

    - Foreground service dataSync type has 6-hour limit

    - Package visibility enforcement tightened

    - Private Space for hiding apps


    Android 16 (API 36 — 2026):

    - Predictive back gesture enforcement (must support or breaks)

    - Photo picker improvements

    - Health Connect integration

    - Richer widget APIs

    - Stricter background work limits


    Key patterns:

    - Target the latest SDK but test on older devices

    - Use AndroidX compat libraries for backward compatibility

    - Handle new permission requirements gracefully

    6. PREDICTIVE BACK GESTURE

    Predictive Back = system-level back gesture with preview animation. User swipes from edge and sees a preview of where they'll go.


    Requirements (API 34+ enforced on API 36):

    1. Set android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true" in manifest

    2. Migrate from onBackPressed() to OnBackPressedCallback

    3. Support system back animations (cross-activity, cross-task)

    class="cm">// Migrating back handling

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        class="cm">// ✅ Modern back handling with OnBackPressedCallback

            override fun handleOnBackPressed() {
                if (hasUnsavedChanges()) {
                    showDiscardDialog()
                } else {
                    class="cm">// Let system handle the back (default animation)
                    isEnabled = false
                    onBackPressedDispatcher.onBackPressed()
                }
            }
        }
        onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback(this, callback)
    }

    7. ACCESSIBILITY

    Google values accessibility. Mentioning it in interviews shows maturity.


    Key practices:

    - contentDescription on all interactive elements

    - Sufficient color contrast (4.5:1 for text)

    - Touch targets >= 48dp

    - Semantic headings for screen readers

    - Focus order matches visual order

    - Support TalkBack navigation

    class="cm">// Compose accessibility
class="an">@Composable
fun AccessibleButton(
    text: String,
    onClick: () -> Unit,
    isBookmarked: Boolean
) {
    IconButton(
        onClick = onClick,
        modifier = Modifier
            .size(48.dp)  class="cm">// Minimum touch target
            .semantics {
                contentDescription = if (isBookmarked) {
                    class="st">"Remove $text from bookmarks"
                } else {
                    class="st">"Add $text to bookmarks"
                }
                role = Role.Button
                stateDescription = if (isBookmarked) class="st">"Bookmarked" else class="st">"Not bookmarked"
            }
    ) {
        Icon(
            imageVector = if (isBookmarked) Icons.Filled.Bookmark else Icons.Outlined.BookmarkBorder,
            contentDescription = null  class="cm">// Described by parent semantics
        )
    }
}

    8. APP LINKS & DEEP LINKS

    Three types of links that open your app:


    Deep Links:

    - Custom scheme URIs: myapp://article/123

    - Matched via intent-filter

    - ⚠️ Any app can register the same scheme — not verified


    Web Links:

    - HTTP/HTTPS URIs: https://example.com/article/123

    - Shows disambiguation dialog if multiple apps handle it


    App Links (verified, recommended):

    - HTTPS only: https://example.com/article/123

    - Verified via Digital Asset Links (assetlinks.json on your domain)

    - No disambiguation dialog — opens directly in your app

    - Falls back to browser if app not installed


    Digital Asset Links:

    Host a JSON file at: https://example.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json Contains your app's package name + signing certificate fingerprint. Android verifies this at install time.

    class="cm">// Intent filter for App Links (AndroidManifest.xml)
class="cm">/*
<activity android:name=class="st">".DeepLinkActivity"
    android:exported=class="st">"true">

    <!-- Deep link (custom scheme) -->
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name=class="st">"android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name=class="st">"android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <category android:name=class="st">"android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
        <data android:scheme=class="st">"myapp" android:host=class="st">"article" />
    </intent-filter>

    <!-- Verified App Link (HTTPS + autoVerify) -->
    <intent-filter android:autoVerify=class="st">"true">
        <action android:name=class="st">"android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name=class="st">"android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <category android:name=class="st">"android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
        <data android:scheme=class="st">"https"
              android:host=class="st">"example.com"
              android:pathPrefix=class="st">"/article" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>
*/

class="cm">// assetlinks.json (hosted at https://example.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json)
class="cm">/*
[{
    class="st">"relation": [class="st">"delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls"],
    class="st">"target": {
        class="st">"namespace": class="st">"android_app",
        class="st">"package_name": class="st">"com.example.app",
        class="st">"sha256_cert_fingerprints": [
            class="st">"AB:CD:EF:12:34:56:..."
        ]
    }
}]
*/

class="cm">// Navigation Component deep links
class ArticleNavigation {

    class="cm">// Type-safe deep link in Navigation Component

            startDestination = class="st">"home"
        ) {
            composable(
                route = class="st">"article/{articleId}",

                        uriPattern = class="st">"https:class="cm">//example.com/article/{articleId}"
                    }
