    9. DYNAMIC FEATURE MODULES

    Play Feature Delivery: Download parts of your app on demand. Requires Android App Bundle (AAB) — not APKs.


    Delivery modes:

    install-time → installed with the base app (like a regular module)

    on-demand → downloaded when user triggers the feature

    conditional → installed only on devices matching conditions (API, country, hardware)


    Benefits:

    - Smaller initial download size (base APK is smaller)

    - Users only download features they actually use

    - Reduces install abandonment (large apps lose users)


    When to use:

    - Large features used by a small % of users (e.g., AR try-on, video editor)

    - Country-specific features (payment methods, compliance)

    - Premium/paid features


    SplitInstallManager API:

    - Request feature install, monitor progress, handle errors

    - Deferred install (download when on Wi-Fi)

    class="cm">// On-demand feature installation
class FeatureInstaller(private val context: Context) {

    private val splitInstallManager: SplitInstallManager =
        SplitInstallManagerFactory.create(context)

    fun installFeature(
        featureName: String,
        onProgress: (Float) -> Unit,
        onSuccess: () -> Unit,
        onError: (Exception) -> Unit
    ) {
        val request = SplitInstallRequest.newBuilder()
            .addModule(featureName)
            .build()

        splitInstallManager.startInstall(request)
            .addOnSuccessListener { sessionId ->
                class="cm">// Monitor installation progress
                splitInstallManager.registerListener { state ->
                    when (state.status()) {
                        SplitInstallSessionStatus.DOWNLOADING -> {
                            val progress = state.bytesDownloaded().toFloat() /
                                state.totalBytesToDownload()
                            onProgress(progress)
                        }
                        SplitInstallSessionStatus.INSTALLED -> {
                            onSuccess()
                        }
                        SplitInstallSessionStatus.REQUIRES_USER_CONFIRMATION -> {
                            class="cm">// Large download — system asks for user confirmation
                            splitInstallManager.startConfirmationDialogForResult(
                                state, context as Activity, REQUEST_CODE
                            )
                        }
                        SplitInstallSessionStatus.FAILED -> {
                            onError(Exception(class="st">"Install failed: ${state.errorCode()}"))
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
            .addOnFailureListener { exception ->
                onError(exception)
            }
    }

    fun isFeatureInstalled(featureName: String): Boolean {
        return splitInstallManager.installedModules.contains(featureName)
    }

    companion object {
        private const val REQUEST_CODE = 1001
    }
}

    10. PRIVACY SANDBOX (OVERVIEW)

    Android Privacy Sandbox = Google's initiative to replace cross-app tracking with privacy-preserving alternatives. Phasing out Advertising ID.


    Key APIs:


    1. Topics API (interest-based ads without cross-app tracking):

    - Device locally classifies apps into interest "topics" (e.g., Sports, Travel)

    - Returns 3 topics per epoch (1 week) — coarse-grained, not per-app

    - Ad SDKs receive topics to show relevant ads without knowing which apps are installed

    - User can view and remove topics in Settings


    2. Attribution Reporting API:

    - Measures ad conversions (ad click → app install/purchase)

    - Reports are delayed and aggregated — no real-time per-user tracking

    - Replaces direct referrer tracking


    3. SDK Runtime (API 34+):

    - Third-party ad SDKs run in an isolated sandbox process

    - Cannot access the app's storage, permissions, or identifiers

    - Reduces data leakage from ad SDKs


    Why this matters for Google interviews:

    - Shows awareness of Google's current strategic direction

    - Privacy-first thinking is valued at Google

    - Understanding the trade-offs between privacy and ad monetization

    - May be asked: "How would you handle ad attribution without GAID?" Answer: Use Attribution Reporting API with aggregated reports.

    11. LARGE SCREEN & ADAPTIVE LAYOUTS

    Google is heavily pushing support for foldables, tablets, and Chromebooks. Apps that don't adapt lose ranking and users on these growing form factors.


    Window Size Classes (Jetpack):

    Compact → phone portrait (< 600dp width)

    Medium → tablet portrait, foldable unfolded, large phone landscape (600-840dp) Expanded → tablet landscape, desktop (> 840dp)


    Use WindowSizeClass to choose layout strategy, NOT screen orientation.


    Canonical Layouts (Google's recommended patterns):

    List-Detail → list on left, detail on right (email, messaging)

    Feed → single-column on compact, multi-column on expanded

    Supporting Panel → main content + side panel (maps, editors)


    Key APIs:

    - WindowSizeClass (Material 3): calculateWindowSizeClass(activity)

    - adaptive-navigation (Jetpack): NavigationSuiteScaffold auto-switches between bottom nav (compact), nav rail (medium), and nav drawer (expanded)

    - WindowInfoTracker: observe fold state and hinge position for foldables

    class="an">@Composable
fun AdaptiveArticleScreen(windowSizeClass: WindowSizeClass) {
    when (windowSizeClass.widthSizeClass) {
        WindowWidthSizeClass.Compact -> {
            class="cm">// Phone: single-pane, navigate to detail screen
            ArticleListScreen()
        }
        WindowWidthSizeClass.Medium, WindowWidthSizeClass.Expanded -> {
            class="cm">// Tablet/Foldable: list-detail side by side
            Row {
                ArticleListScreen(modifier = Modifier.weight(0.4f))
                ArticleDetailScreen(modifier = Modifier.weight(0.6f))
            }
        }
    }
}

            )

    ) {

        class="cm">// On Expanded: renders NavigationDrawer

}

    Interview Question: How do you make your app work well on foldables? A: Use WindowSizeClass to choose layout (not orientation). Observe fold state via WindowInfoTracker to avoid placing content on the hinge. Support drag-and-drop for multi-window. Test with the foldable emulator profiles in Android Studio.


    Interview Tip: 💡 Google evaluates apps on large screens for Play Store featuring.

    Mentioning adaptive layouts shows awareness of Google's current priorities.

    12. CREDENTIAL MANAGER API

    Credential Manager = unified Jetpack API for sign-in (replaces deprecated SmartLock, One Tap Sign-In, and legacy FIDO2 APIs).


    Supports:

    - Passkeys (FIDO2 WebAuthn — passwordless, phishing-resistant)

    - Passwords (saved in Google Password Manager)

    - Federated identity (Sign in with Google)


    Why passkeys matter:

    - Google is actively pushing passkey adoption

    - No password to phish, leak, or reuse

    - Backed by device biometrics (fingerprint/face)

    - Cross-device via Google Account sync


    Key classes:

    CredentialManager → entry point, created via CredentialManager.create(context)

    GetCredentialRequest → request to retrieve an existing credential CreatePublicKeyCredentialRequest → request to create a new passkey

    GetPasswordOption → option to retrieve a saved password GetPublicKeyCredentialOption → option to retrieve a passkey

    suspend fun signIn(context: Context): String? {
    val credentialManager = CredentialManager.create(context)

    val request = GetCredentialRequest(listOf(
        GetPasswordOption(),                    class="cm">// Saved passwords
        GetPublicKeyCredentialOption(           class="cm">// Passkeys
            requestJson = generatePasskeyRequestJson()
        )
    ))

    return try {
        val result = credentialManager.getCredential(context, request)
        when (val credential = result.credential) {
            is PasswordCredential -> {
                class="cm">// Authenticate with username/password
                authenticate(credential.id, credential.password)
            }
            is PublicKeyCredential -> {
                class="cm">// Verify passkey assertion with your server
                verifyPasskeyAssertion(credential.authenticationResponseJson)
            }
            else -> null
        }
    } catch (e: GetCredentialCancellationException) {
        null  class="cm">// User cancelled
    } catch (e: NoCredentialException) {
        null  class="cm">// No saved credentials — show manual sign-in
    }
}
    Interview Tip: 💡 "For new apps, I implement Credential Manager with passkey

    support as the primary sign-in method, with password as fallback. Passkeys are Google's strategic direction and eliminate entire categories of attacks."

    13. PHOTO PICKER

    Photo Picker (API 33+, backported to API 19 via Google Play services):

    System-provided UI for selecting photos/videos. NO runtime permissions required — the system grants access only to the specific items the user selects.


    Why use it:

    ✅ No READ_MEDIA_IMAGES permission needed

    ✅ Privacy-preserving — app only sees selected items

    ✅ Consistent UI across devices

    ✅ Supports single/multi selection and media type filtering


    When NOT to use it:

    ❌ If you need to browse all media (gallery app, file manager)

    ❌ If you need access to file metadata beyond the content URI

    class="cm">// Single photo selection
class PhotoPickerActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private val pickMedia = registerForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia()
    ) { uri ->
        if (uri != null) {
            class="cm">// User selected a photo — use the URI
            loadImage(uri)
        }
    }

    private val pickMultipleMedia = registerForActivityResult(
        ActivityResultContracts.PickMultipleVisualMedia(maxItems = 5)
    ) { uris ->
        if (uris.isNotEmpty()) {
            processSelectedMedia(uris)
        }
    }

    fun openPhotoPicker() {
        class="cm">// Pick images only (no video)
        pickMedia.launch(PickVisualMediaRequest(
            ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia.ImageOnly
        ))
    }

    fun openMultiPicker() {
        class="cm">// Pick images and video
        pickMultipleMedia.launch(PickVisualMediaRequest(
            ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia.ImageAndVideo
        ))
    }
}

    Interview Question: How do you handle image selection in a modern Android app? A: Use the system Photo Picker — no permissions, privacy-preserving, consistent UX. For custom gallery UI, use READ_MEDIA_IMAGES (API 33+) or READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED (API 34+) for partial access. For document files, use Storage Access Framework (SAF).

    14. CAMERAX & MEDIA3

    CameraX (Jetpack):

    Lifecycle-aware camera API that abstracts device-specific quirks.


    Use cases:

    Preview → show camera viewfinder ImageCapture → take photos VideoCapture → record video ImageAnalysis → process frames (barcode scanning, ML)


    Key benefits over Camera2:

    ✅ Lifecycle-aware — binds to LifecycleOwner, auto start/stop

    ✅ Device-specific fixes built in (CameraX Extensions for HDR, Night, etc.)

    ✅ Much less boilerplate than Camera2

    ✅ Concurrent use cases (preview + analysis + capture)


    Architecture:

    ProcessCameraProvider → bind use cases to a lifecycle CameraSelector → choose front/back camera Preview.SurfaceProvider → surface for viewfinder

    fun bindCamera(
    lifecycleOwner: LifecycleOwner,
    previewView: PreviewView
) {
    val cameraProviderFuture = ProcessCameraProvider.getInstance(previewView.context)
    cameraProviderFuture.addListener({
        val cameraProvider = cameraProviderFuture.get()

        val preview = Preview.Builder().build().apply {
            setSurfaceProvider(previewView.surfaceProvider)
        }

        val imageCapture = ImageCapture.Builder()
            .setCaptureMode(ImageCapture.CAPTURE_MODE_MINIMIZE_LATENCY)
            .build()

        val imageAnalysis = ImageAnalysis.Builder()
            .setBackpressureStrategy(ImageAnalysis.STRATEGY_KEEP_ONLY_LATEST)
            .build()
            .apply {
                setAnalyzer(Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()) { imageProxy ->
                    class="cm">// Process frame (e.g., ML Kit barcode scanning)
                    imageProxy.close()
                }
            }

        val cameraSelector = CameraSelector.DEFAULT_BACK_CAMERA

        cameraProvider.unbindAll()
        cameraProvider.bindToLifecycle(
            lifecycleOwner, cameraSelector, preview, imageCapture, imageAnalysis
        )
    }, ContextCompat.getMainExecutor(previewView.context))
}

    Media3 (Jetpack, replaces ExoPlayer standalone):

    Unified media playback library.


    Key components:

    ExoPlayer → the player engine (now under Media3 namespace)

    MediaSession → publish playback state to system (lock screen, Bluetooth)

    MediaController → client-side control of a MediaSession

    PlayerView → ready-made UI for video playback (View system)


    When to mention in interviews:

    - Chat app system design → video message playback

    - News feed design → auto-play video in feed

    - Music player → background playback with MediaSession


    Key features:

    ✅ Adaptive streaming (HLS, DASH)

    ✅ Caching (CacheDataSource for offline playback)

    ✅ DRM (Widevine, PlayReady)

    ✅ Compositor for transitions and effects


    Interview Tip: 💡 "For video playback, I use Media3 ExoPlayer with lifecycle-aware

    binding. For feed auto-play, I observe item visibility in LazyColumn and play/pause the player based on the >50% visibility threshold."

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: How do you decide what to put in each module? A: Follow the dependency rule: features depend on core, not each other. Core modules provide shared infrastructure (network, DB, models). Feature modules contain screens + ViewModels for one feature. Use the "could another team own this?" test.


    Q2: How do Baseline Profiles interact with Cloud Profiles? A: Developer Baseline Profiles are bundled with the app. Cloud Profiles are crowd-sourced from user devices via Play. Both are merged by ART for optimal compilation. Baseline Profiles help first-time users; Cloud Profiles help over time.


    Q3: When would you use KMP vs Flutter vs React Native? A: KMP: native UI per platform, share business logic, gradual adoption. Flutter: single codebase for UI + logic, fast prototyping, custom UI. React Native: JS ecosystem, web team doing mobile. Google recommends KMP for Android+iOS with native quality.


    Q4: How do you handle the predictive back gesture for custom back handling? A: Use OnBackPressedCallback with isEnabled flag. Enable when there's custom back behavior (unsaved changes, bottom sheet). Disable to let system handle default animation. Never override onBackPressed().


    Q5: What are the key Gradle performance optimizations? A: Enable configuration cache, build cache, parallel builds. Use version catalogs (centralized deps). Convention plugins (DRY config). Avoid unnecessary plugins. Use buildSrc sparingly (invalidates all caches).


    Q6: How do you support foldables and tablets in a Compose app? A: Use WindowSizeClass from Material 3 to pick layout strategy:

    Compact → single pane, Medium → nav rail + content, Expanded → list-detail. Use NavigationSuiteScaffold to auto-switch between bottom nav, rail, and drawer. Observe fold state via WindowInfoTracker to avoid placing content on the hinge. Test with foldable emulator profiles in Android Studio.


    Q7: What is the Credential Manager API and why does it matter? A: Unified Jetpack API for sign-in that replaces SmartLock, One Tap, and FIDO2. Supports passkeys (phishing-resistant, biometric-backed), passwords, and federated identity (Sign in with Google). Passkeys are Google's strategic direction for authentication — no password to leak or phish.


    Q8: When should you use the system Photo Picker vs requesting media permissions? A: Photo Picker for most cases — no permissions needed, privacy-preserving. Request READ_MEDIA_IMAGES only if you need to browse all media (gallery app). On API 34+, READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED enables partial access where the user selects specific files each session.

    1. SEALED CLASSES & INTERFACES

    Sealed = restricted hierarchy. All subclasses known at compile time. Compiler can verify exhaustive when expressions.


    sealed class → can have state (constructor parameters) sealed interface → multiple inheritance, no state in the sealed itself

    class="cm">// Sealed interface for UI state — compiler enforces handling all cases
sealed interface UiState<out T> {
    data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>
    data class Success<T>(val data: T) : UiState<T>
    data class Error(val message: String, val cause: Throwable? = null) : UiState<Nothing>
    data object Empty : UiState<Nothing>
}

class="cm">// Usage — exhaustive when (no else needed)
fun <T> renderState(state: UiState<T>) {
    when (state) {
        is UiState.Loading -> showLoadingSpinner()
        is UiState.Success -> showData(state.data)
        is UiState.Error -> showError(state.message)
        is UiState.Empty -> showEmptyState()
        class="cm">// Compiler error if any case is missing
    }
}

class="cm">// Sealed class for network result with data
sealed class NetworkResult<out T> {
    data class Success<T>(val data: T) : NetworkResult<T>()
    data class HttpError(val code: Int, val body: String) : NetworkResult<Nothing>()
    data class NetworkError(val exception: IOException) : NetworkResult<Nothing>()
    data class UnknownError(val exception: Throwable) : NetworkResult<Nothing>()

    val isSuccess get() = this is Success

    fun getOrNull(): T? = (this as? Success)?.data

    fun getOrThrow(): T = when (this) {
        is Success -> data
        is HttpError -> throw HttpException(code, body)
        is NetworkError -> throw exception
        is UnknownError -> throw exception
    }

    fun <R> map(transform: (T) -> R): NetworkResult<R> = when (this) {
        is Success -> Success(transform(data))
        is HttpError -> this
        is NetworkError -> this
        is UnknownError -> this
    }
}

    2. KOTLIN DELEGATES

    Kotlin delegates allow reusing property behavior.


    Built-in delegates:

    by lazy {} → initialized on first access, thread-safe by default by Delegates.observable() → notified on every change

    by Delegates.vetoable() → can reject changes

    by map → reads from a Map


    Custom delegates: implement ReadOnlyProperty or ReadWriteProperty

    class="cm">// by lazy — thread-safe lazy initialization
class ExpensiveClass {
    val database: AppDatabase by lazy {
        Room.databaseBuilder(context, AppDatabase::class.java, class="st">"app.db").build()
    }
    class="cm">// Created only when first accessed. Thread-safe (LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED)
}

class="cm">// by Delegates.observable — react to changes
class UserPreferences {
    var theme: String by Delegates.observable(class="st">"light") { _, old, new ->
        if (old != new) {
            applyTheme(new)
            analytics.logThemeChange(old, new)
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// Custom delegate — SharedPreferences delegate
class PreferenceDelegate<T>(
    private val prefs: SharedPreferences,
    private val key: String,
    private val defaultValue: T
) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> {

    class="an">@Suppress(class="st">"UNCHECKED_CAST")
    override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T {
        return when (defaultValue) {
            is Boolean -> prefs.getBoolean(key, defaultValue) as T
            is String -> prefs.getString(key, defaultValue) as T
            is Int -> prefs.getInt(key, defaultValue) as T
            is Long -> prefs.getLong(key, defaultValue) as T
            is Float -> prefs.getFloat(key, defaultValue) as T
            else -> throw IllegalArgumentException(class="st">"Unsupported type")
        }
    }

    override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) {
        prefs.edit().apply {
            when (value) {
                is Boolean -> putBoolean(key, value)
                is String -> putString(key, value)
                is Int -> putInt(key, value)
                is Long -> putLong(key, value)
                is Float -> putFloat(key, value)
                else -> throw IllegalArgumentException(class="st">"Unsupported type")
            }
            apply()
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// Usage
class Settings(prefs: SharedPreferences) {
    var darkMode: Boolean by PreferenceDelegate(prefs, class="st">"dark_mode", false)
    var username: String by PreferenceDelegate(prefs, class="st">"username", class="st">"")
    var fontSize: Int by PreferenceDelegate(prefs, class="st">"font_size", 14)
}

    3. EXTENSION FUNCTIONS & PROPERTIES

    Extensions add functions/properties to existing classes without inheritance. Resolved STATICALLY (at compile time), not dynamically.


    ⚠️ If the class has a member function with the same signature, the member function wins (extensions don't override members).

    class="cm">// Context extensions — commonly used in Android
fun Context.showToast(message: String, duration: Int = Toast.LENGTH_SHORT) {
    Toast.makeText(this, message, duration).show()
}

fun Context.dpToPx(dp: Float): Int {
    return (dp * resources.displayMetrics.density).roundToInt()
}

val Context.screenWidth: Int
    get() = resources.displayMetrics.widthPixels

class="cm">// Flow extensions
fun <T> Flow<T>.throttleFirst(windowDuration: Long): Flow<T> = flow {
    var lastEmissionTime = 0L
    collect { value ->
        val currentTime = System.currentTimeMillis()
        if (currentTime - lastEmissionTime >= windowDuration) {
            lastEmissionTime = currentTime
            emit(value)
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// Result extensions for cleaner error handling
inline fun <T> Result<T>.onEach(
    onSuccess: (T) -> Unit,
    onFailure: (Throwable) -> Unit
): Result<T> {
    this.onSuccess(onSuccess)
    this.onFailure(onFailure)
    return this
}

    4. GENERICS & VARIANCE

    Variance defines subtyping relationship for generic types.


    Invariant (default):

    MutableList<Dog> is NOT a subtype of MutableList<Animal> → Can read AND write


    Covariant (out):

    List<Dog> IS a subtype of List<Animal> → Can only READ (produce), not write → Use for return types, immutable collections


    Contravariant (in):

    Comparator<Animal> IS a subtype of Comparator<Dog> → Can only WRITE (consume), not read → Use for parameter types, consumers


    Star projection (*):

    List<*> → unknown type, can read as Any?, can't write

    class="cm">// Covariant — produces T
interface Source<out T> {
    fun next(): T  class="cm">// ✅ Can return T
    class="cm">// fun add(item: T)  // ❌ Compile error — can't consume T
}

class="cm">// Contravariant — consumes T
interface Sink<in T> {
    fun put(item: T)  class="cm">// ✅ Can accept T
    class="cm">// fun get(): T    // ❌ Compile error — can't produce T
}

class="cm">// Real-world example
class Repository<out T>(private val items: List<T>) {
    fun getAll(): List<T> = items

    6. INLINE FUNCTIONS

    inline → function body is inserted at the call site (no function object created)


    Benefits:

    - No lambda allocation overhead

    - Can use reified type parameters

    - Non-local returns allowed


    noinline → prevents specific lambda parameter from being inlined crossinline → prevents non-local returns in lambda used in another context

    8. DESIGN PATTERNS IN ANDROID

    Observer Pattern:

    LiveData, StateFlow, Flow — observe data changes Compose's state system — UI recomposes on state change


    Factory Pattern:

    ViewModelProvider.Factory — creates ViewModels with dependencies Retrofit.create() — creates API service implementations


    Builder Pattern:

    OkHttpClient.Builder, Notification.Builder, Room.databaseBuilder Kotlin: use default parameters + apply() instead of explicit builders


    Adapter Pattern:

    RecyclerView.Adapter — adapts data model to views Retrofit Converter — adapts JSON to Kotlin objects


    Repository Pattern:

    Abstract data access, provide single source of truth


    Strategy Pattern:

    Different Dispatchers for different work types Different serializers based on content type


    Singleton Pattern:

    Kotlin's object keyword Hilt's @Singleton scope Room.databaseBuilder with .build() cached


    Decorator Pattern:

    OkHttp Interceptor chain — each interceptor wraps the next Compose Modifier chain — each modifier decorates the composable

    10. KOTLIN CONTRACTS

    Contracts = compiler hints that tell the Kotlin compiler about function behavior it can't otherwise infer.


    Why they exist:

    The compiler can't always analyze function bodies — especially for higher-order functions or custom check functions. Contracts bridge this gap.


    Two main contract types:


    1. callsInPlace — tells compiler how many times a lambda is invoked → Enables smart initialization analysis → Used by: run, let, apply, also, with, synchronized


    2. returns(true/false) implies (condition) — conditional effects → Enables smart casts after custom check functions → Used by: require(), check(), isNullOrEmpty(), isNullOrBlank()

    class="cm">// callsInPlace contract — enables definite initialization
class="an">@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
inline fun <R> executeExactlyOnce(block: () -> R): R {
    contract {
        callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE)
    }
    return block()
}

class="cm">// Without contract, this would be a compile error:
class="cm">//   class="st">"Variable 'result' must be initialized"
fun demonstrateCallsInPlace() {
    val result: String
    executeExactlyOnce {
        result = class="st">"initialized"  class="cm">// Compiler trusts this runs exactly once
    }
    println(result)  class="cm">// ✅ Compiles — compiler knows result is initialized
}

class="cm">// returns implies contract — enables smart casts
class="an">@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun requireNotBlank(value: String?): Boolean {
    contract {
        returns(true) implies (value != null)
    }
    return value != null && value.isNotBlank()
}

fun demonstrateReturnsImplies(name: String?) {
    if (requireNotBlank(name)) {
        class="cm">// ✅ Smart cast: name is String (not String?) here
        println(name.length)
    }
}

class="an">@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun Any?.isNonNullString(): Boolean {
    contract {
        returns(true) implies (thisclass="an">@isNonNullString is String)
    }
    return this is String
}

fun demonstrateTypeCheck(value: Any?) {
    if (value.isNonNullString()) {
        class="cm">// ✅ Smart cast: value is String here
        println(value.uppercase())
    }
}

    How stdlib uses contracts (why require/check enable smart casts):


    public inline fun require(value: Boolean) { contract { returns() implies value } if (!value) throw IllegalArgumentException() }


    public inline fun checkNotNull<T>(value: T?): T { contract { returns() implies (value != null) } if (value == null) throw IllegalStateException() return value }


    ⚠️ Contracts are experimental (as of Kotlin 2.x) and unchecked by the compiler — the compiler trusts them. A wrong contract can lead to unsound code.


    Interview Tip: 💡 You don't need to write contracts often, but understanding

    them explains why require(), check(), and scope functions work so smoothly with Kotlin's type system.

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: When would you use sealed interface vs sealed class? A: sealed interface when you need multiple inheritance or don't need shared state. sealed class when subtypes share common properties. Prefer sealed interface for ADTs (algebraic data types) like UiState.


    Q2: Explain covariance with a real Android example. A: List<Button> can be assigned to List<View> because List is covariant (declared as List<out E>). You can read Views from it but can't add Buttons to a List<View> reference.


    Q3: Why is lazy initialization important on Android? A: Reduces cold start time — don't initialize expensive objects until needed. Example: by lazy for Database, Retrofit, heavy computations. Thread-safe by default (SYNCHRONIZED mode).


    Q4: What's the difference between object and companion object? A: object: singleton, exists independently. Has its own class. companion object: associated with a class, one per class. Members accessible via ClassName.member. Can implement interfaces.


    Q5: How do extension functions work under the hood? A: Compiled to static functions with the receiver as the first parameter. fun String.addExclamation() → StringKt.addExclamation(String str) Resolved statically — no virtual dispatch. If class has member with same signature, member wins.

    1. SYSTEM DESIGN FRAMEWORK — 6-STEP APPROACH

    Step 1: REQUIREMENTS FRAMING (5 min) Functional Requirements:

    - What can the user do? (CRUD, search, share, etc.)

    - What are the core screens/flows? Non-Functional Requirements:

    - Offline support?

    - Real-time updates?

    - Performance targets? (startup < 500ms, scroll 60fps)

    - Scale? (DAU, data volume)

    - Security requirements?


    Step 2: SCALE ESTIMATION (2 min)

    - Back-of-envelope calculations

    - DAU → concurrent users → requests/second

    - Data size per user → total storage → cache budget

    - Network bandwidth requirements


    Step 3: HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURE (5 min)

    - Name your pattern and justify it in one sentence

    - Draw the layer diagram (UI → ViewModel → Repository → DataSources)

    - Identify major components


    Step 4: COMPONENT WALKTHROUGH (15 min)

    - Detail each major component

    - Data models and their relationships

    - API contract (request/response)

    - Caching strategy

    - Sync mechanism


    Step 5: FAILURE MODE ANALYSIS (5 min)

    - What happens when network drops?

    - What happens on process death?

    - What happens with conflicting edits?

    - Auth token expiration mid-request?

    - Database migration failure?


    Step 6: TRADE-OFFS & ALTERNATIVES (3 min)

    - What would you do differently at 10x scale?

    - Alternatives considered and why you rejected them

    - What technical debt does this design accept?

enum class SyncStatus { SYNCED, PENDING, CONFLICT }

class="cm">// Conflict resolution strategy
class ConflictResolver {

    Conflict Resolution Strategies:


    1. Last-Write-Wins (LWW):

    - Simple: higher timestamp wins

    - Risk: silent data loss


    2. Server-Wins:

    - Server version always takes priority

    - Client changes may be lost


    3. Client-Wins:

    - Local version always takes priority

    - Other devices' changes may be lost


    4. Merge (recommended for text):

    - 3-way merge using common ancestor

    - If auto-merge fails, show both versions to user


    For Google interview: discuss trade-offs of each approach.

        fun resolve(local: NoteEntity, remote: NoteEntity, ancestor: NoteEntity?): NoteEntity {
        class="cm">// Field-level merge strategy
        return NoteEntity(
            id = local.id,
            title = if (local.title != ancestor?.title) local.title else remote.title,
            content = mergeContent(local.content, remote.content, ancestor?.content),
            updatedAt = maxOf(local.updatedAt, remote.updatedAt),
            serverVersion = remote.serverVersion,
            localVersion = local.localVersion + 1,
            syncStatus = SyncStatus.SYNCED
        )
    }

    private fun mergeContent(local: String, remote: String, ancestor: String?): String {
        class="cm">// Simplified — real implementation would use OT or CRDT
        if (ancestor == null) return local
        if (local == ancestor) return remote
        if (remote == ancestor) return local
        class="cm">// Both changed — conflict, keep both
        return class="st">"$local\n---CONFLICT---\n$remote"
    }
}

class="cm">// Sync engine using WorkManager
class NoteSyncWorker(
    context: Context,
    params: WorkerParameters,
    private val noteDao: NoteDao,
    private val api: NoteApi,
    private val conflictResolver: ConflictResolver
) : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {

    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        return try {

    1. Push local changes

                val pendingNotes = noteDao.getPendingSync()
            for (note in pendingNotes) {
                val result = api.upsertNote(note.toRequest())
                when {
                    result.isSuccess -> {
                        noteDao.update(note.copy(
                            syncStatus = SyncStatus.SYNCED,
                            serverVersion = result.getOrThrow().version
                        ))
                    }
                    result.isConflict -> {
                        val serverNote = api.getNote(note.id).getOrThrow()
                        val resolved = conflictResolver.resolve(note, serverNote.toEntity(), null)
                        noteDao.update(resolved)
                    }
                }
            }

    2. Pull remote changes

                val lastSyncTime = noteDao.getLastSyncTime()
            val remoteChanges = api.getChanges(since = lastSyncTime)
            for (remote in remoteChanges) {
                val local = noteDao.getById(remote.id)
                if (local == null || local.syncStatus == SyncStatus.SYNCED) {
                    noteDao.upsert(remote.toEntity().copy(syncStatus = SyncStatus.SYNCED))
                }
                class="cm">// If local has pending changes, skip — will resolve on next push
            }

            Result.success()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            if (runAttemptCount < 5) Result.retry() else Result.failure()
        }
    }
}

    private val maxMemory = (Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / 1024).toInt()
    private val cacheSize = maxMemory / 8
    private val memoryCache = object : LruCache<String, Bitmap>(cacheSize) {
        override fun sizeOf(key: String, bitmap: Bitmap): Int {
            return bitmap.byteCount / 1024
        }
    }

    class="cm">// Disk cache
    private val diskCache = DiskLruCache.open(
        File(context.cacheDir, class="st">"image_cache"),
        1, 1, 100L * 1024 * 1024  class="cm">// 100 MB
    )

    class="cm">// Request deduplication
    private val inflightRequests = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Deferred<Bitmap?>>()
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO + SupervisorJob())

    suspend fun load(
        url: String,
        width: Int = 0,
        height: Int = 0
    ): Bitmap? {
        val cacheKey = generateKey(url, width, height)

    1. Memory cache check

            memoryCache.get(cacheKey)?.let { return it }

    2. Deduplicate concurrent requests for same image

            inflightRequests[cacheKey]?.let {
            return it.await()
        }

        val deferred = scope.async {
            try {

    3. Disk cache check

                    val diskBitmap = loadFromDisk(cacheKey)
                if (diskBitmap != null) {
                    memoryCache.put(cacheKey, diskBitmap)
                    returnclass="an">@async diskBitmap
                }

    4. Network download

                    val networkBitmap = downloadAndDecode(url, width, height)
                if (networkBitmap != null) {
                    memoryCache.put(cacheKey, networkBitmap)
                    saveToDisk(cacheKey, networkBitmap)
                }
                networkBitmap
            } finally {
                inflightRequests.remove(cacheKey)
            }
        }
        inflightRequests[cacheKey] = deferred

        return deferred.await()
    }

    private fun generateKey(url: String, width: Int, height: Int): String {
        return class="st">"${url}_${width}x${height}".hashCode().toString()
    }

    private fun downloadAndDecode(url: String, reqWidth: Int, reqHeight: Int): Bitmap? {

    }

}

    Key Discussion Points:


    1. Memory pressure: LruCache eviction, respond to onTrimMemory()

    2. Disk cache: DiskLruCache with journaling for crash safety

    3. Sampling: BitmapFactory.Options.inSampleSize to decode at target size

    4. Lifecycle: cancel requests when target View is recycled/detached

    5. Bitmap pooling: reuse Bitmap memory (inBitmap) to reduce GC

    6. Thread pool: dedicated for decoding (CPU-bound), separate for network (IO)

    Send: UI → ViewModel → Repository → Room (PENDING) → WebSocket → Server ACK → Room (SENT) → Server delivers → Room (DELIVERED) → Recipient reads → Room (READ)


    Receive: WebSocket → Repository → Room → Flow → ViewModel → UI (or FCM → WorkManager → Repository → Room when backgrounded)

class="cm">// WebSocket connection management
class ChatWebSocketClient(
    private val okHttpClient: OkHttpClient,
    private val messageDao: MessageDao,
    private val scope: CoroutineScope
) {
    private var webSocket: WebSocket? = null
    private val _connectionState = MutableStateFlow<ConnectionState>(ConnectionState.Disconnected)
    val connectionState: StateFlow<ConnectionState> = _connectionState.asStateFlow()

    private val _incomingMessages = MutableSharedFlow<ServerMessage>(
        extraBufferCapacity = 100,
        onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST
    )
    val incomingMessages: SharedFlow<ServerMessage> = _incomingMessages.asSharedFlow()

    fun connect(authToken: String) {
        val request = Request.Builder()
            .url(class="st">"wss:class="cm">//chat.example.com/ws")
            .header(class="st">"Authorization", class="st">"Bearer $authToken")
            .build()

        webSocket = okHttpClient.newWebSocket(request, object : WebSocketListener() {
            override fun onOpen(webSocket: WebSocket, response: Response) {
                _connectionState.value = ConnectionState.Connected
            }

            override fun onMessage(webSocket: WebSocket, text: String) {
                val message = Json.decodeFromString<ServerMessage>(text)
                scope.launch { _incomingMessages.emit(message) }
            }

            override fun onFailure(webSocket: WebSocket, t: Throwable, response: Response?) {
                _connectionState.value = ConnectionState.Error(t)
                scheduleReconnect()
            }

            override fun onClosed(webSocket: WebSocket, code: Int, reason: String) {
                _connectionState.value = ConnectionState.Disconnected
            }
        })
    }

    private fun scheduleReconnect() {
        scope.launch {
            var delay = 1000L
            while (_connectionState.value !is ConnectionState.Connected) {
                delay(delay)
                delay = minOf(delay * 2, 30_000)  class="cm">// Exponential backoff, max 30s
                connect(getStoredToken())
            }
        }
    }

    fun send(message: String): Boolean {
        return webSocket?.send(message) ?: false
    }

    fun disconnect() {
        webSocket?.close(1000, class="st">"User disconnected")
    }
}

sealed interface ConnectionState {
    data object Connected : ConnectionState
    data object Connecting : ConnectionState
    data object Disconnected : ConnectionState
    data class Error(val throwable: Throwable) : ConnectionState
}

    Key Design Decisions to Discuss:


    1. Message Ordering: Use server-assigned timestamps for final ordering, local sequence numbers for optimistic display.


    2. Offline Queue: Messages saved to Room with PENDING status. When online, WorkManager or WebSocket reconnect sends pending messages.


    3. Pagination: Load messages from Room with Paging 3. Older messages fetched from API and cached in Room.


    4. Push Notifications: FCM for when WebSocket is disconnected. Data message (not notification message) for custom handling.


    5. E2E Encryption: Signal Protocol (libsignal). Keys stored in Android Keystore. Key exchange on first contact.


    6. Reconnection: Exponential backoff with jitter. On reconnect, fetch missed messages since last known timestamp.

    5. DESIGN: NEWS FEED

    Requirements:

    - Scrollable feed of posts (text, images, video)

    - Pull-to-refresh

    - Infinite scroll with pagination

    - Like, comment, share actions

    - Efficient image/video loading

    - Offline reading of cached content


    Key Components:


    1. Feed ViewModel:

    - Paging 3 with RemoteMediator

    - Room as cache, API as remote source


    2. Image Loading:

    - Coil with memory + disk cache

    - Placeholder → low-res thumbnail → full image


    3. Video:

    - ExoPlayer with preloading

    - Auto-play when >50% visible

    - Pause when scrolled away


    4. RecyclerView/LazyColumn Optimization:

    - Stable keys for items

    - DiffUtil for minimal updates

    - View recycling across view types

    - Prefetch for smooth scrolling


    5. Real-time Updates:

    - New post indicator (don't auto-scroll)

    - Like count updates via WebSocket/SSE

    - Optimistic UI updates for user actions

    6. DESIGN: ANALYTICS SDK

    Requirements:

    - Track events (screen views, clicks, custom events)

    - Batch and send periodically (minimize network calls)

    - Persist events if network unavailable

    - Minimal performance impact

    - Thread-safe

    - Battery-friendly


    Architecture:

    Event → Queue (in-memory) → Batcher → Disk (if threshold/timer) → WorkManager → API upload → Clear from disk

    class AnalyticsSDK private constructor(private val context: Context) {

    private val eventQueue = Channel<AnalyticsEvent>(Channel.UNLIMITED)
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO + SupervisorJob())
    private val db: AnalyticsDatabase by lazy { AnalyticsDatabase.create(context) }

    init {
        class="cm">// Consumer: batch events and persist
        scope.launch {
            val batch = mutableListOf<AnalyticsEvent>()
            for (event in eventQueue) {
                batch.add(event)
                if (batch.size >= BATCH_SIZE) {
                    persistBatch(batch.toList())
                    batch.clear()
                    scheduleUpload()
                }
            }
        }

        class="cm">// Periodic flush
        scope.launch {
            while (true) {
                delay(FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS)
                flushPendingEvents()
            }
        }
    }

    fun track(eventName: String, properties: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap()) {
        val event = AnalyticsEvent(
            name = eventName,
            properties = properties,
            timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis(),
            sessionId = SessionManager.currentSessionId
        )
        eventQueue.trySend(event)
    }

    private suspend fun persistBatch(events: List<AnalyticsEvent>) {
        db.eventDao().insertAll(events.map { it.toEntity() })
    }

    private fun scheduleUpload() {
        val uploadWork = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<AnalyticsUploadWorker>()
            .setConstraints(Constraints.Builder()
                .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED)
                .build())
            .build()
        WorkManager.getInstance(context)
            .enqueueUniqueWork(class="st">"analytics_upload", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, uploadWork)
    }

    companion object {
        private const val BATCH_SIZE = 50
        private const val FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS = 30_000L

        class="an">@Volatile private var instance: AnalyticsSDK? = null

        fun init(context: Context): AnalyticsSDK {
            return instance ?: synchronized(this) {
                instance ?: AnalyticsSDK(context.applicationContext).also { instance = it }
            }
        }
    }
}

    7. DESIGN: FILE DOWNLOADER LIBRARY

    Requirements:

    - Download files from URL with pause/resume support

    - Progress reporting per download

    - Multiple parallel downloads with queue management

    - Survive process death and device reboot

    - Retry on failure with backoff

    - Notification for each active download


    Architecture:

    UI → DownloadManager API → Room (state) → WorkManager (execution) → OkHttp with Range headers → Disk


    Room stores: URL, file path, status, bytes downloaded, total bytes WorkManager: one worker per download, unique work by URL OkHttp: HTTP Range header for resume support Flow: progress updates from worker → UI

    class="cm">// Download state persisted in Room
class="an">@Entity(tableName = class="st">"downloads")
data class DownloadEntity(
    class="an">@PrimaryKey val id: String = UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
    val url: String,
    val fileName: String,
    val destinationPath: String,
    val status: DownloadStatus = DownloadStatus.QUEUED,
    val bytesDownloaded: Long = 0,
    val totalBytes: Long = -1,  class="cm">// -1 = unknown until server responds
    val createdAt: Long = System.currentTimeMillis(),
    val error: String? = null,
    val retryCount: Int = 0
)

enum class DownloadStatus { QUEUED, DOWNLOADING, PAUSED, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED }

class="an">@Dao
interface DownloadDao {
    class="an">@Query(class="st">"SELECT * FROM downloads ORDER BY createdAt DESC")
    fun observeAll(): Flow<List<DownloadEntity>>

    class="an">@Query(class="st">"SELECT * FROM downloads WHERE id = :id")
    suspend fun getById(id: String): DownloadEntity?

    class="an">@Upsert
    suspend fun upsert(download: DownloadEntity)

    class="an">@Query(class="st">"UPDATE downloads SET status = :status WHERE id = :id")
    suspend fun updateStatus(id: String, status: DownloadStatus)

    class="an">@Query(class="st">"UPDATE downloads SET bytesDownloaded = :bytes WHERE id = :id")
    suspend fun updateProgress(id: String, bytes: Long)
}

class="cm">// Download worker with resume support via HTTP Range headers
class FileDownloadWorker(
    context: Context,
    params: WorkerParameters,
    private val downloadDao: DownloadDao,
    private val okHttpClient: OkHttpClient
) : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {

    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        val downloadId = inputData.getString(class="st">"download_id") ?: return Result.failure()
        val download = downloadDao.getById(downloadId) ?: return Result.failure()

        downloadDao.updateStatus(downloadId, DownloadStatus.DOWNLOADING)

        return try {
            val file = File(download.destinationPath)
            val existingBytes = if (file.exists()) file.length() else 0L

            class="cm">// Range header for resume support
            val request = Request.Builder()
                .url(download.url)
                .apply {
                    if (existingBytes > 0) {
                        addHeader(class="st">"Range", class="st">"bytes=$existingBytes-")
                    }
                }
                .build()

            okHttpClient.newCall(request).execute().use { response ->
                if (!response.isSuccessful && response.code != 206) {
                    throw IOException(class="st">"Unexpected code: ${response.code}")
                }

                val totalBytes = if (response.code == 206) {
                    existingBytes + (response.body?.contentLength() ?: 0)
                } else {
                    response.body?.contentLength() ?: -1
                }

                downloadDao.upsert(download.copy(totalBytes = totalBytes))

                val sink = file.appendingSink().buffer()
                val source = response.body?.source() ?: throw IOException(class="st">"Empty body")

                var bytesRead = existingBytes
                val buffer = ByteArray(8192)
                var read: Int

                while (source.read(buffer).also { read = it.toInt() } != -1L) {
                    sink.write(buffer, 0, read)
                    bytesRead += read

                    class="cm">// Report progress
                    downloadDao.updateProgress(downloadId, bytesRead)
                    setProgress(workDataOf(
                        class="st">"progress" to bytesRead,
                        class="st">"total" to totalBytes
                    ))
                }
                sink.flush()
                sink.close()
            }

            downloadDao.updateStatus(downloadId, DownloadStatus.COMPLETED)
            Result.success()
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            if (runAttemptCount < 3) {
                downloadDao.updateStatus(downloadId, DownloadStatus.QUEUED)
                Result.retry()
            } else {
                downloadDao.upsert(download.copy(
                    status = DownloadStatus.FAILED,
                    error = e.message
                ))
                Result.failure()
            }
        }
    }
}

    Key Discussion Points:


    1. Resume: HTTP Range header + append to existing file. Server must support 206 Partial Content. If not, restart from scratch.


    2. Parallel downloads: Each download is a separate WorkManager unique work. Limit concurrency with a custom Configuration (max workers).


    3. Queue management: Room tracks all downloads. UI observes via Flow. Priority queue can be implemented with a priority field in entity.


    4. Pause/Resume: Pause = cancel the worker + save bytesDownloaded in Room. Resume = re-enqueue work, worker reads bytesDownloaded and sets Range header.


    5. Notifications: setForeground(ForegroundInfo) in CoroutineWorker for ongoing notification with progress bar.


    6. Integrity: After download, verify checksum (MD5/SHA-256) if server provides one.

    8. DESIGN: OBSERVABILITY / LOGGING SDK

    Requirements:

    - Structured logging (tag, level, message, metadata)

    - Crash reporting (uncaught exception handler)

    - Performance metrics (startup time, frame drops, network latency)

    - Batched upload to backend (minimize network calls)

    - Persist logs to disk if network unavailable

    - Minimal impact on app performance and battery


    Architecture:

    App code → Logger API → In-memory ring buffer → Flush to disk → WorkManager → Batch upload to backend → Crash handler → Immediate disk write → Upload on next launch


    Log levels: VERBOSE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL


    Sampling:

    - DEBUG/VERBOSE: only in debug builds (never ship)

    - INFO: sample at 10-50% of sessions to reduce volume

    - WARN/ERROR: always log, always upload

    - FATAL (crash): always log, persist immediately, upload on next launch


    Privacy considerations:

    - NEVER log PII (emails, passwords, tokens, phone numbers)

    - Strip sensitive fields before logging

    - Allow users to opt out of analytics/logging

    - Comply with GDPR/CCPA — include session ID, not user ID, unless consented


    Integration with existing tools:

    - Firebase Crashlytics: crash reports + non-fatals, auto stack deobfuscation

    - Play Console Android Vitals: ANRs, crash rates, startup time, battery

    - Perfetto: system-level traces for debugging performance

    - Custom backend: for proprietary metrics and business-specific logging

    data class LogEntry(
    val level: LogLevel,
    val tag: String,
    val message: String,
    val metadata: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(),
    val timestamp: Long = System.currentTimeMillis(),
    val sessionId: String,
    val threadName: String = Thread.currentThread().name,
    val stackTrace: String? = null
)

enum class LogLevel { VERBOSE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL }

class ObservabilitySDK private constructor(private val context: Context) {

    private val buffer = ArrayDeque<LogEntry>(BUFFER_CAPACITY)
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO + SupervisorJob())
    private val sessionId = UUID.randomUUID().toString()

    fun log(level: LogLevel, tag: String, message: String, metadata: Map<String, String> = emptyMap()) {
        if (level.ordinal < minLogLevel.ordinal) return

        val entry = LogEntry(
            level = level,
            tag = tag,
            message = message,
            metadata = metadata,
            sessionId = sessionId
        )

        synchronized(buffer) {
            buffer.addLast(entry)
            if (buffer.size >= FLUSH_THRESHOLD) {
                flushBufferToDisk()
            }
        }
    }

    fun installCrashHandler() {
        val defaultHandler = Thread.getDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler()
        Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler { thread, throwable ->
            log(
                level = LogLevel.FATAL,
                tag = class="st">"CRASH",
                message = throwable.message ?: class="st">"Unknown crash",
                metadata = mapOf(class="st">"thread" to thread.name)
            )
            class="cm">// Flush immediately — process is about to die
            flushBufferToDisk()
            defaultHandler?.uncaughtException(thread, throwable)
        }
    }

    private fun flushBufferToDisk() {
        val entries: List<LogEntry>
        synchronized(buffer) {
            entries = buffer.toList()
            buffer.clear()
        }
        scope.launch {
            class="cm">// Persist to local file or Room, then schedule upload
            persistEntries(entries)
            scheduleUpload()
        }
    }

    private suspend fun persistEntries(entries: List<LogEntry>) { class="cm">/* Write to disk */ }

    private fun scheduleUpload() {
        WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueueUniqueWork(
            class="st">"log_upload",
            ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP,
            OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<LogUploadWorker>()
                .setConstraints(Constraints.Builder()
                    .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED)
                    .build())
                .build()
        )
    }

    companion object {
        private const val BUFFER_CAPACITY = 500
        private const val FLUSH_THRESHOLD = 100
        private var minLogLevel = LogLevel.INFO
    }
}

    Key Discussion Points:


    1. Ring buffer: Fixed-size in-memory buffer avoids OOM. Oldest entries evicted if not flushed fast enough.


    2. Crash reporting: Install UncaughtExceptionHandler, flush synchronously, then delegate to original handler. Upload on next app launch.


    3. Performance metrics: Track via FrameMetrics API (API 24+) for jank, reportFullyDrawn() for startup. Send as structured log entries.


    4. Batched upload: Reduces battery and network usage. Compress (gzip) before upload. Back-pressure: if disk queue grows too large, drop lowest-severity entries.

    9. COMMON MOBILE-SPECIFIC CONSTRAINTS

    Always discuss these in mobile system design:


    1. Network: Hostile environment — drops, slow, metered → Offline-first, retry with backoff, request deduplication


    2. Battery: Background work is heavily restricted → WorkManager, batch operations, avoid polling


    3. Memory: Limited heap (256MB-512MB typical) → LRU caches, bitmap sampling, leak detection


    4. Storage: Users care about app size → On-demand resources, aggressive caching policy with eviction


    5. Process Death: App can be killed at any time → Restore state from SavedStateHandle + persistent storage


    6. Security: Device can be rooted, APK can be decompiled → Keystore for secrets, cert pinning, obfuscation


    7. Lifecycle: Screens can be created/destroyed unpredictably → Lifecycle-aware components, scoped work


    8. Fragmentation: Thousands of device configs → Responsive layouts, API level checks, Compat libraries

    PRACTICE QUESTIONS

    Q1: How do you handle sync conflicts in an offline-first app? A: Depends on the data type:

    - Last-Write-Wins for simple fields (user profile)

    - 3-way merge for text (notes, documents)

    - CRDTs for concurrent data structures (counters, sets)

    - Manual resolution (show both versions to user) Always discuss: What's the cost of data loss vs. complexity?


    Q2: Design a file download manager with pause/resume support. A: Room tracks download state (URL, progress, status, temp file path). OkHttp with Range headers for resume. WorkManager for background execution. CoroutineWorker with progress reporting. Notification for progress. Unique work per URL.


    Q3: How would you implement optimistic UI updates? A: Update local state immediately (Room + StateFlow). Send request to server in background. On success: update sync status. On failure: revert local state, show error. Example: Like button — show liked immediately, sync later.


    Q4: How do you handle token expiration in a WebSocket connection? A: Server sends a "token_expired" message. Client refreshes token, reconnects with new token. During refresh, queue outgoing messages. After reconnect, replay pending messages + fetch missed messages using last known server timestamp.

    16 -- Interview Questions & Mock Q&A

    16 — INTERVIEW QUESTIONS & MOCK Q&A

    Google SDE-2 Android Developer — Domain Round



    How This Round Works at Google


  • Duration: 45-60 minutes
  • Format: Deep technical discussion with code on whiteboard/shared editor
  • Interviewer: Senior Android engineer from Google
  • Expectation: Production-quality thinking, not textbook answers
  • Follow-ups: Expect 2-3 levels of follow-up questions going deeper


    • TIER 1: MOST FREQUENTLY ASKED (Expect 2-3 of these)


    Q1: Explain the Activity lifecycle. What happens when Activity A launches Activity B?


    Expected Answer:


    Activity lifecycle callbacks: onCreate → onStart → onResume → onPause → onStop → onDestroy


    When A launches B (B is opaque):

    A.onPause()
B.onCreate()
B.onStart()
B.onResume()
A.onStop()    ← A stops AFTER B is fully visible

    Follow-ups:

  • What if B is transparent/dialog? → A only reaches onPause, never onStop
  • Where should you save state? → onSaveInstanceState (after onStop on API 28+)
  • What survives config change? → ViewModel survives, Bundle survives, nothing else
  • What about process death? → ViewModel is lost, only Bundle and persistent storage survive


    • Q2: Compare StateFlow and SharedFlow. When would you use each?


    Expected Answer:


    FeatureStateFlowSharedFlow
    Initial valueRequiredNot required
    ReplayAlways 1 (latest)Configurable (0, 1, N)
    Equality checkYes (conflated)No
    Best forUI StateEvents/Signals

    class="cm">// StateFlow — UI State (always has a current value)
private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
val uiState: StateFlow<UiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow()

class="cm">// SharedFlow — One-time events (no replay = no re-delivery)
private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>(replay = 0)
val events: SharedFlow<UiEvent> = _events.asSharedFlow()

class="cm">// Channel — Guaranteed delivery events (navigation, toast)
private val _navigation = Channel<NavEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED)
val navigation = _navigation.receiveAsFlow()

    Follow-up: Why Channel over SharedFlow for navigation?

    → Channel buffers events and delivers exactly once. SharedFlow with replay=0 loses events if no collector is active (e.g., during config change).



    Q3: How does Jetpack Compose handle recomposition? How do you optimize it?


    Expected Answer:


    Compose tracks which composables READ which State<T> objects. When a state changes, only composables that read it are re-executed ("smart recomposition").


    Recomposition can be skipped if:

  • All parameters are stable (primitives, @Stable/@Immutable classes)
  • Parameters haven't changed (by equality)

    • Optimization techniques:

    class="cm">// 1. Use derivedStateOf to avoid unnecessary recomposition
val showButton by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 5 } }

class="cm">// 2. Defer state reads to later phases
Modifier.offset { IntOffset(x.toInt(), 0) }  class="cm">// Layout phase, not Composition

class="cm">// 3. Use ImmutableList instead of List
fun Items(items: ImmutableList<Item>)  class="cm">// Skippable

class="cm">// 4. Use key() for stable identity
LazyColumn { items(articles, key = { it.id }) { ... } }

class="cm">// 5. Use collectAsStateWithLifecycle (not collectAsState)
val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    Follow-up: What are the 3 phases of Compose rendering?

    → Composition (what to show), Layout (where to place), Drawing (how to render). Reading state in a later phase avoids triggering earlier phases.



    Q4: Explain structured concurrency in Kotlin coroutines.


    Expected Answer:


    Structured concurrency = coroutines form a parent-child hierarchy with these guarantees:

  • Parent waits for all children to complete
  • Cancelling parent cancels all children
  • Child failure cancels parent and siblings (unless SupervisorJob)
  • Coroutines can only be launched in a CoroutineScope

    • class="cm">// ✅ Structured — automatically cancelled when ViewModel is cleared
viewModelScope.launch {
    val user = async { fetchUser() }
    val posts = async { fetchPosts() }
    updateUI(user.await(), posts.await())
}

class="cm">// ❌ Breaks structured concurrency
GlobalScope.launch { class="cm">/* Leaked coroutine — never cancelled */ }

    Follow-up: What's the difference between coroutineScope and supervisorScope?

    → coroutineScope: one child failure cancels all siblings. supervisorScope: siblings continue even if one fails. Use supervisorScope for partial failure tolerance (e.g., loading user profile where posts can fail but user data is essential).



    Q5: How would you architect an offline-first app?


    Expected Answer:


    Core principle: Room is the Single Source of Truth. UI reads from Room, never directly from network.


    UI → ViewModel → Repository → Room (SSOT)
                      ↓
               Network (sync)

    Pattern:

  • UI observes Room via Flow<List<T>>
  • Repository checks if cache is stale
  • If stale, fetch from API and upsert into Room
  • Room Flow automatically emits updated data to UI
  • Writes go to Room immediately (optimistic), sync to server via WorkManager

    • Conflict resolution: Last-Write-Wins for simple data, 3-way merge for text, user resolution for complex conflicts.


    override fun observeArticles(): Flow<List<Article>> =

    val remote = api.getArticles()
    articleDao.upsertAll(remote.map { it.toEntity() })

}


    Q6: How does Hilt work? Explain scoping.


    Expected Answer:


    Hilt generates Dagger components at compile time for Android classes.


    Component hierarchy (outer → inner):

    SingletonComponent (Application)
  └── ActivityRetainedComponent (survives config change)
        └── ViewModelComponent (per ViewModel)
        └── ActivityComponent (per Activity)
              └── FragmentComponent (per Fragment)

    class="cm">// Singleton — one instance for app lifetime
class="an">@Module
class="an">@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object NetworkModule {
    class="an">@Provides class="an">@Singleton
    fun provideRetrofit(): Retrofit = ...
}

class="cm">// ViewModel injection

class MyViewModel class="an">@Inject constructor(
    private val useCase: GetArticlesUseCase,
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle

class="cm">// class="an">@Binds for interface → implementation mapping (more efficient than class="an">@Provides)

    Follow-up: What's the difference between @Provides and @Binds?

    → @Provides: creates instances, can have logic. @Binds: maps interface to implementation, must be abstract, generates less code.



    TIER 2: FREQUENTLY ASKED (Expect 1-2 of these)


    Q7: Explain ViewModel. How does it survive configuration changes?


    ViewModel is stored in ViewModelStore, which is retained via NonConfigurationInstance mechanism. When Activity is destroyed for config change, the ViewModelStore is transferred to the new Activity instance.


    Key facts:

  • Survives config change ✅
  • Does NOT survive process death ❌ (use SavedStateHandle)
  • Has viewModelScope (cancelled in onCleared())
  • Should NEVER hold View or Activity references


    • Q8: What are `LaunchedEffect`, `DisposableEffect`, and `SideEffect`?


    class="cm">// LaunchedEffect — coroutine work, restarts on key change
LaunchedEffect(userId) {
    val user = repository.fetchUser(userId)
}

class="cm">// DisposableEffect — register/unregister pattern
DisposableEffect(lifecycleOwner) {
    val observer = LifecycleEventObserver { ... }
    lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(observer)
    onDispose { lifecycleOwner.lifecycle.removeObserver(observer) }
}

class="cm">// SideEffect — runs every recomposition (sync non-Compose state)
SideEffect {
    analytics.setUserProperty(class="st">"screen", screenName)
}


    Q9: How do you handle one-time events in MVVM?


    Problem: StateFlow re-delivers the last value to new collectors. Navigation events, toasts, snackbars should fire once.


    Solution: Use Channel + receiveAsFlow():

    private val _events = Channel<UiEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED)
val events = _events.receiveAsFlow()

_events.send(UiEvent.ShowToast(class="st">"Success"))

LaunchedEffect(Unit) {

        when (event) {
            is UiEvent.ShowToast -> snackbarHostState.showSnackbar(event.message)
            is UiEvent.Navigate -> navController.navigate(event.route)
        }
    }

    Q11: How do you prevent memory leaks in Android?


    Common leaks and fixes:


    Leak SourceFix
    Static Activity referenceUse Application Context or WeakReference
    Handler with Activity refUse lifecycleScope.launch
    Fragment View bindingNull out _binding in onDestroyView
    Unregistered listenersUnregister in matching lifecycle callback
    ViewModel holding View refNever pass View/Activity to ViewModel
    Anonymous inner classesUse static class + WeakReference
    Coroutine scope outliving componentUse viewModelScope / lifecycleScope

    Detection: LeakCanary (auto in debug), Memory Profiler (manual heap dumps).



    Q12: WorkManager vs other background APIs


    APIUse CaseSurvives reboot?
    WorkManagerDeferrable, guaranteed work✅
    CoroutinesImmediate, in-app work❌
    Foreground ServiceLong-running visible taskDepends
    AlarmManagerExact-time triggers✅

    WorkManager is the default answer for almost all background work:

  • Constraints (network, battery, charging)
  • Chaining (sequential and parallel)
  • Retry with backoff
  • Unique work (prevent duplicates)
  • Observable progress


    • Q13: Notifications & Channels


    Expected Answer:


    NotificationChannel (API 26+): Group notifications by type (messages, promotions, alerts). Each channel has user-controllable importance level:

  • IMPORTANCE_HIGH → heads-up notification
  • IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT → sound + status bar
  • IMPORTANCE_LOW → no sound, status bar only
  • IMPORTANCE_MIN → no sound, no status bar

    • class="cm">// Create channel (safe to call repeatedly — no-op if exists)

notificationManager.createNotificationChannel(channel)

    context, 0, intent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT
)

    .setContentTitle(class="st">"New message")

  • API 31+: PendingIntent must specify FLAG_MUTABLE or FLAG_IMMUTABLE
  • API 33+: POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission required
  • Notification styles: BigTextStyle, InboxStyle, MessagingStyle (for chat)

    LayerTest TypeTools
    ViewModel / UseCaseUnit testJUnit, Turbine, MockK
    RepositoryUnit test (fakes)JUnit, fake data sources
    Room DAOIntegration testAndroidJUnit4, in-memory DB
    Compose UIUI testComposeTestRule

  • Use mocks (MockK/Mockito) only when fakes are impractical (e.g., Android framework classes)

    Q15: Performance Diagnosis


    Expected Answer:


    Diagnosing slow app startup:

  • Measure: adb shell am start -W (TotalTime), reportFullyDrawn(), Macrobenchmark
  • Profile: Android Studio Profiler or Perfetto trace during cold start
  • Common culprits: heavy Application.onCreate(), synchronous disk I/O on main thread, large view hierarchies, eager DI initialization

    • Tools:

  • Perfetto: System-level tracing — CPU, memory, disk I/O, frame rendering
  • Macrobenchmark: Automated startup/scroll benchmarks in CI
  • Baseline Profiles: AOT-compile hot paths for 20-30% faster startup
  • Android Vitals (Play Console): Production crash rate, ANR rate, startup time, stuck frames

    TIER 3: DEEP DIVE QUESTIONS (For strong candidates)


    Q16: Explain the Compose Snapshot system.


    Compose uses a snapshot system (similar to software transactional memory) to track state reads and writes. When mutableStateOf() is read during composition, the snapshot records it. When the state value changes, all compositions that read it are invalidated and scheduled for recomposition.



    Q17: How does the Binder IPC mechanism work?


    Client → Proxy → Parcel → Binder Driver (kernel) → Server process → unparcel → execute → return path. Everything in Android uses Binder: startActivity(), bindService(), ContentResolver. Transaction limit ~1MB per process.



    Q18: Design a pagination system for a chat app.


  • Messages loaded from Room with PagingSource
  • Oldest-first loading (scroll up to load older messages)
  • RemoteMediator fetches older messages from API, stores in Room
  • New incoming messages via WebSocket → insert to Room → Flow emits → UI updates
  • Handle: message ordering, gap detection, duplicate prevention


    • BEHAVIORAL TIPS FOR GOOGLE


  • Think out loud — explain your reasoning as you go
  • Discuss trade-offs — never present one solution as perfect
  • Mention scale — Google apps serve billions of users
  • Ask clarifying questions — don't assume requirements
  • Write clean code — even on whiteboard, proper naming and structure
  • Mention testing — how would you test this?
  • Be honest — if you don't know something, say "I haven't used this directly, but here's my understanding..."


    • RAPID FIRE — Quick Answers to Know


  • repeatOnLifecycle vs launchWhenStarted? → repeatOnLifecycle cancels and restarts; launchWhenStarted just suspends (deprecated, can waste resources)
  • remember vs rememberSaveable? → remember survives recomposition; rememberSaveable also survives config change + process death
  • by viewModels() vs by activityViewModels()? → Fragment-scoped vs Activity-scoped ViewModel
  • data class vs class for UI state? → data class for immutable state (copy, equals, hashCode for free)
  • Why Flow over LiveData? → Kotlin-native, no Android dependency, richer operators, works in domain/data layers
  • flatMapLatest vs flatMapConcat? → Latest cancels previous (search); Concat is sequential (ordered processing)
  • App Bundle vs APK? → Bundle lets Play generate optimized APKs per device (15-20% smaller)
  • @Stable vs @Immutable? → @Immutable: all properties never change. @Stable: changes are observable via Compose State
  • Process death test? → ADB: adb shell am kill <package>, or Android Studio terminate button
  • What is callbackFlow? → Wraps callback-based APIs as a Flow; needs awaitClose to unregister the callback when the flow collector cancels
  • Compose Navigation type-safe routes? → Use Kotlin @Serializable classes as route types instead of string routes (Navigation 2.8+)
  • onTrimMemory? → System callback signaling memory pressure; clear caches at appropriate levels (TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOW, TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN)
  • ProGuard vs R8? → R8 replaced ProGuard as default; faster, Kotlin-aware, single-step DEX+shrink, same rule format
