    3. Delegates.notNull<T>() — like lateinit but for primitives (since lateinit doesn't support primitive types).

    class LazyInitExample {
    class="cm">// lazy — initialized on first access, thread-safe, cached
    val heavyObject: ExpensiveParser by lazy {
        println(class="st">"Creating parser...")
        ExpensiveParser()
    }

    class="cm">// lateinit — initialized later, before use
    lateinit var injectedService: ApiService

    class="cm">// notNull — for primitive types that can't use lateinit
    var maxRetries: Int by Delegates.notNull()

    fun setup() {
        maxRetries = 3
        class="cm">// Can now use maxRetries safely
    }
}

    SECTION 4: ANDROID — BASE

    Q: Why does an Android App lag?

    Android renders UI at 60 fps (16.67ms per frame). Lag ("jank") occurs when a frame takes longer than this budget. Root causes:


    1. Main thread blockage — network calls, DB reads, heavy computation on the UI thread starve the choreographer of time to draw.


    2. Overdraw — the same pixel is drawn multiple times per frame. Diagnose: Developer Options → Debug GPU overdraw.


    3. Deep view hierarchies — measure/layout/draw passes scale with tree depth. Each nested ViewGroup multiplies traversal cost.


    4. Expensive onDraw() / layout — custom views doing allocations inside onDraw(), or repeated requestLayout() calls trigger extra passes.


    5. Garbage collection pauses — frequent small allocations (e.g., inside onDraw or onBindViewHolder) cause GC pressure, stalling the main thread.


    6. Bitmap / image decoding on main thread — loading large images without downsampling or async decoding.


    7. RecyclerView misuse — no ViewHolder reuse, inflating in onBindViewHolder, calling notifyDataSetChanged() instead of DiffUtil.


    Tools for diagnosis:

    - Android Profiler (CPU, Memory, Energy)

    - Systrace / Perfetto for frame-level analysis

    - Layout Inspector for view hierarchy depth

    - StrictMode for accidental disk/network on main thread

    fun enableStrictModeForDebug() {
    if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
        StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(
            StrictMode.ThreadPolicy.Builder()
                .detectDiskReads()
                .detectDiskWrites()
                .detectNetwork()
                .penaltyLog()
                .build()
        )
        StrictMode.setVmPolicy(
            StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder()
                .detectLeakedClosableObjects()
                .detectActivityLeaks()
                .penaltyLog()
                .build()
        )
    }
}

    Q: What is Context? How is it used?

    Context is an abstract class that provides access to application-specific resources and classes, as well as calls for app-level operations like launching activities, broadcasting, receiving intents, etc.


    It is the bridge between your code and the Android system.


    Two main concrete types:


    Application Context (applicationContext)

    - Singleton tied to the app process lifetime

    - Safe for DI graphs, singletons, repositories, databases

    - CANNOT show dialogs, inflate themed views, or start activities without FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK


    Activity Context (this in Activity)

    - Tied to the Activity lifecycle; destroyed with it

    - Required for UI operations: dialogs, toasts, inflating themed views

    - Storing a long-lived reference to it causes memory leaks


    Common uses:

    - Accessing resources: context.getString(R.string.app_name)

    - Starting components: context.startActivity(), context.startService()

    - Accessing system services: context.getSystemService(...)

    - File operations: context.filesDir, context.cacheDir

    - SharedPreferences: context.getSharedPreferences(...)

    - Inflating layouts: LayoutInflater.from(context)


    Rule of thumb: Use Application Context for anything that outlives an Activity. Use Activity Context for anything UI-related.

    class MyRepository(private val context: Context) {
    class="cm">// Uses applicationContext to avoid leaking an Activity
    private val appContext = context.applicationContext

    fun getCacheDir(): File = appContext.cacheDir

    fun getSystemService(): ConnectivityManager =
        appContext.getSystemService(Context.CONNECTIVITY_SERVICE) as ConnectivityManager
}

    Q: How does Zygote make Android apps start faster?

    Zygote is a special daemon process that starts at boot time. It pre-loads the entire Android framework (core libraries, common classes, resources) and the Dalvik/ART runtime into memory.


    When a new app process is needed, the system tells Zygote to fork().


    Why fork() is fast:

    1. Copy-on-Write (COW) — the forked process shares the same physical memory pages as Zygote. Pages are only copied when written to.

    2. No re-initialization — the new process already has the runtime, core libraries, and framework classes loaded and initialized.

    3. Pre-warmed heap — common objects are already in memory.


    Without Zygote, every app launch would need to:

    - Start a new ART/Dalvik VM from scratch

    - Load and link all framework classes

    - Initialize the entire Java standard library This would add 1-3 seconds to every cold start.


    Process:

    init → Zygote starts → preloads framework → ActivityManagerService requests new process → Zygote.fork() → child becomes the app process → ActivityThread.main() runs → Application.onCreate() → Activity.onCreate()

    Q: Tell all the Android application components.

    Android has exactly four application components. Each serves a distinct purpose and has its own lifecycle:


    1. Activity — a single screen with a UI. Entry point for user interaction. Managed by the Activity stack within Tasks.


    2. Service — performs long-running operations in the background without UI. Types:

    - Started Service: runs until explicitly stopped (startService)

    - Bound Service: provides client-server interface (bindService)

    - Foreground Service: user-visible ongoing work with notification


    3. BroadcastReceiver — responds to system-wide broadcast announcements. Examples: battery low, screen off, network change, boot completed. Can be registered in manifest (static) or at runtime (dynamic).


    4. ContentProvider — manages shared app data and provides a standard interface for other apps to query/modify it via content:// URIs. Examples: Contacts, MediaStore, your own app's data to other apps.


    All four must be declared in AndroidManifest.xml (except dynamic BroadcastReceivers). They can be activated via Intents (Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver) or ContentResolver (ContentProvider).

    Q: What is the project structure of an Android Application?

    Standard Android project structure (Gradle-based):


    MyApp/

    ├── build.gradle.kts              (project-level: repositories, classpath)
├── settings.gradle.kts           (module declarations)
├── gradle.properties             (JVM args, AndroidX flags)
├── local.properties              (SDK path — NOT committed to VCS)
│
├── app/                          (main application module)
│   ├── build.gradle.kts          (module-level: plugins, deps, SDK versions)
│   └── src/
│       ├── main/
│       │   ├── AndroidManifest.xml
│       │   ├── java/  or  kotlin/   (source code by package)
│       │   ├── res/
│       │   │   ├── layout/          (XML layouts)
│       │   │   ├── drawable/        (vector/bitmap assets)
│       │   │   ├── values/          (strings.xml, colors.xml, themes.xml)
│       │   │   ├── mipmap/          (launcher icons)
│       │   │   └── navigation/      (NavGraph XMLs)
│       │   └── assets/              (raw files accessed via AssetManager)
│       ├── test/                    (unit tests — runs on JVM)
│       └── androidTest/             (instrumentation tests — runs on device)
│
├── feature-module/               (optional: dynamic feature modules)
└── core/                         (optional: shared library module)

    Key points for interview:

    - build.gradle.kts defines compileSdk, minSdk, targetSdk, dependencies

    - res/ is type-safe via R class; assets/ is raw file access

    - Build variants (debug/release) and product flavors allow configuration

    - Gradle wrapper (gradlew) ensures consistent builds across machines

    Q: What is AndroidManifest.xml?

    AndroidManifest.xml is the declaration file every Android app must have at the root of the app module. It provides essential information about the app to the Android build tools, the OS, and Google Play.


    What it declares:


    1. Package name / Application ID — unique identifier for the app

    2. Application components — all Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers, ContentProviders must be declared here

    3. Permissions — both requested (<uses-permission>) and defined (<permission>)

    4. Hardware/software features — <uses-feature> (camera, GPS, etc.)

    5. Minimum and target API levels (also in build.gradle, which overrides)

    6. Intent filters — what implicit intents each component responds to

    7. App-level configuration — theme, backup rules, network security config


    Important attributes:

    android:exported — whether other apps can start the component android:launchMode — Activity instantiation behavior android:configChanges — opt out of recreation on config changes android:process — run a component in a separate process android:permission — restrict who can start a component


    The manifest is merged from multiple sources during build:

    app manifest + library manifests + build variant manifests Conflicts are resolved via merge rules or tools:replace attribute.

    Q: What is the Application class?

    The Application class is the base class for maintaining global application state. It is instantiated before any Activity, Service, or Receiver and lives for the entire lifetime of the app process.


    Common uses:

    - Initialize libraries (Timber, Koin, Hilt, Coil, Firebase)

    - Set up crash reporting

    - Register ActivityLifecycleCallbacks for global Activity monitoring

    - Provide applicationContext to DI graph


    Must be declared in AndroidManifest:

    <application android:name=".MyApplication" ... />


    Lifecycle:

    - onCreate() is the first code that runs when the process starts

    - onTerminate() is NEVER called on production devices (only in emulator)

    - onTrimMemory(level) is called when the system needs memory

    - onConfigurationChanged() for system-wide config changes


    Anti-patterns:

    - Don't use it as a global variable dumping ground

    - Don't do heavy work in onCreate() — it blocks the first Activity launch

    - Use lazy initialization or App Startup library for deferred init

    class MyApplication : Application() {

    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
            Timber.plant(Timber.DebugTree())
        }
        registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks(object : ActivityLifecycleCallbacks {
            override fun onActivityCreated(activity: Activity, bundle: Bundle?) {
                Timber.d(class="st">"Created: ${activity::class.simpleName}")
            }
            override fun onActivityStarted(activity: Activity) {}
            override fun onActivityResumed(activity: Activity) {}
            override fun onActivityPaused(activity: Activity) {}
            override fun onActivityStopped(activity: Activity) {}
            override fun onActivitySaveInstanceState(activity: Activity, bundle: Bundle) {}
            override fun onActivityDestroyed(activity: Activity) {}
        })
    }

    override fun onTrimMemory(level: Int) {
        super.onTrimMemory(level)
        if (level >= TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATE) {
            class="cm">// Clear image caches, reduce memory footprint
            ImageLoader.getInstance().clearMemoryCache()
        }
    }
}

    SECTION 5: ACTIVITY AND FRAGMENT

    Q: Why is it recommended to use only the default constructor to create a Fragment?

    When Android recreates a Fragment (after config change or process death), it uses reflection to call the no-arg default constructor. If a Fragment only has a parameterized constructor, the system cannot recreate it and throws an InstantiationException.


    The correct way to pass data to a Fragment is via arguments Bundle:


    - The arguments Bundle is automatically saved and restored by the system

    - It survives both configuration changes and process death

    - The Fragment can read arguments in onCreate() or later


    Modern approach: Use FragmentFactory for constructor injection, or use Hilt's @AndroidEntryPoint which handles this automatically.

    class UserFragment : Fragment() {

    companion object {
        private const val ARG_USER_ID = class="st">"user_id"

        fun newInstance(userId: String): UserFragment {
            return UserFragment().apply {
                arguments = bundleOf(ARG_USER_ID to userId)
            }
        }
    }

    private val userId: String by lazy {
        requireArguments().getString(ARG_USER_ID)!!
    }
}

class="cm">// With FragmentFactory (for constructor injection):
class MyFragmentFactory(
    private val repository: UserRepository
) : FragmentFactory() {
    override fun instantiate(classLoader: ClassLoader, className: String): Fragment {
        return when (className) {
            UserDetailFragment::class.java.name -> UserDetailFragment(repository)
            else -> super.instantiate(classLoader, className)
        }
    }
}

    Q: What is Activity and its lifecycle?

    An Activity represents a single screen with a user interface. It is the primary entry point for user interaction.


    Full lifecycle (in order):


    onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) → Called once when Activity is first created or recreated. → Initialize views, bind data, set content view. → savedInstanceState is non-null if recreating.


    onStart() → Activity becomes VISIBLE but not yet interactive. → Register UI-related observers.


    onResume() → Activity is in FOREGROUND and interactive (user can touch). → Resume camera, animations, sensors.


    onPause() → Activity is partially obscured (dialog, multi-window). → Release exclusive resources (camera). Keep it fast.


    onStop() → Activity is no longer visible. → Release heavy resources, save data to DB, stop animations.


    onDestroy() → Activity is finishing or being destroyed by system. → isFinishing == true: user leaving; false: config change.


    onRestart() → Coming back from stopped state. onStop → onRestart → onStart.


    onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) is called BEFORE onStop() (after onPause on older APIs, after onStop on API 28+).

    Q: What is the difference between onCreate() and onStart()?

    onCreate():

    - Called ONCE per Activity creation (or recreation after destruction)

    - Activity is NOT visible yet

    - Purpose: one-time setup — inflate layout, initialize ViewModel, set up RecyclerView, read Intent extras, restore saved state

    - Receives savedInstanceState Bundle (null on first creation)


    onStart():

    - Called every time the Activity becomes visible

    - Called AFTER onCreate() on first launch, and after onRestart() when returning from background

    - Activity is VISIBLE but NOT interactive

    - Purpose: start UI-related updates — register observers, refresh data that may have changed while stopped


    Key difference: onCreate() is for initialization; onStart() is for visibility-related setup that may need to happen multiple times.


    Example: A user navigates away (onStop) then returns (onRestart → onStart). onCreate() is NOT called again, but onStart() IS.

    Q: When only onDestroy is called for an activity without onPause() and onStop()?

    This happens when finish() is called from within onCreate().


    If an Activity calls finish() in onCreate(), the system skips onPause() and onStop() entirely and goes directly to onDestroy(). The Activity was never visible or interactive, so there is nothing to pause or stop.


    Example scenario: An Activity checks for login status in onCreate(). If the user is not authenticated, it redirects to the login screen immediately.

    class ProtectedActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        if (!isUserLoggedIn()) {
            startActivity(Intent(this, LoginActivity::class.java))
            finish() class="cm">// Goes directly to onDestroy, skipping onPause and onStop
            return
        }
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_protected)
    }
}

    Q: Why do we need to call setContentView() in onCreate() of Activity class?

    setContentView() inflates the XML layout and attaches the resulting view hierarchy to the Activity's window (DecorView). It must be called in onCreate() because:


    1. View setup methods (findViewById, ViewBinding) need the view tree to already exist — they must run AFTER setContentView().


    2. The view hierarchy should be ready BEFORE onStart() (when the Activity becomes visible). If called later, the user might see a blank screen.


    3. onRestoreInstanceState() (called between onStart and onResume) expects views to exist so it can restore their state (scroll positions, EditText text, etc.).


    4. It is idempotent in onCreate() — on recreation after config change, the layout is re-inflated fresh with the new configuration's resources.


    Alternatives to setContentView():

    - Pass layout ID to AppCompatActivity constructor: class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity(R.layout.my)

    - Use ViewBinding: binding = ActivityMainBinding.inflate(layoutInflater); setContentView(binding.root)

    - Compose: setContent { MyComposableScreen() }

    Q: What is onSaveInstanceState() and onRestoreInstanceState() in activity?

    onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle):

    - Called when the system might destroy the Activity (before config change, before going to background, before process death).

    - Save transient UI state: scroll position, selected tab, draft text.

    - Called AFTER onStop() on API 28+, after onPause() on older APIs.

    - NOT called when user explicitly destroys (back press, finish()).

    - Bundle limit: ~1MB (Binder transaction limit). Save only small data.


    onRestoreInstanceState(savedInstanceState: Bundle):

    - Called AFTER onStart() and BEFORE onResume().

    - Only called if there IS saved state (savedInstanceState is non-null).

    - Alternative: check savedInstanceState in onCreate() — both work.

    - Advantage of onRestoreInstanceState(): you know for certain state exists, no null-checking needed.


    The system automatically saves/restores View state for views with IDs (EditText text, ScrollView position, CheckBox state). Custom transient state must be handled manually.

    class StatefulActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private var currentTabIndex = 0

    override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
        super.onSaveInstanceState(outState) class="cm">// saves view hierarchy state
        outState.putInt(class="st">"TAB_INDEX", currentTabIndex)
    }

    override fun onRestoreInstanceState(savedInstanceState: Bundle) {
        super.onRestoreInstanceState(savedInstanceState) class="cm">// restores view hierarchy state
        currentTabIndex = savedInstanceState.getInt(class="st">"TAB_INDEX", 0)
        selectTab(currentTabIndex)
    }
}

    Q: What is Fragment and its lifecycle?

    A Fragment is a reusable portion of UI within an Activity. It has its own lifecycle, receives its own input events, and can be added/removed while the Activity is running.


    Fragment lifecycle (in order):


    onAttach(context) → Fragment attached to Activity. Access host here.

    onCreate(bundle) → Initialize non-view state. Arguments available.

    onCreateView() → Inflate and return the view hierarchy.

    onViewCreated() → View is ready. Set up observers, listeners, RV.

    onStart() → Fragment visible (mirrors Activity.onStart).

    onResume() → Fragment interactive (mirrors Activity.onResume).

    onPause() → Losing focus.

    onStop() → No longer visible.

    onDestroyView() → View hierarchy destroyed. Null out bindings!

    onDestroy() → Fragment instance destroyed.

    onDetach() → Fragment detached from Activity.


    Critical distinction: VIEW lifecycle vs INSTANCE lifecycle.

    - When a Fragment goes on the back stack, onDestroyView is called but onDestroy is NOT. The instance stays alive but has no view.

    - When popped from back stack, onCreateView → onViewCreated is called again on the SAME instance.

    - This is why you must null out ViewBinding in onDestroyView().

    Q: What is Bundle in Android?

    Bundle is a key-value map for passing data between Android components. It implements Parcelable, so it can cross process boundaries via IPC.


    Supported types: primitives, String, Parcelable, Serializable, arrays/ArrayLists of these, and nested Bundles.


    Common uses:

    - Intent extras: intent.putExtra("key", value)

    - Fragment arguments: fragment.arguments = bundleOf(...)

    - Activity saved state: onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle)

    - FragmentResult API: setFragmentResult("key", bundle)

    - Navigation Safe Args (compiled down to Bundle)


    Size limitation: ~1MB total for Binder transaction. Exceeding this throws TransactionTooLargeException. Store only IDs and small state; pass large data via ViewModel, database, or file.

    fun bundleExamples() {
    class="cm">// Creating bundles
    val bundle = Bundle().apply {
        putString(class="st">"name", class="st">"John")
        putInt(class="st">"age", 30)
        putParcelable(class="st">"user", userParcelable)
    }

    class="cm">// Kotlin-idiomatic
    val bundle2 = bundleOf(
        class="st">"name" to class="st">"John",
        class="st">"age" to 30
    )

    class="cm">// Reading
    val name = bundle.getString(class="st">"name") class="cm">// nullable
    val age = bundle.getInt(class="st">"age", -1)  class="cm">// with default
}

    Q: What are "launchMode"?

    Launch modes control how a new instance of an Activity is associated with the current task and back stack. Set in AndroidManifest.xml:


    1. standard (default):

    - A new instance is created every time, regardless of existing instances.

    - Task: [A] → startActivity(A) → [A, A]

    - Use case: most Activities.


    2. singleTop:

    - If the same Activity is already at the TOP of the stack, the existing instance is reused via onNewIntent(). Otherwise, a new instance is created.

    - Task: [A, B] → startActivity(B, singleTop) → [A, B] (B gets onNewIntent)

    - Task: [A, B] → startActivity(A, singleTop) → [A, B, A] (A not on top)

    - Use case: search results, notification destinations.


    3. singleTask:

    - Only one instance exists in the system. If it exists in any task, that task is brought to front and all Activities above it are destroyed.

    - Task: [A, B, C] → startActivity(A, singleTask) → [A] (B, C destroyed)

    - Use case: app home/dashboard.


    4. singleInstance:

    - Like singleTask, but the Activity is the ONLY Activity in its task. Any Activity started from it goes into a different task.

    - Use case: phone dialer, payment screen.


    5. singleInstancePerTask (API 31+):

    - Allows one instance per task. Can exist in multiple tasks simultaneously.


    Intent flags (FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK, FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP, etc.) can override manifest-declared launchMode at runtime.

    Q: What is the difference between a Fragment and an Activity?

    Activity:

    - Full-screen window that acts as a host for the UI

    - Managed directly by the system (ActivityManager)

    - Has its own lifecycle managed by the OS

    - Declared in AndroidManifest.xml

    - Entry point for user interaction (can be launched by Intents)

    - Each Activity has its own back stack entry by default


    Fragment:

    - A modular portion of UI hosted WITHIN an Activity

    - Managed by FragmentManager (not the OS directly)

    - Lifecycle is tied to (but distinct from) its host Activity

    - NOT declared in manifest

    - Cannot exist without a host Activity

    - Multiple Fragments can be displayed side-by-side (tablets)

    - Can be added/removed/replaced at runtime

    - Has its own back stack (managed by FragmentManager)


    Key architectural difference: Activities are OS-level components with heavyweight creation (involves IPC with ActivityManagerService). Fragments are lightweight, managed entirely in-process by FragmentManager.


    Modern recommendation: Single-Activity architecture with Fragments (or Compose) for each screen, using Navigation Component.

    Q: When should you use a Fragment rather than an Activity?

    Use Fragments when:


    1. Multi-pane layouts — tablets showing list + detail side by side.


    2. Single-Activity architecture — modern best practice. One Activity hosts all Fragments via Navigation Component. Benefits:

    - Shared ViewModel scoped to navigation graph

    - Smoother transitions/animations between screens

    - Shared elements (toolbar, bottom nav) don't recreate

    - Easier deep linking


    3. ViewPager/Tab layouts — each page is a Fragment.


    4. Reusable UI components — same Fragment in multiple Activities/contexts.


    5. Dynamic UI — add/remove/replace portions of the screen at runtime.


    Use separate Activities when:

    - Completely independent flows (e.g., a settings module)

    - Different process requirements (android:process in manifest)

    - Entry points from other apps (deep links that need Intent filters)

    - Totally different UI paradigms (e.g., camera Activity)

    Q: What is the difference between FragmentPagerAdapter vs FragmentStatePagerAdapter?

    Both are used with ViewPager (deprecated; prefer ViewPager2 with FragmentStateAdapter). The key difference is memory management:


    FragmentPagerAdapter:

    - Keeps ALL Fragment instances in memory (only detaches their views).

    - Calls detach() when Fragment goes off-screen → view destroyed, instance stays in FragmentManager.

    - Fast re-navigation (no re-creation), but uses more memory.

    - Best for: small, fixed number of tabs (3-5).


    FragmentStatePagerAdapter:

    - DESTROYS Fragment instances when off-screen (saves their state via Bundle).

    - Calls remove() → Fragment and its view are both destroyed.

    - Uses less memory but recreation is slower.

    - Best for: large or dynamic number of pages (feeds, galleries).


    Modern replacement (ViewPager2):

    FragmentStateAdapter — behaves like FragmentStatePagerAdapter with RecyclerView-based diffing and better lifecycle handling.

    Q: What is the difference between adding/replacing fragment in backstack?

    add() — places a new Fragment ON TOP of the existing Fragment in the container.

    - The old Fragment is NOT destroyed; it remains in the view hierarchy.

    - Both Fragments are active simultaneously.

    - The old Fragment's lifecycle does NOT change (no onPause/onStop).

    - Use case: overlays, dialogs, stacking content.


    replace() — removes ALL existing Fragments in the container, then adds the new one.

    - The old Fragment goes through onDestroyView() (if added to back stack) or full onDestroy() (if not added to back stack).

    - Only one Fragment is active in the container at a time.

    - Use case: standard screen navigation.


    With addToBackStack():

    - add + backstack: pressing Back removes the top Fragment, old one shows.

    - replace + backstack: pressing Back recreates old Fragment's view (onCreateView is called again since onDestroyView was called).

    fun fragmentTransactionExamples(fragmentManager: FragmentManager) {
    class="cm">// add: stacks on top, old Fragment stays alive
    fragmentManager.commit {
        add(R.id.container, FragmentB())
        addToBackStack(class="st">"add_b")
    }

    class="cm">// replace: removes old, adds new; old view destroyed if on back stack
    fragmentManager.commit {
        replace(R.id.container, FragmentC())
        addToBackStack(class="st">"replace_c")
    }
}

    Q: How would you communicate between two Fragments?

    Four modern approaches (in order of preference):


    1. Shared ViewModel (recommended for same Activity scope):

    Both Fragments observe the same ViewModel scoped to the Activity or a shared navigation graph.


    2. Fragment Result API (for one-shot results between Fragments):

    Fragment B sets a result; Fragment A listens for it. Works across the FragmentManager without coupling.


    3. Navigation Component with SavedStateHandle:

    Previous destination can observe a key set by the current destination.


    4. Shared ViewModel scoped to Navigation graph:

    Both Fragments share a ViewModel scoped to a nested nav graph.


    Anti-patterns:

    - Casting getActivity() to a specific Activity type (tight coupling)

    - Static variables or event buses (hard to track, lifecycle-unaware)

    class="cm">// Approach 1: Shared ViewModel
class SharedViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _selectedItem = MutableLiveData<Item>()
    val selectedItem: LiveData<Item> = _selectedItem

    fun select(item: Item) { _selectedItem.value = item }
}

class ListFragment : Fragment() {
    private val sharedVM: SharedViewModel by activityViewModels()

    fun onItemClicked(item: Item) {
        sharedVM.select(item)
    }
}

class DetailFragment : Fragment() {
    private val sharedVM: SharedViewModel by activityViewModels()

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onViewCreated(view, savedInstanceState)
        sharedVM.selectedItem.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { item ->
            displayItem(item)
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// Approach 2: Fragment Result API
class FragmentB : Fragment() {
    fun onDone() {
        setFragmentResult(class="st">"request_key", bundleOf(class="st">"result" to class="st">"some_value"))
        parentFragmentManager.popBackStack()
    }
}

class FragmentA : Fragment() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setFragmentResultListener(class="st">"request_key") { _, bundle ->
            val result = bundle.getString(class="st">"result")
        }
    }
}

    Q: What is retained Fragment?

    A retained Fragment (setRetainInstance(true)) survives Activity destruction on configuration changes. The Fragment instance is NOT destroyed; only its view is destroyed and recreated. It skips onDestroy() and onCreate() during the config change cycle.


    Lifecycle on config change (retained):

    onPause → onStop → onDestroyView → (Activity destroyed/recreated) → onCreateView → onViewCreated → onStart → onResume


    This was commonly used to hold large data across config changes BEFORE ViewModel was introduced.


    DEPRECATED: setRetainInstance() is deprecated since Fragment 1.3.0. Use ViewModel instead — it provides the same benefit (surviving config changes) with better separation of concerns, testability, and support for SavedStateHandle (process death survival).

    Q: What is the purpose of addToBackStack() while committing fragment transaction?

    addToBackStack(name) records the FragmentTransaction so that it can be reversed when the user presses the Back button.


    Without addToBackStack():

    - The transaction is committed but NOT reversible

    - Pressing Back will finish the Activity (default back behavior)

    - Replaced Fragments are fully destroyed (onDestroy + onDetach)


    With addToBackStack():

    - The transaction is pushed onto the Fragment back stack

    - Pressing Back pops the transaction, reversing it

    - Replaced Fragments are only view-destroyed (onDestroyView), not instance-destroyed — the instance stays in FragmentManager

    - When popped, the Fragment's view is recreated (onCreateView again)


    The optional name parameter lets you pop to a specific transaction:

    fragmentManager.popBackStack("name", FragmentManager.POP_BACK_STACK_INCLUSIVE)


    popBackStack() is asynchronous. Use popBackStackImmediate() for synchronous.

    SECTION 6: VIEWS AND VIEWGROUPS

    Q: What is View in Android?

    View is the fundamental building block for UI in Android. Every UI element (Button, TextView, ImageView, EditText) is a subclass of android.view.View.


    A View occupies a rectangular area on screen and is responsible for:

    - Drawing itself (onDraw(Canvas))

    - Handling events (touch, click, key)

    - Measuring its size (onMeasure(widthSpec, heightSpec))

    - Laying out its position (onLayout())


    The rendering pipeline for each frame:

    Measure → Layout → Draw


    1. Measure pass: each View determines its own size. Parent calls child.measure() with MeasureSpec constraints.

    2. Layout pass: each View is positioned. Parent calls child.layout() with left, top, right, bottom coordinates.

    3. Draw pass: each View renders to Canvas. The hardware renderer draws the View tree to a Surface.


    Every View has: visibility, alpha, padding, elevation, background, layout parameters, and a unique (optional) ID.

    Q: Difference between View.GONE and View.INVISIBLE?

    View.VISIBLE (0):

    - View is visible and participates in layout.


    View.INVISIBLE (4):

    - View is NOT visible but STILL takes up space in the layout.

    - It is measured and laid out normally; just not drawn.

    - Other views are positioned as if it were visible.


    View.GONE (8):

    - View is NOT visible and does NOT take up any space.

    - It is excluded from the measure/layout pass entirely.

    - Other views fill the space it would have occupied.


    Performance consideration: changing from GONE to VISIBLE triggers a full measure + layout pass because the view hierarchy changes. INVISIBLE → VISIBLE only requires a draw pass (cheaper). If you toggle visibility frequently, INVISIBLE may be more performant.


    In ConstraintLayout specifically, GONE views still participate in constraint resolution (other views' constraints to the GONE view are honored as if it had zero size), which is a unique and useful behavior.

    Q: Can you create a custom view? How?

    Yes. Three main approaches:


    1. Extend an existing View (e.g., AppCompatTextView) — add behavior.

    2. Extend View directly — full custom drawing via Canvas.

    3. Extend ViewGroup — custom layout logic for children.


    Key methods to override:

    onMeasure(widthMeasureSpec, heightMeasureSpec) — determine size. Must call setMeasuredDimension() at the end. onDraw(canvas: Canvas) — render content using Canvas API. onTouchEvent(event: MotionEvent) — handle touch input. onSizeChanged(w, h, oldW, oldH) — react to size changes.


    Best practices:

    - Never allocate objects in onDraw() (causes GC jank).

    - Pre-allocate Paint, Path, Rect objects in init{} or constructor.

    - Support custom XML attributes via attrs.xml and obtainStyledAttributes.

    - Call invalidate() to trigger redraw, requestLayout() for size changes.

    - Implement onSaveInstanceState/onRestoreInstanceState for state.

    class CircleProgressView class="an">@JvmOverloads constructor(
    context: Context,
    attrs: AttributeSet? = null,
    defStyleAttr: Int = 0
) : View(context, attrs, defStyleAttr) {

    private val paint = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG).apply {
        style = Paint.Style.STROKE
        strokeWidth = 12f
        color = Color.BLUE
        strokeCap = Paint.Cap.ROUND
    }

    private val rect = RectF()
    var progress: Float = 0f
        set(value) {
            field = value.coerceIn(0f, 1f)
            invalidate() class="cm">// trigger redraw
        }

    override fun onMeasure(widthMeasureSpec: Int, heightMeasureSpec: Int) {
        val size = minOf(
            MeasureSpec.getSize(widthMeasureSpec),
            MeasureSpec.getSize(heightMeasureSpec)
        )
        setMeasuredDimension(size, size)
    }

    override fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas) {
        val inset = paint.strokeWidth / 2
        rect.set(inset, inset, width - inset, height - inset)
        canvas.drawArc(rect, -90f, 360f * progress, false, paint)
    }
}

    Q: What are ViewGroups and how are they different from Views?

    ViewGroup is a subclass of View that serves as a container for other Views (children). It defines the layout structure.


    View:

    - A leaf node — draws itself, no children

    - Examples: TextView, Button, ImageView, EditText


    ViewGroup:

    - An internal node — contains and positions child Views

    - Responsible for measuring and laying out children

    - Examples: LinearLayout, RelativeLayout, ConstraintLayout, FrameLayout, RecyclerView, ScrollView


    Every ViewGroup must implement:

    onMeasure() — measure itself and all children onLayout() — position each child within its bounds


    The View tree (hierarchy) is a tree structure with ViewGroups as internal nodes and Views as leaves. The root is DecorView, which contains the system chrome (status bar, nav bar) and your content view.

    Q: What is a Canvas?

    Canvas is the drawing surface provided to a View in its onDraw() method. It provides methods to draw shapes, text, bitmaps, and paths onto a backing Bitmap or hardware-accelerated surface.


    Common Canvas operations:

    drawRect(), drawCircle(), drawArc() — geometric shapes drawText() — text rendering drawBitmap() — image rendering drawPath() — complex shapes from Path objects translate(), rotate(), scale(), skew() — transformations save() / restore() — save/restore transformation state clipRect(), clipPath() — restrict drawing area


    Canvas works with Paint objects that define HOW to draw:

    - Color, alpha, stroke width, style (fill vs stroke)

    - Text size, font, alignment

    - Anti-aliasing, shadows, color filters, shaders


    Under hardware acceleration (default since API 14), Canvas operations are recorded into a DisplayList and rendered by the GPU. Some Canvas operations are not hardware-accelerated (e.g., drawBitmapMesh).

    Q: What is a SurfaceView?

    SurfaceView provides a dedicated drawing Surface that is rendered on a SEPARATE window layer from the normal View hierarchy. This allows drawing on a background thread without blocking the UI thread.


    Normal View vs SurfaceView:

    - View: draws on the main thread in the app's window

    - SurfaceView: draws on ANY thread into its own Surface/window


    How it works:

    - SurfaceView creates a "hole" in the View hierarchy

    - A separate Surface is composited BELOW the app window

    - Drawing happens via SurfaceHolder.lockCanvas() → draw → unlockCanvasAndPost()

    - Can run a rendering loop on a background thread


    Use cases:

    - Camera preview

    - Video playback (MediaPlayer, ExoPlayer)

    - Game rendering loops

    - Heavy real-time graphics (charts, waveforms)


    Downsides:

    - Cannot be transformed (animated, scaled, rotated) like regular Views

    - Z-ordering limitations (always behind or in front of window)


    Alternative: TextureView — draws to a SurfaceTexture, so it CAN be transformed and animated like a normal View, but is slightly less performant than SurfaceView. Another option: GLSurfaceView for OpenGL.

    Q: Relative Layout vs Linear Layout

    LinearLayout:

    - Arranges children in a single direction: horizontal or vertical

    - Uses layout_weight for proportional distribution of space

    - Simple, predictable positioning

    - Performance: single measure pass (unless weights are used — weights trigger a SECOND measure pass, doubling cost)

    - Best for: simple row/column arrangements


    RelativeLayout:

    - Positions children relative to each other or the parent

    - Rules: toLeftOf, below, alignParentEnd, centerInParent, etc.

    - Can achieve complex layouts without nesting

    - Performance: ALWAYS does TWO measure passes (to resolve relative dependencies), regardless of complexity

    - Best for: flat layouts where children have spatial relationships


    Performance comparison:

    - LinearLayout (no weights) < RelativeLayout (always 2 passes)

    - LinearLayout (with weights) ≈ RelativeLayout (both do 2 passes)

    - Deep nesting of either is bad — each level multiplies measure passes


    Modern recommendation: Use ConstraintLayout — it achieves complex layouts with a FLAT hierarchy (no nesting) and has an optimized constraint solver that typically does a single measure pass.

    Q: Tell about Constraint Layout optimization

    ConstraintLayout is optimized for flat hierarchies. Instead of nesting multiple LinearLayouts/RelativeLayouts, you express relationships as constraints, and the Cassowary-based solver resolves positions in a single (or minimal) measure/layout pass.


    Key optimizations:


    1. Flat hierarchy — eliminates nested measure/layout passes. Nested LinearLayout (3 levels) = 2^3 = 8 measure passes. ConstraintLayout (flat) = 1-2 measure passes.


    2. Chains — replicate LinearLayout weight behavior without nesting. Spread, spread_inside, packed, and weighted chains.


    3. Guidelines & Barriers — virtual views with zero rendering cost. Barriers adapt to the largest child dynamically.


    4. ConstraintLayout 2.0 features:

    - Flow: virtual layout for wrapping rows/columns

    - MotionLayout: declarative animations with constraints

    - Layer: group transforms without nesting


    5. match_constraint (0dp) — lets the solver determine size based on constraints rather than content, reducing measure iterations.


    When to prefer ConstraintLayout:

    - Complex layouts that would require 2+ levels of nesting

    - Responsive layouts that need percentage-based sizing

    - Animations between two constraint states (MotionLayout)


    When simpler layouts suffice:

    - Simple vertical/horizontal list → LinearLayout

    - Stacking overlapping views → FrameLayout

    Q: Do you know what is the view tree? How can you optimize its depth?

    The view tree is the hierarchical structure of all Views and ViewGroups that make up the UI. The root is the DecorView (system-provided), which contains the content view set by setContentView().


    Why depth matters:

    - Measure, layout, and draw passes traverse the tree recursively.

    - Each level of nesting multiplies the cost of these passes.

    - Deep trees cause jank, especially with RelativeLayout or LinearLayout with weights (which do 2 measure passes per level).


    Optimization strategies:


    1. Use ConstraintLayout to flatten nested layouts into a single level.


    2. Use <merge> tag — eliminates a redundant FrameLayout when including a layout via <include>.


    3. Use <ViewStub> — lazy inflation. The view is not inflated until explicitly requested, saving measure/layout cost for hidden views.


    4. Remove unnecessary wrappers — audit with Layout Inspector.


    5. Use RecyclerView instead of ScrollView with many children.


    6. Consider Jetpack Compose — Compose's layout system does NOT have multi-pass measurement. Each composable is measured exactly ONCE, regardless of nesting depth.


    Tools:

    - Layout Inspector (Android Studio) — visualize tree and measure times

    - lint (Android Lint) — warns about deep hierarchies (>10 levels)

    - Systrace / Perfetto — profile measure/layout/draw per frame

    SECTION 7: RECYCLERVIEW

    Q: What is the difference between ListView and RecyclerView?

    ListView (legacy):

    - ViewHolder pattern is optional (manual optimization)

    - Only supports vertical scrolling

    - Built-in click listeners (onItemClickListener)

    - Dividers are built-in

    - No built-in animation support for add/remove

    - addHeaderView/addFooterView for headers/footers

    - Adapter: BaseAdapter, ArrayAdapter, CursorAdapter


    RecyclerView (modern replacement):

    - ViewHolder pattern is ENFORCED (mandatory)

    - LayoutManager supports vertical, horizontal, grid, staggered

    - No built-in click listener (set on ViewHolder)

    - ItemDecoration for custom dividers, spacing, decorations

    - Built-in item animations (DefaultItemAnimator)

    - Supports DiffUtil for efficient list updates

    - ItemTouchHelper for drag-and-drop, swipe-to-dismiss

    - Pluggable architecture: Adapter, LayoutManager, ItemDecoration, ItemAnimator are all independently replaceable

    - ViewPool for sharing ViewHolders across nested RecyclerViews


    RecyclerView is always preferred. ListView is effectively deprecated.

    Q: How does RecyclerView work?

    RecyclerView works by recycling ViewHolder objects as the user scrolls.


    Core loop:

    1. LayoutManager requests the next View from RecyclerView.

    2. RecyclerView checks the Recycler (cache) for a reusable ViewHolder:

    a. Scrap (attached views being re-laid out) — used as-is b. Cache (recently detached, by position) — used as-is, no rebind c. ViewCacheExtension (custom cache, optional) d. RecycledViewPool (by viewType) — must rebind (onBindViewHolder)

    3. If no cached ViewHolder found → Adapter.onCreateViewHolder() inflates a new one.

    4. Adapter.onBindViewHolder(holder, position) binds data to the ViewHolder.

    5. LayoutManager positions the View on screen.

    6. When a View scrolls off screen, it goes into the cache/pool.


    Cache hierarchy (in lookup order):

    Scrap → mCachedViews (default size 2) → ViewCacheExtension → RecycledViewPool


    Key insight: onCreateViewHolder() is expensive (inflation). onBindViewHolder() is cheap (data binding). RecyclerView minimizes creates by recycling. The pool holds up to 5 ViewHolders per viewType by default.

    Q: RecyclerView Optimization — Scrolling Performance Improvement

    Key optimizations for smooth 60fps scrolling:


    1. setHasFixedSize(true) — if the RecyclerView size doesn't depend on adapter content, skip re-measuring on every data change.


    2. Use DiffUtil / ListAdapter — calculate minimal changes instead of notifyDataSetChanged() which rebinds everything.


    3. Avoid inflation in onBindViewHolder() — all view creation should be in onCreateViewHolder(). onBind should only set data.


    4. Avoid allocations in onBindViewHolder() — no new objects, no string concatenation, pre-format data in the ViewModel.


    5. Use RecycledViewPool — share ViewHolders across nested RecyclerViews. pool.setMaxRecycledViews(viewType, count)


    6. setItemViewCacheSize(n) — increase off-screen cache for faster reverse scroll (default is 2).


    7. Efficient image loading — use Coil/Glide with proper sizing, placeholder, and cache policies. Cancel loads in onViewRecycled().


    8. setRecycledViewPool() for nested horizontal RecyclerViews — reuse ViewHolders across rows.


    9. Avoid nested RecyclerView in RecyclerView when possible; use ConcatAdapter or a flat list with multiple view types.


    10. Use View.setHasTransientState(true) sparingly — it prevents recycling.

    class OptimizedAdapter(
    private val onClick: (Item) -> Unit
) : ListAdapter<Item, OptimizedAdapter.ItemViewHolder>(ItemDiffCallback()) {

    override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int): ItemViewHolder {
        val binding = ItemRowBinding.inflate(
            LayoutInflater.from(parent.context), parent, false
        )
        return ItemViewHolder(binding)
    }

    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: ItemViewHolder, position: Int) {
        holder.bind(getItem(position))
    }

    inner class ItemViewHolder(
        private val binding: ItemRowBinding
    ) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(binding.root) {

        init {
            binding.root.setOnClickListener {
                val pos = bindingAdapterPosition
                if (pos != RecyclerView.NO_POSITION) {
                    onClick(getItem(pos))
                }
            }
        }

        fun bind(item: Item) {
            binding.titleText.text = item.title
            binding.subtitleText.text = item.subtitle
        }
    }
}

class ItemDiffCallback : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<Item>() {
    override fun areItemsTheSame(old: Item, new: Item) = old.id == new.id
    override fun areContentsTheSame(old: Item, new: Item) = old == new
}

    Q: Optimizing Nested RecyclerView

    Nested RecyclerViews (common pattern: vertical outer + horizontal inner) have specific performance challenges.


    Optimizations:


    1. Share RecycledViewPool — inner RecyclerViews should share a single pool so ViewHolders recycled from one row can be reused in another.


    2. Set initial prefetch item count — tells the LayoutManager how many items the inner RecyclerView will need during the next frame. (innerLayoutManager as LinearLayoutManager).initialPrefetchItemCount = 4


    3. Cache inner RecyclerView layout state — when the outer row is recycled, save the inner RecyclerView's scroll position and LayoutManager state in onViewRecycled(), restore in onBindViewHolder().


    4. setRecycledViewPool(sharedPool) on each inner RecyclerView.


    5. setItemViewCacheSize(0) on inner RecyclerViews — push items directly to the shared pool instead of per-RV cache.


    6. Consider flattening — use ConcatAdapter with headers to avoid nesting.

    class OuterAdapter : RecyclerView.Adapter<OuterAdapter.OuterViewHolder>() {

    private val sharedPool = RecyclerView.RecycledViewPool()

    class OuterViewHolder(
        itemView: View,
        private val innerRv: RecyclerView
    ) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(itemView)

    override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int): OuterViewHolder {
        val view = LayoutInflater.from(parent.context)
            .inflate(R.layout.row_outer, parent, false)
        val innerRv = view.findViewById<RecyclerView>(R.id.innerRecyclerView)
        innerRv.setRecycledViewPool(sharedPool)
        innerRv.setItemViewCacheSize(0)
        (innerRv.layoutManager as LinearLayoutManager).initialPrefetchItemCount = 4
        return OuterViewHolder(view, innerRv)
    }

    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: OuterViewHolder, position: Int) {
        class="cm">// bind inner adapter data
    }

    override fun getItemCount(): Int = 0 class="cm">// placeholder
}

    Q: What are the components of a RecyclerView?

    RecyclerView has a pluggable architecture with these components:


    1. RecyclerView.Adapter — bridges data to ViewHolders. Responsible for creating ViewHolders and binding data to them.


    2. RecyclerView.ViewHolder — holds references to views in a single item. Avoids repeated findViewById calls.


    3. RecyclerView.LayoutManager — positions items on screen. Built-in: LinearLayoutManager, GridLayoutManager, StaggeredGridLayoutManager. Custom LayoutManagers are possible for non-standard layouts.


    4. RecyclerView.ItemDecoration — draws decorations (dividers, spacing, badges) around or over items without modifying item views.


    5. RecyclerView.ItemAnimator — animates item changes (add, remove, move, change). Default: DefaultItemAnimator with fade/translate effects.


    6. RecyclerView.Recycler — manages the caching of ViewHolders (scrap, cache, pool). Internal to RecyclerView but accessible for custom LayoutManagers.


    7. SnapHelper — snaps items to specific positions after scroll. LinearSnapHelper (center snap), PagerSnapHelper (one-page snap).


    8. ItemTouchHelper — handles drag-and-drop and swipe-to-dismiss gestures.

    Q: Explain the role of RecyclerView.Adapter and RecyclerView.ViewHolder

    RecyclerView.Adapter<VH>:

    - Creates ViewHolder instances (onCreateViewHolder) — inflates the layout

    - Binds data to ViewHolders (onBindViewHolder) — sets text, images, etc.

    - Reports dataset size (getItemCount)

    - Handles multiple view types (getItemViewType)

    - Notifies RecyclerView of data changes (notifyItemInserted, etc.)

    - Modern: extend ListAdapter<T, VH> for built-in DiffUtil support


    RecyclerView.ViewHolder:

    - Wraps a single item view and caches references to its child views

    - Created once, then reused (recycled) for different data positions

    - Holds the itemView reference and knows its adapter position

    - Key properties: bindingAdapterPosition, absoluteAdapterPosition

    - Should set click listeners in init{} (not in onBind) for efficiency


    The separation of Adapter and ViewHolder enables the recycling pattern:

    the Adapter knows HOW to create and bind, the ViewHolder knows WHAT views exist. This avoids expensive inflation and findViewById on every scroll.

    Q: What is a LayoutManager in RecyclerView?

    LayoutManager is responsible for measuring and positioning item views within the RecyclerView and determining the policy for when to recycle items that are no longer visible.


    Built-in LayoutManagers:


    1. LinearLayoutManager

    - Vertical or horizontal scrolling list

    - Options: reverseLayout, stackFromEnd


    2. GridLayoutManager

    - Grid with configurable span count

    - SpanSizeLookup for variable span sizes per item


    3. StaggeredGridLayoutManager

    - Staggered grid where items can have different heights

    - Pinterest-style layout


    Key responsibilities:

    - Decide which items are visible (layout)

    - Position items (left, top, right, bottom)

    - Handle scroll events

    - Report scroll state and position

    - Support prefetching for smoother scrolling

    - Handle accessibility traversal order


    Custom LayoutManager: override onLayoutChildren() and scrollVerticallyBy() for non-standard layouts (circular, carousel, etc.).

    fun setupRecyclerView(recyclerView: RecyclerView) {
    class="cm">// Linear
    recyclerView.layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(
        recyclerView.context,
        LinearLayoutManager.VERTICAL,
        false
    )

    class="cm">// Grid with varying spans
    val gridLayoutManager = GridLayoutManager(recyclerView.context, 3)
    gridLayoutManager.spanSizeLookup = object : GridLayoutManager.SpanSizeLookup() {
        override fun getSpanSize(position: Int): Int {
            return if (position == 0) 3 else 1 class="cm">// header spans full width
        }
    }
}

    Q: How do you handle multiple view types in a single RecyclerView?

    Override getItemViewType(position) in the Adapter to return different integer constants for different view types. Then create the appropriate ViewHolder in onCreateViewHolder() based on the viewType parameter.


    RecyclerView uses viewType to ensure a ViewHolder of type A is never reused for type B — they have separate pools.

    sealed class FeedItem {
    data class Header(val title: String) : FeedItem()
    data class Post(val id: Int, val content: String) : FeedItem()
    data class Ad(val imageUrl: String) : FeedItem()
}

class FeedAdapter : ListAdapter<FeedItem, RecyclerView.ViewHolder>(FeedDiffCallback()) {

    companion object {
        private const val TYPE_HEADER = 0
        private const val TYPE_POST = 1
        private const val TYPE_AD = 2
    }

    override fun getItemViewType(position: Int): Int = when (getItem(position)) {
        is FeedItem.Header -> TYPE_HEADER
        is FeedItem.Post -> TYPE_POST
        is FeedItem.Ad -> TYPE_AD
    }

    override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int): RecyclerView.ViewHolder {
        val inflater = LayoutInflater.from(parent.context)
        return when (viewType) {
            TYPE_HEADER -> HeaderViewHolder(inflater.inflate(R.layout.item_header, parent, false))
            TYPE_POST -> PostViewHolder(inflater.inflate(R.layout.item_post, parent, false))
            TYPE_AD -> AdViewHolder(inflater.inflate(R.layout.item_ad, parent, false))
            else -> throw IllegalArgumentException(class="st">"Unknown viewType: $viewType")
        }
    }

    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: RecyclerView.ViewHolder, position: Int) {
        when (val item = getItem(position)) {
            is FeedItem.Header -> (holder as HeaderViewHolder).bind(item)
            is FeedItem.Post -> (holder as PostViewHolder).bind(item)
            is FeedItem.Ad -> (holder as AdViewHolder).bind(item)
        }
    }
}

    Q: What is DiffUtil and how does it improve RecyclerView performance?

    DiffUtil computes the minimal set of update operations (insert, remove, move, change) needed to transform one list into another using Eugene Myers' difference algorithm.


    Without DiffUtil: notifyDataSetChanged() rebinds EVERY visible item, loses item animations, and is O(n) regardless of actual changes.


    With DiffUtil: only changed items are rebound; animations play for inserts, removals, and moves. This is crucial for large lists.


    Two ways to use:


    1. DiffUtil.calculateDiff(callback) — manual, runs on calling thread. Should be done on background thread for large lists.


    2. ListAdapter / AsyncListDiffer — wraps DiffUtil with automatic background thread diffing. This is the recommended approach.


    DiffUtil.ItemCallback<T>:

    areItemsTheSame(old, new) → same identity? (compare IDs) areContentsTheSame(old, new) → same content? (compare all fields) getChangePayload(old, new) → optional partial bind info


    Performance: O(N + D^2) where N = list size, D = number of edits. For very large lists (10k+), even this can be slow — paginate instead.

    class UserDiffCallback : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<User>() {
    override fun areItemsTheSame(oldItem: User, newItem: User) =
        oldItem.id == newItem.id

    override fun areContentsTheSame(oldItem: User, newItem: User) =
        oldItem == newItem

    override fun getChangePayload(oldItem: User, newItem: User): Any? {
        class="cm">// Return partial change info for efficient partial rebind
        return if (oldItem.name != newItem.name) class="st">"name_changed" else null
    }
}

class UserAdapter : ListAdapter<User, UserAdapter.UserVH>(UserDiffCallback()) {

    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: UserVH, position: Int, payloads: MutableList<Any>) {
        if (payloads.contains(class="st">"name_changed")) {
            holder.updateName(getItem(position).name) class="cm">// partial rebind
        } else {
            super.onBindViewHolder(holder, position, payloads) class="cm">// full rebind
        }
    }
}

    Q: What is the purpose of RecyclerView.setHasFixedSize(true)?

    When setHasFixedSize(true) is called, you are telling RecyclerView that changes in adapter content will NOT change the size of the RecyclerView itself (only the number/content of items changes, not the RV dimensions).


    Why it helps performance:

    - Without it, every adapter notify call triggers requestLayout() on the RecyclerView, which in turn causes a full measure/layout pass of the RecyclerView AND its parent hierarchy.

    - With it, RecyclerView skips the requestLayout() call and only re-layouts its children internally.


    When to use: when the RecyclerView has match_parent or a fixed dp size. When NOT to use: when the RecyclerView uses wrap_content (its size depends on the number of items).

    Q: How do you update a specific item in RecyclerView?

    Several approaches, from most to least efficient:


    1. ListAdapter.submitList(newList) with DiffUtil (recommended):

    Automatically computes and dispatches minimal updates.


    2. notifyItemChanged(position) — rebinds a single item. notifyItemChanged(position, payload) — partial rebind with payload.


    3. notifyItemInserted(position) / notifyItemRemoved(position) / notifyItemMoved(fromPos, toPos) — specific structural changes.


    4. notifyItemRangeChanged(positionStart, itemCount) — rebind a range.


    5. notifyDataSetChanged() — WORST. Rebinds everything, no animations. Only use as last resort.


    Payload-based partial update for efficiency:

    fun partialUpdateExample(adapter: RecyclerView.Adapter<*>) {
    class="cm">// Full rebind of position 5
    adapter.notifyItemChanged(5)

    class="cm">// Partial rebind — only the class="st">"likes" count changed
    adapter.notifyItemChanged(5, class="st">"likes_updated")
}

class="cm">//     } else {

class="cm">//     }

    Q: What is SnapHelper?

    SnapHelper helps RecyclerView snap items to specific positions after a scroll or fling gesture completes. Without it, items can stop at any arbitrary scroll position.


    Built-in SnapHelpers:


    1. LinearSnapHelper — snaps the closest item to the CENTER of the RecyclerView. Used for carousel-like centered item selection.


    2. PagerSnapHelper — snaps one page at a time (like ViewPager). Only one item is scrolled per fling, always fully visible.


    Usage:

    val snapHelper = LinearSnapHelper() snapHelper.attachToRecyclerView(recyclerView)


    Custom SnapHelper: override these methods:

    calculateDistanceToFinalSnap(layoutManager, targetView) → [dx, dy] findSnapView(layoutManager) → which View to snap to findTargetSnapPosition(layoutManager, velocityX, velocityY) → target pos


    Use cases: horizontal carousels, date pickers, time selectors, and any paginated horizontal list.

    fun setupSnapHelper(recyclerView: RecyclerView) {
    val snapHelper = PagerSnapHelper()
    snapHelper.attachToRecyclerView(recyclerView)

    class="cm">// Get the currently snapped position
    recyclerView.addOnScrollListener(object : RecyclerView.OnScrollListener() {

            if (newState == RecyclerView.SCROLL_STATE_IDLE) {
                val snappedView = snapHelper.findSnapView(recyclerView.layoutManager!!)
                val position = recyclerView.layoutManager!!.getPosition(snappedView!!)
                class="cm">// position is the currently centered item
            }
