    Q: What is Recomposition?

    Recomposition is the process of re-invoking composable functions when their inputs (state) change, to update the UI.


    HOW IT WORKS:

    1. Initial composition: all composables run and build the UI tree.

    2. State changes: a MutableState/StateFlow value is modified.

    3. Compose invalidates all composables that READ the changed state.

    4. Recomposition: only invalidated composables re-execute.

    5. Compose diffs the new output with the old and applies minimal changes.


    KEY RULES:


    • Composable functions can run in any order — don't depend on execution order.

    • Can run in parallel — don't write to shared mutable state in composables.

    • Recomposition skips unchanged composables — if inputs are the same, skip.

    • Recomposition is optimistic — assumes state won't change again mid-recomposition.

    • Side effects must use dedicated APIs (LaunchedEffect, etc.)


    SMART RECOMPOSITION: Compose skips recomposition of a composable if ALL its parameters are "stable" and haven't changed. Stable types:

    - Primitives (Int, String, Boolean, Float, etc.)

    - @Stable or @Immutable annotated classes

    - Lambda types (by reference equality)


    Performance tip: Use @Immutable for data classes passed to composables. Use remember { } to cache expensive computations across recompositions.

    Q: What is State in Compose? remember vs rememberSaveable

    STATE in Compose is any value that can change over time and affects the UI. When state changes, Compose recomposes the composables that read it.


    MutableState<T> — Compose's observable state holder. Created via mutableStateOf(initialValue). When .value changes, all composables reading it are recomposed.


    REMEMBER — Caches a value across recompositions within the same composition. Without remember, the value would reset on every recomposition. Survives: recomposition. Lost on: configuration change, process death, composable leaving composition.


    REMEMBER SAVEABLE — Like remember, but also survives configuration changes and process death (stores in savedInstanceState Bundle). Automatically works for Bundle-compatible types (primitives, String, etc.). For custom types, provide a Saver or use @Parcelize.


    ┌─────────────────────┬──────────────┬────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│                     │ Recomposition│ Config Change  │ Process Death    │
├─────────────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────┼──────────────────┤
│ mutableStateOf      │ ✗ Resets     │ ✗ Lost         │ ✗ Lost           │
│ remember { }        │ ✓ Survives   │ ✗ Lost         │ ✗ Lost           │
│ rememberSaveable {} │ ✓ Survives   │ ✓ Survives     │ ✓ Survives       │
│ ViewModel state     │ ✓ Survives   │ ✓ Survives     │ ✗ Lost*          │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────────┘

    * Use SavedStateHandle in ViewModel for process death.

    class="an">@Composable
fun Counter() {
    class="cm">// remember: survives recomposition
    var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }

    class="cm">// rememberSaveable: survives config change + process death
    var savedCount by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(0) }

    Column {
        Text(class="st">"Count (remember): $count")
        Text(class="st">"Count (saveable): $savedCount")
        Button(onClick = { count++; savedCount++ }) {
            Text(class="st">"Increment")
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// Custom Saver for non-Bundle types
data class City(val name: String, val country: String)

val CitySaver = run {
    val nameKey = class="st">"name"
    val countryKey = class="st">"country"
    mapSaver(
        save = { mapOf(nameKey to it.name, countryKey to it.country) },
        restore = { City(it[nameKey] as String, it[countryKey] as String) }
    )
}

class="an">@Composable
fun CityPicker() {
    var selectedCity by rememberSaveable(stateSaver = CitySaver) {
        mutableStateOf(City(class="st">"Tokyo", class="st">"Japan"))
    }
}

    Q: Stateful composable vs Stateless composable

    STATEFUL COMPOSABLE — Owns and manages its own state internally. Uses remember/rememberSaveable to hold state. Harder to test and reuse because behavior is internal.


    STATELESS COMPOSABLE — Receives state as parameters and emits events via callbacks (lambdas). Has no internal state. Easy to test, reuse, preview, and compose.


    Best practice: Extract state up (State Hoisting). The composable that USES the state should be stateless; the CALLER manages state.

    class="cm">// ❌ Stateful — harder to test and reuse
class="an">@Composable
fun StatefulSearchBar() {
    var query by remember { mutableStateOf(class="st">"") }
    TextField(
        value = query,
        onValueChange = { query = it },
        placeholder = { Text(class="st">"Search...") }
    )
}

class="cm">// ✓ Stateless — caller manages state
class="an">@Composable
fun StatelessSearchBar(
    query: String,
    onQueryChange: (String) -> Unit,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier
) {
    TextField(
        value = query,
        onValueChange = onQueryChange,
        placeholder = { Text(class="st">"Search...") },
        modifier = modifier
    )
}

class="cm">// Stateful wrapper that hoists state
class="an">@Composable
fun SearchScreen(viewModel: SearchViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    StatelessSearchBar(
        query = state.query,
        onQueryChange = viewModel::onQueryChanged
    )
}

    Q: What are side effects? LaunchedEffect vs DisposableEffect

    A SIDE EFFECT is any operation that escapes the scope of a composable function:

    network calls, database writes, analytics events, navigation, showing toasts, etc.


    Composables should be side-effect free for predictable behavior. When you need side effects, use dedicated Effect APIs that are lifecycle-aware.


    LAUNCHED EFFECT — Runs a suspend function when the composable enters the composition. Re-launches when key changes. Cancels when composable leaves. Use for: one-shot loading, navigation events, snackbar.


    DISPOSABLE EFFECT — Runs a block on enter and provides onDispose {} for cleanup. Use for: registering/unregistering listeners, observers, callbacks. Like LaunchedEffect, re-runs when key changes (disposing previous first).

    class="an">@Composable
fun UserDetailScreen(userId: String, viewModel: UserDetailViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    class="cm">// LaunchedEffect: load data when userId changes
    LaunchedEffect(userId) {
        viewModel.loadUser(userId)
    }

    class="cm">// LaunchedEffect for one-shot event collection
    val snackbarHostState = remember { SnackbarHostState() }
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        viewModel.errorEvents.collect { message ->
            snackbarHostState.showSnackbar(message)
        }
    }
}

class="an">@Composable
fun LocationTracker(onLocationUpdate: (Location) -> Unit) {
    val context = LocalContext.current

    class="cm">// DisposableEffect: register listener on enter, unregister on leave
    DisposableEffect(Unit) {
        val locationManager = context.getSystemService(Context.LOCATION_SERVICE) as LocationManager
        val listener = LocationListener { location -> onLocationUpdate(location) }

        locationManager.requestLocationUpdates(
            LocationManager.GPS_PROVIDER, 1000L, 10f, listener
        )

        onDispose {
            locationManager.removeUpdates(listener)
        }
    }
}

    Q: rememberCoroutineScope use cases

    rememberCoroutineScope() provides a CoroutineScope tied to the composable's lifecycle. The scope is cancelled when the composable leaves the composition.


    USE CASE: Launching coroutines from event handlers (callbacks).


    LaunchedEffect vs rememberCoroutineScope:

    - LaunchedEffect: runs automatically on composition / key change.

    - rememberCoroutineScope: gives you a scope to launch manually from callbacks.


    Common use cases:

    - Scroll to item on button click (lazyListState.animateScrollToItem)

    - Show snackbar on user action

    - Perform animation on click

    - Save data on button press

    class="an">@Composable
fun ScrollableList(items: List<String>) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()
    val coroutineScope = rememberCoroutineScope()

    Column {
        Button(onClick = {
            coroutineScope.launch {
                listState.animateScrollToItem(0) class="cm">// needs suspend
            }
        }) {
            Text(class="st">"Scroll to Top")
        }

        LazyColumn(state = listState) {
            items(items) { item -> Text(item, modifier = Modifier.padding(16.dp)) }
        }
    }
}

class="an">@Composable
fun SnackbarExample() {
    val snackbarHostState = remember { SnackbarHostState() }
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()

    Scaffold(snackbarHost = { SnackbarHost(snackbarHostState) }) { padding ->
        Button(
            onClick = {
                scope.launch {
                    val result = snackbarHostState.showSnackbar(
                        message = class="st">"Item deleted",
                        actionLabel = class="st">"Undo",
                        duration = SnackbarDuration.Short
                    )
                    if (result == SnackbarResult.ActionPerformed) {
                        class="cm">// Undo delete
                    }
                }
            },
            modifier = Modifier.padding(padding)
        ) {
            Text(class="st">"Delete")
        }
    }
}

    Q: How to observe Flows and LiveData states in Compose UI?

    Compose provides extension functions to collect observable streams as State.


    STATEFLOW / FLOW:

    collectAsStateWithLifecycle() — Lifecycle-aware (recommended). Starts collecting in STARTED, stops in STOPPED. Prevents UI updates when app is in background.


    collectAsState() — Not lifecycle-aware. Collects as long as composable is in composition. Use only when lifecycle awareness isn't needed.


    LIVEDATA:

    observeAsState() — Converts LiveData to Compose State. Automatically observes/un-observes with composition lifecycle.


    Dependency: implementation "androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose:2.7.x"

    class="an">@Composable
fun UserScreen(viewModel: UserViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    class="cm">// StateFlow → State (lifecycle-aware, recommended)
    val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    class="cm">// Flow → State
    val messages by viewModel.messages.collectAsStateWithLifecycle(initialValue = emptyList())

    class="cm">// LiveData → State
    val legacyData by viewModel.legacyLiveData.observeAsState(initial = class="st">"")

    when {
        uiState.isLoading -> CircularProgressIndicator()
        uiState.error != null -> ErrorScreen(uiState.error!!)
        else -> UserList(uiState.users)
    }
}

    Q: derivedStateOf, rememberUpdatedState explained

    DERIVED STATE OF — Creates a state that is computed from other states. Only triggers recomposition when the DERIVED value changes, not when the source state changes. Great for filtering/transforming state.


    Without derivedStateOf: Every scroll position change (hundreds per second) would trigger recomposition of the "Show button" logic. With derivedStateOf: Only recomposes when shouldShow flips true↔false.


    REMEMBER UPDATED STATE — Captures the latest value of a parameter in a long-lived lambda (e.g., inside LaunchedEffect).


    Problem: LaunchedEffect(Unit) captures the initial value of a lambda. If the lambda changes (new callback), the effect still uses the old one. rememberUpdatedState ensures the latest value is always used.

    class="cm">// derivedStateOf
class="an">@Composable
fun ContactList(contacts: List<Contact>) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()

    val showScrollToTop by remember {
        derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 5 }
    }

    Box {
        LazyColumn(state = listState) {
            items(contacts) { ContactItem(it) }
        }
        if (showScrollToTop) {
            FloatingActionButton(onClick = { class="cm">/* scroll */ }) {
                Icon(Icons.Default.ArrowUpward, contentDescription = class="st">"Scroll to top")
            }
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// rememberUpdatedState
class="an">@Composable
fun SplashScreen(onTimeout: () -> Unit) {
    val currentOnTimeout by rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout)

    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        delay(3000)
        currentOnTimeout() class="cm">// always calls the latest onTimeout, not the initial one
    }

    class="cm">// Splash UI...
}

    Q: What is State Hoisting?

    State Hoisting is the pattern of moving state UP from a composable to its caller, making the composable stateless. The caller passes state DOWN as parameters and receives events UP as callbacks.


    Pattern: (value: T, onValueChange: (T) -> Unit)


    Benefits:

    • Single source of truth — state lives in one place.

    • Encapsulation — only the state owner can modify it.

    • Shareability — hoisted state can be shared with multiple composables.

    • Testability — stateless composables are easy to test.

    • Reusability — composable works with any state source.


    How far to hoist? Hoist to the LOWEST COMMON ANCESTOR that needs it. If only one screen uses it → ViewModel. If shared → navigation-level ViewModel.

    class="cm">// Hoisted state pattern
class="an">@Composable
fun EditableUserProfile(
    name: String,
    onNameChange: (String) -> Unit,
    email: String,
    onEmailChange: (String) -> Unit,
    onSave: () -> Unit,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier
) {
    Column(modifier = modifier.padding(16.dp)) {
        OutlinedTextField(value = name, onValueChange = onNameChange, label = { Text(class="st">"Name") })
        OutlinedTextField(value = email, onValueChange = onEmailChange, label = { Text(class="st">"Email") })
        Button(onClick = onSave) { Text(class="st">"Save") }
    }
}

class="cm">// Caller (screen-level composable) owns the state
class="an">@Composable
fun ProfileScreen(viewModel: ProfileViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    EditableUserProfile(
        name = state.name,
        onNameChange = viewModel::onNameChange,
        email = state.email,
        onEmailChange = viewModel::onEmailChange,
        onSave = viewModel::saveProfile
    )
}

    Q: Explain CompositionLocal

    CompositionLocal provides implicit data passing through the composition tree without explicitly passing it as parameters to every composable.


    Think of it as "scoped dependency injection" for composables.


    Built-in examples:

    LocalContext.current — current Android Context

    LocalDensity.current — screen density

    LocalConfiguration.current — device configuration

    LocalLifecycleOwner.current — lifecycle owner

    LocalFocusManager.current — focus management


    Two types:

    staticCompositionLocalOf — rarely changes; when it does, entire subtree recomposes.

    compositionLocalOf — can change often; only recomposes readers.


    USE CASES:

    • Theming (MaterialTheme uses CompositionLocals internally)

    • Feature flags

    • Analytics/logging context

    • Navigation controller access


    ⚠️ Use sparingly. Overuse makes code harder to understand because dependencies are implicit. Prefer explicit parameters when feasible.

    data class AppConfig(val isDarkMode: Boolean, val apiBaseUrl: String)

val LocalAppConfig = compositionLocalOf<AppConfig> {
    error(class="st">"No AppConfig provided")
}

class="an">@Composable
fun AppRoot() {
    val config = AppConfig(isDarkMode = true, apiBaseUrl = class="st">"https:class="cm">//api.example.com")

    CompositionLocalProvider(LocalAppConfig provides config) {
        AppContent() class="cm">// all children can access LocalAppConfig.current
    }
}

class="an">@Composable
fun DeepNestedChild() {
    val config = LocalAppConfig.current
    Text(class="st">"API: ${config.apiBaseUrl}")
}

    Q: Jetpack Compose Phases

    Compose renders UI in THREE phases (similar to View's measure/layout/draw):


    1. COMPOSITION (What to show)

    - Executes @Composable functions.

    - Builds/updates the UI tree (slot table).

    - Reads state to determine what to display.

    - Produces a tree of LayoutNodes.


    2. LAYOUT (Where to place it)

    - Measures each node (like onMeasure in View).

    - Places nodes at specific positions (like onLayout).

    - Single-pass measurement: each child measured once (no double taxation).

    - Uses Constraints (min/max width/height).


    3. DRAWING (How to render it)

    - Draws each node to the Canvas.

    - Renders text, shapes, images, etc.

    - Canvas operations (drawRect, drawText, etc.)


    PERFORMANCE INSIGHT:

    State reads in later phases don't trigger earlier phases.

    - State read in DRAWING → only re-draws (no re-layout, no re-composition).

    - State read in LAYOUT → re-layout + re-draw (no re-composition).

    - State read in COMPOSITION → full re-composition + layout + draw.


    Optimization tip: Use Modifier.graphicsLayer { } for animation state to read state in the DRAWING phase only, skipping composition/layout.


    Example: animating alpha

    ❌ Modifier.alpha(animatedAlpha) → reads in composition

    ✓ Modifier.graphicsLayer { alpha = animatedAlpha } → reads in draw only

    Q: What is the role of Modifier?

    Modifier is Compose's mechanism for decorating or augmenting composables. It replaces XML attributes like layout_width, padding, background, onClick, etc. from the View system.


    KEY PROPERTIES:


    1. CHAINING — Modifiers chain with the dot operator. Order matters! Modifier.padding(8.dp).background(Color.Red) // padding OUTSIDE red bg Modifier.background(Color.Red).padding(8.dp) // padding INSIDE red bg


    2. ORDER MATTERS — Modifiers apply from LEFT to RIGHT (outer to inner). Like wrapping in nested containers.


    3. CATEGORIES:

    Layout: size, fillMaxWidth, padding, offset, wrapContentSize Drawing: background, border, clip, shadow, alpha Input: clickable, toggleable, draggable, scrollable Semantics: semantics, testTag, contentDescription Focus: focusable, focusRequester Other: graphicsLayer, animateContentSize, pointerInput


    4. BEST PRACTICE — Accept Modifier parameter (default = Modifier) as the first optional parameter. Lets callers customize layout from outside.

    class="an">@Composable
fun StyledCard(title: String, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    Card(
        modifier = modifier
            .fillMaxWidth()
            .padding(horizontal = 16.dp, vertical = 8.dp)
            .shadow(4.dp, shape = RoundedCornerShape(12.dp))
            .clip(RoundedCornerShape(12.dp))
            .clickable { class="cm">/* handle click */ }
    ) {
        Text(
            text = title,
            modifier = Modifier.padding(16.dp),
            style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium
        )
    }
}

    Q: What are Semantics?

    Semantics in Compose provide meaning and metadata to UI elements for:


    1. ACCESSIBILITY — TalkBack reads semantics to describe UI to visually impaired users. contentDescription, stateDescription, role.


    2. TESTING — Compose testing APIs find elements by semantics. onNodeWithText(), onNodeWithContentDescription(), onNodeWithTag().


    3. AUTOFILL — System uses semantics to auto-fill form fields.


    Compose automatically merges semantics up the tree. A Button with Text inside automatically has the text as its semantic label.


    clearAndSetSemantics { } — replaces all child semantics with custom ones. semantics(mergeDescendants = true) { } — merges children into one node.

    class="an">@Composable
fun AccessibleToggle(
    label: String,
    checked: Boolean,
    onCheckedChange: (Boolean) -> Unit
) {
    Row(
        modifier = Modifier
            .semantics(mergeDescendants = true) { }
            .toggleable(
                value = checked,
                onValueChange = onCheckedChange,
                role = Role.Switch
            )
            .padding(16.dp),
        verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically
    ) {
        Text(label, modifier = Modifier.weight(1f))
        Switch(
            checked = checked,
            onCheckedChange = null class="cm">// handled by parent Row
        )
    }
}

class="cm">// Testing with semantics
class="cm">// composeTestRule.onNodeWithText(class="st">"Dark Mode").assertIsToggled()
class="cm">// composeTestRule.onNodeWithTag(class="st">"loginButton").performClick()
class="cm">// composeTestRule.onNodeWithContentDescription(class="st">"Profile picture").assertIsDisplayed()

    Q: How do you handle navigation in Jetpack Compose?

    Navigation in Compose uses the Navigation Component for Compose library.


    KEY CONCEPTS:

    NavHost — Container that displays destinations. Manages back stack. NavController — Manages navigation state. Created via rememberNavController(). NavGraph — Collection of destinations (routes). Route — String identifier for a destination (e.g., "profile/{userId}").


    Type-safe navigation (Navigation 2.8+) uses @Serializable data classes as routes.

    class="cm">// Define routes as serializable classes
class="an">@Serializable object HomeRoute
class="an">@Serializable data class ProfileRoute(val userId: String)
class="an">@Serializable data class SettingsRoute(val tab: String = class="st">"general")

class="an">@Composable
fun AppNavigation() {
    val navController = rememberNavController()

    NavHost(navController = navController, startDestination = HomeRoute) {

        composable<HomeRoute> {
            HomeScreen(
                onNavigateToProfile = { userId ->
                    navController.navigate(ProfileRoute(userId))
                },
                onNavigateToSettings = {
                    navController.navigate(SettingsRoute())
                }
            )
        }

        composable<ProfileRoute> { backStackEntry ->
            val route = backStackEntry.toRoute<ProfileRoute>()
            ProfileScreen(userId = route.userId)
        }

        composable<SettingsRoute> { backStackEntry ->
            val route = backStackEntry.toRoute<SettingsRoute>()
            SettingsScreen(initialTab = route.tab)
        }
    }
}

    Navigation best practices:

    • Pass navController only to top-level composable; pass callbacks down.

    • Use ViewModel for navigation events (SharedFlow of navigation actions).

    • Hoist navigation state — screens shouldn't know about NavController.

    • Handle deep links via NavDeepLink in navigation graph.

    Q: Unidirectional data flow in Jetpack Compose

    Unidirectional Data Flow (UDF) means data flows DOWN and events flow UP.


      ┌──────────┐   state (down)    ┌──────────┐
  │ ViewModel│ ────────────────→ │   UI     │
  │          │                   │(Compose) │
  │          │ ←──────────────── │          │
  └──────────┘   events (up)     └──────────┘

    STATE flows DOWN: ViewModel exposes StateFlow → UI collects and renders. EVENTS flow UP: User actions → UI calls ViewModel methods via lambdas.


    Benefits:

    • Single source of truth — state lives in ViewModel only.

    • Predictable — UI is a pure function of state.

    • Testable — test ViewModel by sending events, asserting state.

    • Debuggable — can log/inspect every state change.


    Implementation pattern:

    1. Screen-level state in ViewModel (StateFlow<UiState>).

    2. UI collects state with collectAsStateWithLifecycle().

    3. User interactions call ViewModel methods (click → viewModel.onAction()).

    4. ViewModel updates state → UI re-renders.

    class="cm">// UDF Example
data class TodoUiState(
    val items: List<TodoItem> = emptyList(),
    val inputText: String = class="st">""
)

class TodoViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(TodoUiState())
    val uiState: StateFlow<TodoUiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow()

    fun onInputChanged(text: String) {
        _uiState.update { it.copy(inputText = text) }
    }

    fun onAddTodo() {
        val text = _uiState.value.inputText
        if (text.isBlank()) return
        _uiState.update {
            it.copy(
                items = it.items + TodoItem(text = text),
                inputText = class="st">""
            )
        }
    }
}

class="an">@Composable
fun TodoScreen(viewModel: TodoViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    TodoContent(
        items = state.items,
        inputText = state.inputText,
        onInputChanged = viewModel::onInputChanged, class="cm">// events UP
        onAddClicked = viewModel::onAddTodo
    )
}

class="an">@Composable
fun TodoContent(
    items: List<TodoItem>,       class="cm">// state DOWN
    inputText: String,           class="cm">// state DOWN
    onInputChanged: (String) -> Unit, class="cm">// events UP
    onAddClicked: () -> Unit          class="cm">// events UP
) {
    Column {
        LazyColumn { items(items) { Text(it.text) } }
        Row {
            TextField(value = inputText, onValueChange = onInputChanged)
            Button(onClick = onAddClicked) { Text(class="st">"Add") }

    Q: How to create Custom Layouts in Compose?

    Custom Layouts in Compose let you control exactly how children are measured and placed, beyond what Row/Column/Box provide.


    Use the Layout composable (analogous to custom ViewGroup in View system).


    Steps:

    1. Measure each child with constraints → get Placeables.

    2. Determine the layout's total size.

    3. Place each child at specific coordinates.


    Single-pass measurement: each child is measured ONCE. Use intrinsic measurements if you need to pre-query sizes.

    class="cm">// Staggered grid / flow layout
class="an">@Composable
fun FlowRow(
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,
    horizontalSpacing: Dp = 8.dp,
    verticalSpacing: Dp = 8.dp,
    content: class="an">@Composable () -> Unit
) {
    Layout(
        content = content,
        modifier = modifier
    ) { measurables, constraints ->
        val hSpacingPx = horizontalSpacing.roundToPx()
        val vSpacingPx = verticalSpacing.roundToPx()

        val placeables = measurables.map { it.measure(constraints.copy(minWidth = 0)) }

        var x = 0
        var y = 0
        var rowHeight = 0

        val positions = placeables.map { placeable ->
            if (x + placeable.width > constraints.maxWidth && x > 0) {
                x = 0
                y += rowHeight + vSpacingPx
                rowHeight = 0
            }
            val pos = IntOffset(x, y)
            x += placeable.width + hSpacingPx
            rowHeight = maxOf(rowHeight, placeable.height)
            pos
        }

        val totalHeight = y + rowHeight

        layout(constraints.maxWidth, totalHeight) {
            placeables.forEachIndexed { index, placeable ->
                placeable.placeRelative(positions[index])
            }
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// Modifier.layout for single-element custom layout
class="an">@Composable
fun BaselineAlignedText() {
    Text(
        class="st">"Hello",
        modifier = Modifier.layout { measurable, constraints ->
            val placeable = measurable.measure(constraints)
            val firstBaseline = placeable[FirstBaseline]
            val y = 48.dp.roundToPx() - firstBaseline
            layout(placeable.width, placeable.height + y) {
                placeable.placeRelative(0, y)
            }
        }
    )
}

    SECTION 18 — JAVA (Brief Interview Answers)

    Q: SOLID Principles

    S — Single Responsibility Principle:

    A class should have only one reason to change. Each class handles one concern. Example: UserRepository handles data access, UserValidator handles validation — not both in one class. In Android, ViewModel handles UI state, UseCase handles business logic, Repository handles data.


    O — Open/Closed Principle:

    Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. Add new behavior through inheritance or composition, not by modifying existing code. Example: Define an AnalyticsProvider interface; add new providers (Firebase, Mixpanel) without changing existing code.


    L — Liskov Substitution Principle:

    Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking behavior. If a function accepts Shape, passing Circle or Rectangle must work correctly. Violating LSP: Square extends Rectangle but breaks setWidth/setHeight expectations.


    I — Interface Segregation Principle:

    Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don't use. Prefer multiple small, focused interfaces over one fat interface. Example: Instead of one Repository interface with 20 methods, split into ReadRepository and WriteRepository.


    D — Dependency Inversion Principle:

    High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. ViewModel depends on Repository interface (abstraction), not on RoomRepository (concrete). This is the foundation of DI frameworks.

    Q: OOP Concepts, abstract class vs interface, overloading vs overriding

    FOUR PILLARS OF OOP:

    Encapsulation — Hide internal state, expose through methods. (private fields + public getters)

    Inheritance — Reuse code by extending a parent class. (class Dog : Animal)

    Polymorphism — Same interface, different implementations. (animal.speak() → bark/meow)

    Abstraction — Hide complexity, expose essential features. (interface vs implementation)


    ABSTRACT CLASS vs INTERFACE:


    ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│                  │ Abstract Class       │ Interface                │
├──────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ Constructor      │ Can have             │ Cannot have              │
│ State            │ Can have fields      │ No backing fields (in    │
│                  │                      │ Java), can in Kotlin     │
│ Methods          │ Abstract + concrete  │ Abstract + default       │
│ Inheritance      │ Single (one parent)  │ Multiple (many interfaces│
│ Use when         │ IS-A + shared state  │ CAN-DO (capability)      │
└──────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

    METHOD OVERLOADING — Same name, different parameters (compile-time polymorphism). fun log(message: String) { ... } fun log(message: String, level: Level) { ... }


    METHOD OVERRIDING — Subclass provides specific implementation of a parent method (runtime polymorphism). Uses override keyword in Kotlin.

    Q: String Pool, String immutability

    STRING POOL (String Intern Pool):

    The JVM maintains a special memory area where String literals are stored. When you create "hello", JVM checks the pool first — if it exists, returns the existing reference. This saves memory when the same string appears often.


    val a = "hello" // stored in pool val b = "hello" // reuses same reference from pool println(a === b) // true (same reference)


    val c = String("hello".toCharArray()) // new object, NOT in pool println(a === c) // false (different reference) println(a == c) // true (same content)


    STRING IMMUTABILITY:

    Strings cannot be modified after creation. Any "modification" creates a new String object. This ensures:

    1. Thread safety — no synchronization needed for shared strings.

    2. Hashcode caching — computed once, reused (efficient HashMap keys).

    3. Security — connection strings, class names can't be tampered with.

    4. String Pool works — shared references are safe because strings don't change.


    For mutable string operations, use StringBuilder (not thread-safe, faster) or StringBuffer (thread-safe, slower).

    Q: Access modifiers (private, default, protected, public)

    JAVA ACCESS MODIFIERS:


    ┌──────────────┬───────┬─────────┬────────────┬───────────┐
│              │ Class │ Package │ Subclass   │ World     │
├──────────────┼───────┼─────────┼────────────┼───────────┤
│ private      │  ✓    │  ✗      │  ✗         │  ✗        │
│ default      │  ✓    │  ✓      │  ✗         │  ✗        │
│ protected    │  ✓    │  ✓      │  ✓         │  ✗        │
│ public       │  ✓    │  ✓      │  ✓         │  ✓        │
└──────────────┴───────┴─────────┴────────────┴───────────┘

    KOTLIN ACCESS MODIFIERS:


    private — Visible within the file (top-level) or class.

    internal — Visible within the same MODULE (Gradle module).

    protected — Visible in the class and subclasses (not package).

    public — Default in Kotlin, visible everywhere.


    Key Kotlin difference: No "package-private" (Java's default). Kotlin adds "internal" which is module-scoped — much more useful for multi-module Android projects.

    Q: Generics in Java

    Generics provide type safety at compile time while allowing code reuse across different types. Introduced in Java 5 via type erasure.


    TYPE ERASURE: Generic type information is removed at runtime. List<String> and List<Integer> are both just List at runtime. This is why you can't do if (obj is List<String>) in Java/Kotlin.


    VARIANCE (Kotlin perspective, applies to Java's ? extends / ? super):


    COVARIANCE (out / ? extends) — Producer. Can read T, not write T. List<out Animal> = can assign List<Dog> to it. Java: List<? extends Animal>


    CONTRAVARIANCE (in / ? super) — Consumer. Can write T, not read T. Comparator<in Animal> = can assign Comparator<Any> to it. Java: Comparator<? super Animal>


    INVARIANT — Neither in nor out. MutableList<T> — exact type only.


    MNEMONIC: PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super.


    Reified generics (Kotlin only): inline functions can access generic type at runtime using reified keyword. Useful for type checks and reflection. inline fun <reified T> isType(obj: Any) = obj is T

    Q: What is garbage collector? How does it work?

    The Garbage Collector (GC) automatically frees memory by reclaiming objects that are no longer reachable from any GC root.


    GC ROOTS: Stack variables, static fields, JNI references, thread objects.


    HOW IT WORKS (Generational Collection):


    1. YOUNG GENERATION — Newly created objects.

    - Eden space: all new objects start here.

    - Survivor spaces (S0, S1): objects that survived a minor GC.

    - Minor GC: fast, collects Eden + one Survivor, copies survivors to other.


    2. OLD GENERATION (Tenured) — Objects that survived many minor GCs.

    - Major GC: slower, collects old generation.

    - Triggered when old gen fills up.


    ANDROID-SPECIFIC (ART Runtime):

    - Concurrent Copying GC (default on ART) — minimal pause times.

    - Generational approach: young gen collected more frequently.

    - Compacting GC reduces fragmentation.

    - GC pauses are typically < 2ms on modern devices.


    MEMORY LEAK: When objects that should be GC'd are still referenced (e.g., Activity referenced by a static field). The GC can't collect them. Use LeakCanary to detect leaks in Android apps.

    Q: synchronized keyword, volatile modifier, ThreadPoolExecutor

    SYNCHRONIZED — Ensures only one thread can execute a block/method at a time. Provides both mutual exclusion and memory visibility. @Synchronized fun increment() { count++ } // Kotlin synchronized(lock) { sharedList.add(item) }


    VOLATILE — Ensures visibility of changes across threads. A write to a volatile variable is immediately visible to all other threads. Does NOT provide atomicity — count++ on volatile is still not thread-safe. Use for flags: @Volatile var isRunning = true


    THREAD POOL EXECUTOR — Manages a pool of worker threads. Avoids thread creation overhead. Configurable:

    - corePoolSize: minimum threads kept alive

    - maxPoolSize: maximum threads

    - keepAliveTime: idle thread lifetime

    - workQueue: BlockingQueue for pending tasks


    Android's AsyncTask used a ThreadPoolExecutor internally. Kotlin coroutines use thread pools via Dispatchers (IO = 64 threads max, Default = CPU core count).

    Q: Checked vs Unchecked Exception

    CHECKED EXCEPTIONS (Java only — Kotlin has no checked exceptions):

    Must be caught or declared in method signature (throws clause). Extends Exception (but not RuntimeException). Examples: IOException, SQLException, FileNotFoundException. Purpose: recoverable errors that the caller should handle.


    UNCHECKED EXCEPTIONS:

    Don't need to be caught or declared. Extends RuntimeException. Examples: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, IndexOutOfBoundsException, ClassCastException. Purpose: programming errors (bugs).


    KOTLIN APPROACH: All exceptions are unchecked. No throws clause. Use @Throws annotation for Java interop only. Kotlin philosophy: checked exceptions add boilerplate without improving safety.


    ERROR vs EXCEPTION:

    Error — JVM-level problems, not recoverable (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError). Exception — Application-level problems, potentially recoverable.

    Q: final, finally, finalize

    FINAL (Kotlin: val, no open):

    - final class — cannot be extended (all Kotlin classes are final by default).

    - final method — cannot be overridden.

    - final variable — cannot be reassigned (val in Kotlin).


    FINALLY:

    Block that executes after try/catch regardless of outcome. Used for cleanup: closing streams, releasing resources. try { read() } catch (e: IOException) { handle() } finally { close() } Modern alternative: use() extension (auto-closes resources).


    FINALIZE (DEPRECATED since Java 9):

    Method called by GC before collecting an object. Historically used for cleanup, but unreliable — no guarantee when (or if) it runs. Problems: delays GC, unpredictable timing, performance overhead. Alternative: Cleaner class (Java 9+) or explicit close()/release().

    Q: static keyword in Java

    STATIC in Java means the member belongs to the CLASS, not to instances.


    static field — Shared across all instances. One copy in memory. static method — Called on the class, not on an instance. No access to this.

    static block — Runs once when the class is loaded. Used for initialization.

    static class — Nested class that doesn't hold a reference to the outer class.


    KOTLIN EQUIVALENTS:

    static field/method → companion object { } or top-level functions

    static constant → companion object { const val X = 1 }

    static nested class → class Nested (default, no inner keyword)

    static initializer → init { } in companion object


    ⚠️ Android gotcha: Static fields holding Activity/Context → memory leaks. The static field lives for the entire process lifetime.


    @JvmStatic annotation makes companion object methods/properties appear as actual Java static members for interop.

    Q: Serialization and Deserialization, Parcelable vs Serializable

    SERIALIZATION: Converting an object into a byte stream for storage/transfer. DESERIALIZATION: Reconstructing an object from a byte stream.


    SERIALIZABLE (Java):

    - Marker interface (no methods to implement).

    - Uses reflection → slow.

    - Creates many temporary objects → GC pressure.

    - Simple to implement: just implements Serializable.


    PARCELABLE (Android):

    - Android-specific interface optimized for IPC (Inter-Process Communication).

    - No reflection — manual or generated marshalling/unmarshalling.

    - ~10x faster than Serializable on Android.

    - Used for: Intent extras, Bundle data, Activity/Fragment arguments.

    - With @Parcelize (kotlin-parcelize plugin): auto-generated, zero boilerplate.


    WHEN TO USE:

    Parcelable → passing data between Android components (Intent, Bundle, AIDL). Serializable → saving to disk, network serialization (but prefer Gson/Moshi/Protobuf).


    Kotlin Serialization (kotlinx.serialization):

    Modern alternative for JSON/Protobuf/CBOR. Compile-time, no reflection. @Serializable data class User(val name: String, val age: Int)

├─────────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┤

    - HashMap for large datasets where O(1) lookup matters.

    SECTION 19 — ANDROID JETPACK

    Q: What is Android Jetpack?

    Android Jetpack is a suite of libraries, tools, and guidance from Google to help developers build high-quality Android apps.


    Categories:


    ARCHITECTURE:

    ViewModel, LiveData, Room, DataStore, WorkManager, Navigation, Paging, Lifecycle, SavedState


    UI:

    Jetpack Compose, Fragment, RecyclerView, ViewPager2, ConstraintLayout, Material Design Components, AppCompat


    BEHAVIOR:

    CameraX, Notifications, Permissions, Sharing, Slices, Media


    FOUNDATION:

    AppCompat, Android KTX, Multidex, Test


    Benefits:

    • Backwards compatible — works across Android versions.

    • Follows best practices — lifecycle awareness, testability.

    • Reduces boilerplate — e.g., Room vs raw SQLite.

    • Consistent APIs — all libraries work well together.

    • Maintained by Google — regular updates and bug fixes.

    Q: What is a ViewModel and how is it useful? How does ViewModel work internally?

    ViewModel is a lifecycle-aware component that stores and manages UI-related data. It survives configuration changes (rotation, locale change, etc.).


    WHY USEFUL:

    • Survives config changes — no data loss on rotation.

    • Separation of concerns — UI logic out of Activity/Fragment.

    • Scope — lives as long as its ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity/Fragment/NavBackStackEntry).

    • Coroutine scope — viewModelScope auto-cancels on onCleared().


    HOW IT WORKS INTERNALLY:


    1. ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity/Fragment) has a ViewModelStore. ViewModelStore is a HashMap<String, ViewModel>.


    2. On config change, the Activity is destroyed and recreated, BUT:

    - The NonConfigurationInstances object is retained by the framework.

    - ViewModelStore is stored in NonConfigurationInstances.

    - The new Activity retrieves the same ViewModelStore.


    3. ViewModelProvider.get(MyViewModel::class.java):

    - Checks ViewModelStore for existing instance → returns it.

    - If not found, uses ViewModelProvider.Factory to create one → stores it.


    4. When the Activity TRULY finishes (not config change):

    - Activity.isFinishing == true

    - ViewModelStore.clear() is called

    - Each ViewModel's onCleared() is called

    - viewModelScope is cancelled


    Lifecycle:

    Activity created → ViewModel created (if first time) Config change → Activity destroyed → Activity recreated → same ViewModel Activity finished → ViewModel.onCleared() → GC'd

    class MyViewModel(
    private val repository: UserRepository,
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle class="cm">// survives process death
) : ViewModel() {

    class="cm">// Survives config change
    private val _users = MutableStateFlow<List<User>>(emptyList())
    val users: StateFlow<List<User>> = _users.asStateFlow()

    class="cm">// Survives process death
    val searchQuery = savedStateHandle.getStateFlow(class="st">"query", class="st">"")

    fun setSearchQuery(query: String) {
        savedStateHandle[class="st">"query"] = query
    }

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            repository.getUsers().collect { _users.value = it }
        }
    }

    override fun onCleared() {
        super.onCleared()
        class="cm">// cleanup if needed (viewModelScope is auto-cancelled)
    }
}

    Q: SharedViewModel in Android

    A SharedViewModel is a ViewModel scoped to an Activity (or Navigation graph) that is shared between multiple Fragments. This allows Fragments to communicate without direct references to each other.


    Use case: Master-detail layout, multi-step forms, filter panel.


    Key: Both Fragments request the ViewModel scoped to the SAME owner. In Fragment A: val vm by activityViewModels<SharedViewModel>() In Fragment B: val vm by activityViewModels<SharedViewModel>() Both get the SAME instance because the owner is the Activity.


    With Navigation: scope to a navigation graph. val vm by navGraphViewModels<SharedViewModel>(R.id.checkout_graph)

    class SharedFilterViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _selectedCategory = MutableStateFlow<String?>(null)
    val selectedCategory: StateFlow<String?> = _selectedCategory.asStateFlow()

    fun selectCategory(category: String) { _selectedCategory.value = category }
}

    Modern recommendation: Use StateFlow in ViewModels. Google is moving towards Flow-based APIs. LiveData is still fine for existing codebases.

    Q: What is LiveData? setValue vs postValue

    LiveData is a lifecycle-aware observable data holder class from Android Jetpack.


    KEY PROPERTIES:

    • Lifecycle-aware: only notifies ACTIVE observers (STARTED or RESUMED).

    • No memory leaks: observers are auto-removed when lifecycle is DESTROYED.

    • No crashes from stopped activities: inactive observers don't receive updates.

    • Configuration change safe: observers re-receive the latest value on reattach.

    • Always has the latest data: new observer immediately gets the current value.


    setValue() vs postValue():


    setValue(value) — MUST be called from MAIN THREAD. Sets the value and immediately dispatches to observers. Throws if called from background thread.


    postValue(value) — Can be called from ANY THREAD. Posts a task to main thread to set the value. If called multiple times before main thread processes, only the LAST value is dispatched (intermediate values are dropped).


    ⚠️ postValue() dropping intermediate values is a common interview gotcha. If you postValue("A") then postValue("B") rapidly, observers may only see "B".

    Q: Explain WorkManager and its use cases

    WorkManager is the recommended API for deferrable, guaranteed background work. It runs even if the app exits or the device restarts.


    WHEN TO USE:

    • Upload logs/analytics to server

    • Sync local data with remote

    • Process/compress images

    • Periodic data cleanup

    • Download content for offline use


    TYPES OF WORK:

    OneTimeWorkRequest — Runs once. PeriodicWorkRequest — Runs at intervals (min 15 minutes).


    CONSTRAINTS:

    NetworkType (CONNECTED, UNMETERED), RequiresCharging, RequiresBatteryNotLow, RequiresStorageNotLow, RequiresDeviceIdle


    FEATURES:

    • Chaining: workA.then(workB).then(workC) — sequential pipeline.

    • Parallel: WorkManager.enqueue(listOf(workA, workB)) — run together.

    • Unique work: enqueueUniqueWork() — prevent duplicates.

    • Input/Output data: pass Data objects between chained workers.

    • Backoff policy: LINEAR or EXPONENTIAL retry on failure.

    • Expedited work: run immediately with foreground service.


    UNDER THE HOOD:

    Uses JobScheduler (API 23+), GcmNetworkManager, or AlarmManager + BroadcastReceiver as the backing scheduler depending on API level. Work metadata is stored in a Room database for persistence across reboots.

    class SyncWorker(
    context: Context,
    params: WorkerParameters
) : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {

    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        return try {
            val repository = class="cm">/* get from DI */ SyncRepository()
            repository.syncPendingChanges()
            Result.success()
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            if (runAttemptCount < 3) Result.retry()
            else Result.failure()
        }
    }
}

class="cm">// Enqueue work
val syncRequest = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>()
    .setConstraints(
        Constraints.Builder()
            .setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED)
            .setRequiresBatteryNotLow(true)
            .build()
    )
    .setBackoffCriteria(BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .addTag(class="st">"sync")
    .build()

class="cm">// WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueueUniqueWork(class="st">"sync", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, syncRequest)

    Q: How Does WorkManager Guarantee Task Execution?

    WorkManager guarantees task execution through several mechanisms:


    1. PERSISTENCE — Work requests are stored in a Room database. Even if the app is killed or the device reboots, pending work is persisted and re-scheduled on next boot.


    2. PLATFORM DELEGATION — Delegates to the best available scheduler:

    - API 23+: JobScheduler (system-managed job scheduling)

    - API 14-22: GcmNetworkManager (if GMS available) or AlarmManager + BroadcastReceiver (fallback) These system APIs survive app death and device reboot.


    3. BOOT RECEIVER — WorkManager registers a BroadcastReceiver for BOOT_COMPLETED. On reboot, it re-reads the Room DB and re-schedules all pending work with the platform scheduler.


    4. CONSTRAINT MONITORING — Continuously monitors constraints (network, battery, idle). When all constraints are met, work runs.


    5. RETRY POLICY — On worker failure returning Result.retry(), WorkManager re-enqueues with backoff (linear or exponential).


    IMPORTANT CAVEATS:

    - "Guaranteed" means it WILL run eventually, not immediately.

    - Doze mode and App Standby can delay execution.

    - For immediate work, use setExpedited() (foreground service).

    - OEM battery optimizations may still interfere (Xiaomi, Samsung, Huawei). Direct users to dontkillmyapp.com settings.

    SECTION 20 — OTHER TOPICS

    Q: Serializable vs Parcelable

    (Covered in Section 18 — brief recap)


    Serializable:

    - Java standard interface. Uses reflection. Slow on Android.

    - Simple: just implement interface, no methods needed.

    - Creates many temporary objects → GC pressure.


    Parcelable:

    - Android-specific. No reflection. ~10x faster.

    - Use @Parcelize in Kotlin for zero-boilerplate implementation.

    - Required for passing data in Intents, Bundles, and IPC.


    @Parcelize data class User(val name: String, val age: Int) : Parcelable


    Rule: Always use Parcelable for Android component communication. Use kotlinx.serialization for JSON/disk/network serialization.

    Q: Why Bundle class is used for data passing?

    Bundle is a type-safe key-value container optimized for Android IPC (Inter-Process Communication via Binder).


    WHY BUNDLE (not HashMap)?


    1. PARCELABLE — Bundle implements Parcelable, so it can be sent across process boundaries (Activity ↔ Activity, even across apps).


    2. TYPE-SAFE ACCESSORS — getInt(), getString(), getParcelable<T>(), etc. Prevents ClassCastException that HashMap<String, Any> would allow.


    3. ANDROID FRAMEWORK INTEGRATION — Used by:

    - Intent extras (intent.putExtra / intent.extras)

    - Fragment arguments (fragment.arguments)

    - onSaveInstanceState / onRestoreInstanceState

    - DialogFragment arguments

    - Activity result data


    4. INTERNALLY USES ARRAYMAP — Memory efficient for small datasets (typical for component arguments). Not HashMap.


    5. BINDER TRANSACTION LIMIT — ~1MB per process. Bundle warns you to keep data small. Don't store large objects — store IDs and retrieve from ViewModel/database.


    ALTERNATIVE: Safe Args (Navigation Component) generates type-safe classes for passing arguments between destinations.

    Q: How to secure API keys in Android App?

    ⚠️ No client-side secret is 100% secure. The goal is to make extraction as difficult as possible and minimize damage if keys are compromised.


    STRATEGIES (from least to most secure):


    1. GRADLE/BUILDCONFIG (basic — still in APK) Store in local.properties (gitignored), read in build.gradle. buildConfigField("String", "API_KEY", "\"${localProps['apiKey']}\"")

    ⚠️ Key is still in the APK as a string. Can be extracted with apktool.


    2. NDK / NATIVE CODE Store key in C/C++ .so file. Harder to extract than BuildConfig (needs binary analysis). Still not truly secure — determined attacker can disassemble native code.


    3. OBFUSCATION ProGuard/R8 obfuscates class/method names. Encrypt the key string and decrypt at runtime. Adds a layer but doesn't prevent determined attackers.


    4. BACKEND PROXY (RECOMMENDED) Never put the real API key on the client. Instead:

    Client → Your Backend (with user auth) → Third-party API (with real key). The client authenticates with your server; your server holds the API key. Benefits: rate limiting, key rotation without app update, revocation.


    5. ANDROID KEYSTORE Use for encryption keys / signing keys (not API keys). Hardware-backed secure storage. Keys can't be extracted.


    6. GOOGLE CLOUD SECRET MANAGER / FIREBASE REMOTE CONFIG Fetch keys at runtime (still transmitted to client, but not in APK). Use with certificate pinning and encrypted transport.


    BEST PRACTICE: Sensitive API keys should NEVER be in the APK. Use a backend proxy. For less sensitive keys (Maps, Analytics), use BuildConfig + NDK + restrict key scope (API restrictions on console).

    Q: How does the Android Push Notification system work?

    Android Push Notifications use Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM).


    ARCHITECTURE:


    Your Server → FCM Server → Device (Google Play Services) → Your App


    FLOW:


    1. REGISTRATION:

    a. App starts → FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().token → gets FCM token. b. Token is a unique device+app identifier. c. App sends token to your backend server for storage. d. Token can change — handle onNewToken() callback.


    2. SENDING:

    a. Your server sends HTTP POST to FCM endpoint with:

    - Target: device token, topic, or condition

    - Payload: notification (title/body) and/or data (key-value pairs) b. FCM routes the message to the correct device.


    3. RECEIVING:

    a. Google Play Services maintains a persistent connection to FCM. b. Message arrives → delivered to FirebaseMessagingService. c. Two types of messages:


    NOTIFICATION MESSAGE — Handled by system when app is in background. Shows notification automatically. onMessageReceived() only called when app is in foreground.


    DATA MESSAGE — Always delivered to onMessageReceived() regardless of app state. You build the notification manually. More control.


    Recommendation: Use DATA messages for full control.


    4. HIGH vs NORMAL PRIORITY:

    HIGH — Delivered immediately, can wake device from Doze. Use for messages the user should see promptly (chat messages). NORMAL — May be batched/delayed by Doze. Use for non-urgent (sync triggers).


    TOPICS: Subscribe devices to topics (e.g., "sports_news"). Send to all subscribers at once without managing individual tokens.

    Q: What is Cleartext traffic?

    Cleartext traffic is unencrypted HTTP communication (not HTTPS). Data travels as plain text and can be intercepted by anyone on the network (man-in-the-middle attack).


    ANDROID 9 (API 28)+ DEFAULT:

    Cleartext traffic is BLOCKED by default. All HTTP requests must use HTTPS. Violating this causes: java.net.UnknownServiceException:

    "CLEARTEXT communication to example.com not permitted"


    TO ALLOW (development only):


    1. Network Security Config (recommended):

    res/xml/network_security_config.xml:

    <network-security-config> <domain-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"> <domain includeSubdomains="true">10.0.2.2</domain> <!-- emulator localhost --> </domain-config> </network-security-config>


    AndroidManifest.xml:

    android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config"


    2. Global flag (NOT recommended for production):

    android:usesCleartextTraffic="true" in <application> tag.


    BEST PRACTICE: Always use HTTPS in production. Use Network Security Config to allow cleartext only for specific development domains. Also consider Certificate Pinning for high-security apps.

    Q: What are Annotations? How to create custom Annotation?

    Annotations are metadata attached to code elements (classes, functions, properties, parameters) that can be read at compile time or runtime.


    CATEGORIES:


    1. SOURCE-LEVEL — Read by compiler, discarded after. (@Suppress, @SuppressLint)

    2. CLASS-LEVEL — Stored in .class file but not available at runtime.

    3. RUNTIME — Available via reflection at runtime. (@Retention(RUNTIME))


    COMMON ANDROID ANNOTATIONS:

    @NonNull, @Nullable, @IntDef, @StringDef — null safety & type safety @WorkerThread, @MainThread, @UiThread — thread enforcement @LayoutRes, @DrawableRes, @StringRes — resource type safety @VisibleForTesting — documents that visibility is widened for tests @Keep — prevent ProGuard from removing/obfuscating

    class="cm">// Custom annotation — compile-time validation
class="an">@Target(AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION)
class="an">@Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME)
annotation class RequiresPermission(val permission: String)

class="an">@Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS)
class="an">@Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME)
annotation class Analytics(val screenName: String)

class="cm">// Usage
class="an">@Analytics(screenName = class="st">"HomeScreen")
class HomeActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    class="an">@RequiresPermission(permission = class="st">"android.permission.CAMERA")
    fun openCamera() { class="cm">/* ... */ }
}

class="cm">// Reading annotations at runtime via reflection
fun trackScreen(activity: AppCompatActivity) {
    val annotation = activity::class.java.getAnnotation(Analytics::class.java)
    annotation?.let {
        AnalyticsTracker.logScreenView(it.screenName)
    }
}

    Q: How to show local Notification at an exact time?

    Use AlarmManager for exact-time scheduling + BroadcastReceiver + NotificationManager.


    STEPS:


    1. Schedule alarm with AlarmManager.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() (works in Doze mode for exact timing).


    2. AlarmManager fires PendingIntent → BroadcastReceiver.


    3. BroadcastReceiver creates and shows the Notification.


    IMPORTANT ANDROID 12+ (API 31):

    Must declare SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM permission. Must check canScheduleExactAlarms() before scheduling. <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM" />


    ANDROID 13+ (API 33):

    Must request POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission.


    Alternative: WorkManager with initialDelay for approximate timing. WorkManager is NOT suitable for exact-time notifications because it's subject to batching and Doze delays.

    class NotificationScheduler(private val context: Context) {

    fun scheduleNotification(
        title: String,
        message: String,
        triggerTimeMillis: Long,
        notificationId: Int
    ) {
        val intent = Intent(context, NotificationReceiver::class.java).apply {
            putExtra(class="st">"title", title)
            putExtra(class="st">"message", message)
            putExtra(class="st">"notificationId", notificationId)
        }

        val pendingIntent = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(
            context,
            notificationId,
            intent,
            PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
        )

        val alarmManager = context.getSystemService(Context.ALARM_SERVICE) as AlarmManager

        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.S) {
            if (alarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms()) {
                alarmManager.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(
                    AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, triggerTimeMillis, pendingIntent
                )
            } else {
                class="cm">// Fallback to inexact or guide user to Settings → Alarms & Reminders
                alarmManager.setAndAllowWhileIdle(
                    AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, triggerTimeMillis, pendingIntent
                )
            }
        } else {
            alarmManager.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(
                AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, triggerTimeMillis, pendingIntent
            )
        }
    }
}

class NotificationReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {

    override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
        val title = intent.getStringExtra(class="st">"title") ?: return
        val message = intent.getStringExtra(class="st">"message") ?: return
        val notificationId = intent.getIntExtra(class="st">"notificationId", 0)

        val channelId = class="st">"scheduled_notifications"

        if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.O) {
            val channel = NotificationChannel(
                channelId, class="st">"Scheduled", NotificationManager.IMPORTANCE_HIGH
            )
            val manager = context.getSystemService(NotificationManager::class.java)
            manager.createNotificationChannel(channel)
        }

        val notification = NotificationCompat.Builder(context, channelId)
            .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_notification)
            .setContentTitle(title)
            .setContentText(message)
            .setPriority(NotificationCompat.PRIORITY_HIGH)
            .setAutoCancel(true)
            .build()

        NotificationManagerCompat.from(context).notify(notificationId, notification)
    }
}
